chapters.title: Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Applications
chapters.blurb: The three big non-functional goals every data system is judged by, and the vocabulary for talking about them.

b: Most modern apps are limited by the amount, complexity and speed of change of their data, not by raw CPU.

They’re assembled from standard building blocks: databases (store), caches (speed up reads), search indexes (keyword/filter lookup), stream processing (react to messages async), batch processing (crunch accumulated data periodically).
The categories blur: Redis can act as a message queue; Kafka offers database‑like durability. When you stitch tools together with app code, you have become a data‑system designer.
Functional requirements say what the system does; reliability, scalability and maintainability are non‑functional requirements.
Reliability = keep working correctly even when things go wrong (hardware, software, humans).
A fault is one component deviating from its spec. A failure is the system as a whole no longer delivering the service.
You can’t get faults to zero, so design fault‑tolerant (resilient) systems that stop faults becoming failures.
Deliberately injecting faults (e.g. Netflix’s Chaos Monkey randomly killing processes) keeps the recovery machinery exercised so it works when a real fault arrives.
Exception: security breaches can’t be ‘tolerated’ — prevention beats cure there.
Disks die, RAM goes bad, power fails, someone unplugs the wrong cable.
Disk mean‑time‑to‑failure is roughly 10–50 years, so a 10,000‑disk cluster should expect about one dead disk per day.
Classic answer: redundancy per component — RAID, dual power supplies, hot‑swappable CPUs, batteries and diesel generators.

Shift: with big data volumes and cloud VMs that can vanish without warning, systems increasingly tolerate losing whole machines in software. Bonus: you can do rolling upgrades — patch one node at a time with no downtime.
Hardware faults are mostly independent/random.
Systematic faults: correlated across nodes, so they cause far more failures than random hardware faults.

Examples: a bug triggered by one bad input crashing every instance (the 2012 leap‑second bug in the Linux kernel hung many apps at once); a runaway process eating shared CPU/memory/disk/network; a dependency slowing down or returning corrupt data; cascading failures.
They often lie dormant because the code assumes something about its environment that suddenly stops being true.

No silver bullet. Many small things help: thinking about assumptions and interactions, thorough testing, process isolation, letting processes crash and restart, measuring and monitoring in production, self‑checks (e.g. a queue verifying messages in = messages out).
Humans are unreliable; one study of large internet services found operator configuration errors were the leading cause of outages, with hardware only behind 10–25%.
Design to minimise error opportunities: good abstractions, APIs and admin UIs that make the right thing easy — without being so restrictive people work around them.
Decouple risky places: non‑production sandboxes with real data for experiments.
Test thoroughly at every level, including automated tests for corner cases.
Make recovery fast: quick config rollback, gradual rollout of new code, tools to recompute data.
Detailed, clear monitoring (telemetry) of performance and error rates; plus good management and training.
Not just for nuclear plants: bugs in business apps cost productivity and legal risk; e‑commerce outages cost revenue and reputation.
Even ‘non‑critical’ apps carry responsibility — imagine a parent losing every photo of their kids stored in your app.
Sometimes you may consciously trade reliability for cost (e.g. a prototype), but know you’re doing it.
Scalability = the system’s ability to cope with increased load. It’s not a yes/no label; ask ‘if load grows in way X, what are our options?’
Describe load with load parameters: requests/second, read‑to‑write ratio, simultaneously active users, cache hit rate, etc. — whichever matters for your architecture.
Sometimes the average case is the bottleneck, sometimes a small number of extreme cases is.
Two key operations: post a tweet (~4.6k req/s average, 12k+ at peak) and read the home timeline (~300k req/s).
Approach 1 — read‑time join: insert tweet into one global table; on timeline read, look up everyone you follow and merge their tweets. Cheap writes, expensive reads.

Approach 2 — fan‑out on write: keep a cached timeline ‘mailbox’ per user; when someone tweets, push it into every follower’s cache. Reads become cheap. Works because reads outnumber writes by about two orders of magnitude.
Cost of approach 2: one tweet → ~75 cache writes on average (≈345k writes/s), but a celebrity with 30M+ followers means 30M writes for one tweet.
Final design is a hybrid: fan‑out for most users; celebrities’ tweets are fetched separately at read time and merged.
The key load parameter is the distribution of followers per user (weighted by how often they tweet).
Two ways to ask: increase load with fixed resources — what happens to performance? Or: how much must resources grow to keep performance unchanged?
Batch systems (e.g. Hadoop) care about throughput: records processed per second or total job time.
Online systems care about response time: what the client sees — service time plus network and queueing delays.
Latency (strictly) = how long a request waits to be handled, i.e. latent. Response time ≠ latency, though people mix them.
Response time is a distribution, not a number: context switches, packet loss and TCP retransmits, GC pauses, page faults, a server rack’s vibrations… all add random outliers.
The mean hides how many users actually waited. Use percentiles: sort times; median (p50) = half of requests faster.
High percentiles = tail latencies: p95, p99, p999. p99 = 1.5 s means 1 in 100 requests takes 1.5 s or longer.
Amazon set targets at p99.9 because the slowest requests often belong to its most valuable customers — those with the most data/purchases.
Amazon observed +100 ms response time cut sales by 1%; others report a 1‑second slowdown cutting customer satisfaction by 16%.
Going to p99.99 is usually too costly: those outliers are dominated by random events you can’t control.
SLOs/SLAs are written with percentiles: e.g. median < 200 ms and p99 < 1 s, otherwise the service counts as down.
Head‑of‑line blocking: a few slow requests hold up everything queued behind them, so measure response time on the client side, not only server processing time.
Load‑testing trap: if your test client waits for each response before sending the next, it keeps queues artificially short. Send requests independently of responses.
Tail latency amplification: if one user request fans out to many backend calls in parallel, it’s as slow as the slowest. The more calls, the more likely one hits the tail.
Compute rolling percentiles efficiently with approximations like forward decay, t‑digest or HdrHistogram.
Never average percentiles across machines or time windows — that’s mathematically meaningless. Add histograms instead.
Scaling up (vertical): a bigger machine. Scaling out (horizontal): spread load over many smaller machines = shared‑nothing architecture. Real systems usually mix pragmatically.
Elastic systems add resources automatically when load rises — handy for unpredictable load; manual scaling is simpler and has fewer surprises.
Stateless services are easy to distribute; stateful data systems add a lot of complexity when distributed, so the old wisdom was keep the database on one node until you can’t.
There’s no generic ‘magic scaling sauce’. Architecture follows from assumptions about which operations will be common.
Example: 100,000 req/s of 1 kB each vs 3 req/min of 2 GB each — same data throughput, totally different architectures.
Early‑stage products: iterate on features fast before scaling for hypothetical future load.
Most software cost is ongoing maintenance, not initial build. Three design principles: operability, simplicity, evolvability.

Operability = make life easy for operations teams, who monitor health, find causes of problems, patch, track interactions between systems, plan capacity, set up deployment & config, keep the environment stable, and preserve organisational knowledge.

Data systems help by: giving visibility into runtime behaviour (monitoring), supporting automation, not depending on individual machines (so they can be taken down for maintenance), good documentation, sensible defaults that admins can override, self‑healing with manual control when needed, and predictable behaviour with minimal surprises.
Projects that grow get complex and slow — a ‘big ball of mud’.
Symptoms: state‑space explosion, tight coupling, tangled dependencies, inconsistent naming, performance hacks, special‑casing.
Accidental complexity (Moseley & Marks): complexity that’s not inherent in the problem users see, but arises only from the implementation.

The best tool for removing it is abstraction: a clean façade hiding implementation detail, reusable and improvable in one place. High‑level languages hide machine code; SQL hides on‑disk structures, concurrency and crash recovery.
Requirements never stop changing: new facts, new use cases, business priorities, user requests, new platforms, legal changes, growth forcing architecture changes.
Agile practices (TDD, refactoring) help at small scale; ‘evolvability’ means the same agility at the level of a whole data system.
The easier a system is to understand (simplicity), the easier it is to change — evolvability is tightly linked to good abstractions.

qs.q: What’s the difference between a fault and a failure?
o: A fault is a component deviating from spec; a failure is the whole system no longer providing the service
A fault is a software bug; a failure is a hardware problem
A failure affects one node; a fault affects the cluster
qs.e: Faults are local; failures are system‑wide. The goal of fault tolerance is to stop the former turning into the latter.

qs.q: Why would a company deliberately kill random processes in production?
o: To keep fault‑tolerance machinery continuously exercised and tested
qs.e: Many critical bugs come from poor error handling. Injecting faults on purpose (Chaos Monkey) increases confidence that real faults will be handled.

qs.q: Disks have an MTTF of roughly 10–50 years. In a 10,000‑disk cluster, how often should you expect a disk to die?
qs.e: Large numbers turn rare events into routine ones — roughly one disk per day.

qs.q: Why are software errors often worse than hardware faults?
o: They tend to be correlated across nodes, causing many simultaneous failures
qs.e: Hardware faults are mostly independent. A software bug hits every node running the same code with the same input, e.g. the 2012 leap‑second bug.

qs.q: Which shift made rolling upgrades a natural benefit?
o: Designing systems to tolerate the loss of entire machines in software
qs.e: If the system survives losing a whole machine, you can take nodes down one at a time to patch them without downtime.

qs.q: According to a study of large internet services, what was the leading cause of outages?
qs.e: Human configuration mistakes topped the list; hardware played a role in only about 10–25% of outages.

qs.q: Which is NOT a recommended way to reduce human error?
o: Easy, fast rollback of config changes
Locking interfaces down so tightly that every change needs a workaround
qs.e: Over‑restrictive interfaces push people to work around them. Make the right thing easy instead.

qs.q: What are the three main concerns this book treats as non‑functional requirements?
qs.e: These three are the lens for the whole book.

qs.q: Twitter moved to fan‑out on write mainly because…
o: Writes were far more frequent than reads
Home‑timeline reads outnumber tweet writes by about two orders of magnitude
It removed the need for caches
qs.e: ~300k timeline reads/s vs ~4.6k writes/s: doing work at write time makes the hot path (reads) cheap.

qs.q: What breaks fan‑out on write?
o: Users with tens of millions of followers
qs.e: A single celebrity tweet would mean tens of millions of cache writes. The fix: a hybrid that fetches celebrity tweets at read time.

qs.q: For the Twitter example, which is the key load parameter?
o: Distribution of followers per user (weighted by tweet frequency)
qs.e: It determines the fan‑out write load, which is what decides the architecture.

qs.q: Why prefer percentiles over the arithmetic mean for response times?
o: The mean doesn’t tell you how many users actually experienced a given delay
qs.e: The median tells you what a typical user sees; high percentiles reveal how bad outliers are.

qs.q: Your p99 is 1.5 s. What does that mean?
o: 99 of 100 requests take 1.5 s or longer
1 in 100 requests takes 1.5 s or longer
The slowest request ever was 1.5 s
qs.e: 99% of requests are faster than 1.5 s; the remaining 1% are at least that slow.

qs.q: Why did Amazon target the 99.9th percentile for internal services?
o: The slowest requests often belong to the most valuable customers, who have the most data
qs.e: Customers with long purchase histories cause slower requests — and they’re the ones you least want to annoy.

qs.q: Why not optimise p99.99 too?
o: The cost is usually too high since those outliers are dominated by random events outside your control
qs.e: Diminishing returns: GC pauses, packet loss and similar random events drive the extreme tail.

qs.q: What is head‑of‑line blocking?
o: A cache miss on the first request
A few slow requests holding up the requests queued behind them
The first node in a ring failing
qs.e: Even fast requests look slow when stuck behind slow ones — which is why you measure response time client‑side.

qs.q: A load generator waits for each response before sending the next request. What’s wrong?
o: It keeps queues artificially short, so it underestimates response times
qs.e: Real users don’t wait for each other. The client must send requests independently of responses.

qs.q: One page load calls 10 backend services in parallel. What happens to tail latency?
o: It’s set by the fastest call
The user waits for the slowest call, so more calls means a higher chance of hitting a slow one
qs.e: This is tail latency amplification: a small share of slow backend calls slows a large share of end‑user requests.

qs.q: You have p99 from 5 servers. How do you get the overall p99?
o: Merge the underlying histograms and compute from that
qs.e: Averaging percentiles is mathematically meaningless. Combine the distributions (histograms), then compute.

qs.q: Strictly speaking, ‘latency’ is…
o: The time a request spends waiting to be handled
qs.e: Response time is what the client sees end‑to‑end (service + network + queueing). Latency is the waiting part.

qs.q: Which metric is usually most important for a batch system like Hadoop?
qs.e: Batch jobs care about records per second or total job runtime.

qs.q: Which statement about scaling stateful vs stateless services is right?
o: Both are equally easy to distribute
Stateless services are easy to spread across machines; stateful data systems add much more complexity
Stateful services should always scale out first
qs.e: That’s why the traditional advice was to keep the database on one node (scale up) until scaling out became unavoidable.

qs.q: ‘Shared‑nothing architecture’ refers to…
o: Scaling up on one big machine
Scaling out across many independent machines
qs.e: Each node has its own CPU, RAM and disks; coordination happens over the network.

qs.q: System A: 100,000 req/s of 1 kB each. System B: 3 req/min of 2 GB each. Same data throughput. What follows?
o: They can share the same architecture
qs.e: Scaling architecture is built around assumptions about which operations are common — there is no generic scaling sauce.

qs.q: When is an elastic (auto‑scaling) system most useful?
qs.e: Manually scaled systems are simpler with fewer operational surprises; elasticity pays off with unpredictable load.

qs.q: Accidental complexity is…
o: Complexity not inherent in the problem being solved, arising only from the implementation
qs.e: Term from Moseley & Marks. It’s the kind you can and should remove.

qs.q: What’s the best tool for removing accidental complexity?
qs.e: Good abstractions hide implementation details behind a clean façade — SQL hiding storage, concurrency and recovery is a classic example.

qs.q: Which is NOT something a data system does to support good operability?
o: Provide sensible defaults that can be overridden
Depend on specific individual machines always being up
qs.e: Good systems avoid dependence on individual machines so they can be taken down for maintenance.

qs.q: ‘Evolvability’ is best described as…
o: Agility (like TDD/refactoring) applied at the level of a whole data system
qs.e: Also called extensibility or modifiability; closely tied to simplicity and good abstractions.

qs.q: Which pair shows the line between tool categories blurring?
o: Redis used as a message queue; Kafka offering database‑like durability
qs.e: Modern tools stretch across categories, which is why ‘data system’ is a useful umbrella term.

qs.q: Which of these is a symptom of a ‘big ball of mud’?
qs.e: Others: state‑space explosion, inconsistent terminology, performance hacks and special cases.

qs.q: A message queue checks that messages in equals messages out. Which software‑fault mitigation is this?
o: A self‑check that constantly verifies a guarantee while running
qs.e: Systems that check their own guarantees raise an alarm when assumptions stop holding.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your API’s average latency looks fine, but support tickets say ‘it’s slow’. Your best first move?
o: Look at p95/p99/p999 response times measured from the client side
qs.e: Averages hide the tail. Client‑side percentiles capture queueing and head‑of‑line effects users actually feel.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a new social app has 20 users each followed by millions, and everyone else has ~50 followers. Which timeline design?
o: Fan‑out on write for normal users, read‑time merge for the 20 celebrities
qs.e: Exactly Twitter’s hybrid: avoid giant write amplification for the few, keep reads cheap for the many.

qs.q: Boss scenario: an outage happened after an engineer edited a config in prod. What change best reduces recurrence without slowing everyone down?
o: Gradual rollout plus fast one‑click rollback, tested in a realistic sandbox first
Add a second engineer to watch
qs.e: Design for human error: decouple experiments, roll out gradually, and make recovery quick.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you must report the fleet‑wide p99 for the last hour from per‑minute, per‑server p99s. What do you do?
o: Aggregate per‑minute histograms (e.g. HdrHistogram) and compute p99 from the merged data
qs.e: Percentiles don’t average. Merge distributions, then compute.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a startup with 300 users asks you to design for 100M users on day one. Best advice?
o: Focus on iterating features quickly; design for the load parameters you actually understand
qs.e: Scaling architectures rest on assumptions about load; wrong assumptions waste effort or actively hurt.

qs.q: Boss scenario: every node in your cluster crashed at the same moment after a calendar edge case. Which fault category, and what helps most?
o: Systematic software error; question environmental assumptions, test edge cases, isolate processes and monitor
qs.e: Correlated failures across all nodes are the signature of software errors, like the leap‑second bug.

terms: One component deviating from its spec
The whole system stops providing the required service
Push each new post into every follower’s cached timeline
Response times at high percentiles like p99 or p999
Slow requests delaying the ones queued behind them
Complexity from the implementation, not the problem
Making life easy for the people who run the system
Making it easy to change the system as requirements shift
A number that describes load, e.g. read/write ratio
Contract defining expected performance and availability
Patching one node at a time without downtime

chapters.title: Data Models and Query Languages
chapters.blurb: How you model data shapes what’s easy and what’s painful: relational, document and graph models, and the query languages built around them.

b: Every app stacks data models: real‑world concepts → app objects/APIs → a general model (JSON, tables, graph) → bytes on disk/memory/network → electrical signals.
Each layer hides the complexity of the layer below behind a clean model, so different groups of people can work together.
The choice of model profoundly affects what the software can and can’t do easily.

cards.t: The relational model & the birth of NoSQL
b: Proposed by Edgar Codd in 1970: data organised into relations (tables), each an unordered collection of tuples (rows).
It dominated from the mid‑1980s, originally for business data processing (transactions and batch jobs), and generalised remarkably well.
Earlier competitors (network, hierarchical, object and XML databases) came and went.

NoSQL (a hashtag from ~2009, later read as ‘Not Only SQL’) was driven by: easier scaling to huge datasets or write throughput, preference for free/open source, specialised queries, and frustration with restrictive schemas.
Polyglot persistence: relational and non‑relational stores used side by side.

Most app code is object‑oriented; an awkward translation layer is needed to map objects to tables and rows (the ‘impedance mismatch’). ORMs like ActiveRecord and Hibernate reduce the boilerplate but can’t hide it fully.
Example: a résumé/profile with one user and many positions, schools and contact entries — a one‑to‑many tree.
Relational options: separate tables with foreign keys; structured/JSON/XML columns; or the whole thing as encoded text.
A JSON document fits this tree naturally: one place to look (better locality — one query instead of several joins), and the tree structure is explicit.
Store IDs (region_id) rather than free text (“Greater Seattle Area”): consistent spelling, no ambiguity, easy updates, localisation and better search.
An ID has no meaning to humans, so it never needs to change; meaningful info stored in one place. Removing such duplication is normalization.
Many‑to‑one fits relational databases well (joins), but awkwardly fits document models, where join support is often weak — the app has to emulate joins with extra queries.
Data gets more interconnected as features grow: organisations and schools become entities with their own pages, recommendations link users… pushing toward many‑to‑many.
IBM’s IMS (built for the Apollo programme, 1968) used a hierarchical model — a tree of records, much like JSON. Great for one‑to‑many, bad for many‑to‑many.
The network model (CODASYL) let a record have multiple parents. You navigated by following ‘access paths’ with a cursor, which made queries and schema changes painful.
The relational model laid data out in the open; a query optimizer decides access paths automatically. Add an index and queries use it without being rewritten.
Document databases echo the hierarchical model for nested data, but use document references (like foreign keys) for many‑to‑one — not CODASYL‑style paths.
Document strengths: schema flexibility, locality, a structure closer to app objects for some apps.
Relational strengths: joins and good support for many‑to‑one and many‑to‑many relationships.
If your data is a document‑like tree loaded all at once, use a document model. If it’s highly interconnected, relational or graph.
Deeply nested documents are awkward: you can’t refer directly to a nested item, you need a path.
Document DBs aren’t truly schemaless: the structure is implicit and interpreted when read (schema‑on‑read), like dynamic typing. Relational enforces schema on write, like static typing.
Change example — splitting a full name into first name: document DB handles old docs in app code at read time; relational runs ALTER TABLE plus an UPDATE migration.
ALTER TABLE is usually fast in most DBs; MySQL historically copied the whole table, causing long downtime.
Schema‑on‑read fits heterogeneous data: many object types, or structure decided by external systems you don’t control.
A document is stored as one continuous string (JSON, XML or binary like BSON), so reading the whole thing is efficient.
But the DB loads the full document even if you need a small part, and updates usually rewrite it all, so keep documents small.
Locality isn’t exclusive to document DBs: Google Spanner interleaves child rows within parents; Oracle has multi‑table index clusters; Bigtable‑style stores have column families.
Models are converging: PostgreSQL and MySQL support JSON; RethinkDB supports joins; some MongoDB drivers resolve references. A hybrid is a good path.
Imperative code tells the computer step by step how to compute (loops, conditions). Declarative languages like SQL say what result you want and leave the how to the optimizer.

Benefits: more concise, hides implementation details so the database can improve performance without changing queries, doesn’t guarantee order so the engine is free to reorder, and lends itself to parallel execution.
Web analogy: a CSS selector (declarative) to highlight the selected item vs JavaScript walking the DOM (imperative) — the CSS version keeps working if the page changes.
A model for bulk processing across many machines, somewhere between declarative and imperative.
MongoDB’s version: you supply map and reduce functions as JavaScript snippets; they must be pure (no side effects, no extra queries) so they can run anywhere, in any order, and be re‑run on failure.
Writing two coordinated functions is harder than one query, so MongoDB added a declarative JSON‑based aggregation pipeline — a lesson that NoSQL systems may reinvent SQL in disguise.
When many‑to‑many relationships are everywhere, model data as a graph: vertices (nodes/entities) and edges (relationships/arcs).
Examples: social graphs, the web graph, road and rail networks. Algorithms: shortest path, PageRank.
Graphs can also store very different object types in one store — e.g. people, places, events, check‑ins and comments as one graph.

Property graph (Neo4j, Titan, InfiniteGraph): each vertex has an ID, incoming and outgoing edges, and key‑value properties. Each edge has an ID, a tail vertex, a head vertex, a label for the relationship and properties.
Any vertex can connect to any other — no schema restrictions; you can traverse efficiently in both directions; labels let one graph hold many kinds of relationships. Great for evolvability.
Cypher (Neo4j) is a declarative query language using arrow‑like patterns to match structure, e.g. people born in the US who now live in Europe.
Variable‑length paths (follow ‘within’ edges zero or more times) are trivial in Cypher. The same in SQL needs recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE) — dozens of clumsy lines.
A triple‑store holds everything as (subject, predicate, object), e.g. (Jim, likes, bananas). The object is a primitive value (a property) or another vertex (an edge).
Turtle is a readable notation for triples. RDF is the data model of the semantic web vision; the idea was overhyped, but triples are still useful for apps.
SPARQL is the query language for RDF triple‑stores, more concise than Cypher for similar queries.
Datalog (1980s, academic roots) writes facts as predicate(subject, object) and builds rules step by step. Rules can be combined and reused, which suits complex queries. Used by Datomic and Cascalog.
Other specialised models exist too: genome sequence similarity search (e.g. GenBank) and full‑text search indexes.

qs.q: What was a main driver behind the rise of NoSQL around 2009?
o: The need to scale to very large datasets or very high write throughput, plus frustration with restrictive schemas
qs.e: Others: preference for open source and specialised queries poorly served by relational models.

qs.q: The ‘impedance mismatch’ refers to…
o: Network latency between app and DB
The awkward translation between object‑oriented app code and relational tables
qs.e: ORMs reduce boilerplate but can’t fully hide the difference between the two models.

qs.q: Why does a JSON document fit a résumé profile well?
o: It’s a one‑to‑many tree, so the whole profile lives in one place with good locality
qs.e: One query fetches the whole profile, rather than several queries or a multi‑way join.

qs.q: Why store region_id instead of the text “Greater Seattle Area”?
o: Consistent spelling, easy updates, localisation and better search; an ID never needs to change
qs.e: Meaningful info lives in one place; removing duplication like this is normalization.

qs.q: Which kind of relationship is weakest in typical document databases?
qs.e: Join support is often weak, so the app must emulate joins with multiple queries.

qs.q: What made the CODASYL network model painful to use?
o: You had to navigate access paths manually, so queries and schema changes were hard
It was too slow on SSDs
It only allowed one parent per record
qs.e: The relational model moved access path selection to the query optimizer.

qs.q: In a relational DB, you add an index. What must change in your queries?
o: All queries must name the index
Nothing — the optimizer will use it automatically
qs.e: Declarative queries plus an optimizer decouple what you ask for from how it’s executed.

qs.q: Document databases are more accurately described as…
qs.e: There’s an implicit structure, interpreted when data is read — like dynamic type checking.

qs.q: When is schema‑on‑read especially useful?
o: When all records share one structure
When data is heterogeneous or its structure is set by external systems you don’t control
qs.e: A rigid schema would add overhead without benefit when objects vary widely.

qs.q: What is a downside of document locality?
o: Reading the full document is slow
The DB usually loads and rewrites the whole document even for a small change, so documents should stay small
qs.e: Locality helps when you need most of the document at once; otherwise it’s wasted work.

qs.q: Which is an example of locality in a relational‑style system?
o: Spanner interleaving child rows inside parent rows
qs.e: Oracle multi‑table index clusters and Bigtable column families are similar ideas.

qs.q: Which is NOT an advantage of declarative query languages?
o: The engine can improve performance without query changes
They lend themselves to parallel execution
They require you to specify the exact algorithm
qs.e: That’s imperative code. Declarative languages specify the result, not the algorithm.

qs.q: Why must MapReduce map and reduce functions be pure?
o: So they can run anywhere, in any order, and be safely re‑run on failure
qs.e: No side effects and no extra database queries.

qs.q: Why did MongoDB add the aggregation pipeline?
o: Writing two coordinated functions is harder than one declarative query, and declarative queries can be optimized
qs.e: An example of NoSQL rediscovering the value of declarative querying.

qs.q: In a property graph, what does every edge have?
o: An ID, a tail vertex, a head vertex, a label and properties
qs.e: Vertices have an ID, incoming and outgoing edges and properties.

qs.q: What’s easy in Cypher but clumsy in SQL?
o: Traversing a variable number of edges, like ‘within’ chains of locations
qs.e: SQL needs recursive common table expressions (WITH RECURSIVE) for this.

qs.q: A triple is…
qs.e: The object is either a primitive value or another vertex.

qs.q: What is SPARQL?
o: A query language for RDF triple‑stores
qs.e: It predates Cypher, which borrows its pattern‑matching style.

qs.q: What’s Datalog’s key strength?
o: Rules can be combined and reused, building complex queries step by step
qs.e: Less convenient for one‑off queries, but powerful for complex data.

qs.q: What’s the main problem with the hierarchical (IMS) model?
qs.e: Developers had to duplicate data or manually resolve references — the same problem document DBs face today.

qs.q: Why do graph models help evolvability?
o: Any vertex can connect to any other, and new kinds of edges can be added easily
qs.e: Adapting a graph to new features is easy as data structures change.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you’re building an app that stores self‑contained blog posts with nested comments, always loaded together. What model fits best?
qs.e: A one‑to‑many tree loaded at once benefits from document locality.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a social app’s data is mostly people, places, events and who‑knows‑whom, queried by multi‑hop traversals. What model fits?
qs.e: Highly interconnected many‑to‑many data is the graph model’s home ground.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your document app starts needing ‘show everyone at the same company’ and company pages. What’s happening?
o: Data is becoming many‑to‑one/many‑to‑many, so joins (or a relational/graph model) become important
qs.e: Features tend to make data more interconnected over time.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you must split ‘name’ into ‘first_name’ in a large MySQL table without downtime worries. A teammate suggests a document DB. What is the real trade‑off?
o: Document DBs handle old formats in app code at read time; relational needs a migration (ALTER + UPDATE)
qs.e: Schema‑on‑read moves the burden into application code; schema‑on‑write moves it into migrations.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a front‑end developer highlights the selected menu item by manually walking the DOM in JavaScript. What’s the declarative alternative?
qs.e: The CSS rule keeps working when the page changes; the imperative version is brittle.

terms: Removing duplication by referring to data by ID
Translation friction between objects and tables
Structure is implicit and interpreted when reading
Structure is explicit and enforced when writing
Related data stored together so one read gets it all
Say what result you want, not how to compute it
Vertices and labeled edges, both with properties
Rule‑based query language that builds queries step by step
Several different data stores used side by side
Manual navigation route in the network model

chapters.title: Storage and Retrieval
chapters.blurb: How databases lay data out on disk and find it again: logs, hash indexes, LSM‑trees, B‑trees, and column storage for analytics.

b: Two bash functions: set appends ‘key,value’ to a file; get scans for the last line with that key.
Appending to a log is extremely efficient — many real databases use an append‑only log internally.
But lookups are O(n): every read scans the whole file. That’s why we need indexes.
An index is extra structure derived from the data. It speeds up reads but slows down writes (it must be updated too), so databases don’t index everything by default — you choose.
Keep an in‑memory hash map from each key to the byte offset of its latest value in the data file (Bitcask, Riak’s default engine, does this).
Great when values update often and all keys fit in RAM.
Avoid running out of disk: break the log into segments, then compact them (drop overwritten keys) and merge segments in a background thread.
Details: binary format; deletion via a special tombstone record; snapshot hash maps to disk for faster crash recovery; checksums to detect half‑written records; a single writer thread.
Why append‑only? Sequential writes are much faster, crash recovery and concurrency are simpler, and fragmentation is avoided.
Limits: the hash table must fit in memory, and range queries are inefficient.
Sorted String Table: segment files where key‑value pairs are sorted by key, and each key appears only once per segment.
Merging is simple and efficient, like mergesort, even when files are bigger than memory; when keys repeat across segments, keep the newest.
You don’t need every key in memory: a sparse index (one key every few kilobytes) is enough, then scan from there.
Records between index points can be grouped and compressed into blocks, saving disk space and I/O.
Writes go into an in‑memory balanced tree (memtable, e.g. red‑black or AVL tree). When it passes a threshold (a few MB), write it out as a new SSTable.
Reads check the memtable, then the newest on‑disk segment, then older ones.
Background merging and compaction combine segments and discard old values.
A separate append‑only log on disk protects the memtable from crashes.
Log‑Structured Merge‑Tree is the name; used in LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, HBase; Lucene uses a similar idea for its term dictionary.

Optimisations: Bloom filters to skip lookups for keys that don’t exist; size‑tiered compaction (merge newer, smaller tables into older, bigger ones) vs leveled compaction (key ranges split into levels).
The most widely used index. Breaks the database into fixed‑size pages (traditionally 4 KB) and reads/writes one page at a time, matching the hardware.
Pages refer to child pages, forming a tree; a leaf page holds keys with values or references.
The branching factor (refs per page) is typically several hundred. A four‑level tree of 4 KB pages with branching factor 500 can store up to 256 TB.
Updates overwrite pages in place. Inserting into a full page splits it into two half‑full pages and updates the parent. Depth stays O(log n).
Reliability: a write‑ahead log (redo log) records every change before it’s applied, for crash recovery. Concurrent access needs latches (lightweight locks).
Optimisations: copy‑on‑write pages instead of a WAL (LMDB), abbreviated keys to raise branching, leaf pages laid out in order on disk, sibling pointers between leaves.
Rule of thumb: LSM‑trees are faster for writes; B‑trees are faster for reads.
Write amplification = one write to the DB causing multiple disk writes over its lifetime. B‑trees write every piece at least twice (WAL + page) and whole pages even for small changes.
LSM advantages: often higher write throughput (lower write amplification, sequential writes), better compression and less fragmentation.

LSM downsides: compaction can interfere with ongoing reads/writes, making high‑percentile response times unpredictable; with very high write throughput compaction may fall behind and segments pile up until disk runs out — monitor it.
B‑tree advantage: each key exists in exactly one place, which makes strong transactional semantics (e.g. range locks) easier.
Secondary indexes: keys aren’t unique; store a list of matching rows per key, or make keys unique by appending a row ID.
Values can be the row itself, or a reference into a heap file (avoids duplication; updates are simple if the value stays the same size).
A clustered index stores the row inside the index (e.g. MySQL InnoDB’s primary key). A covering index stores some columns, so certain queries are answered by the index alone.
Concatenated index: several fields in one key, in order (like a phone book by last then first name).
Multi‑dimensional indexes (e.g. R‑trees) handle queries like latitude AND longitude ranges in one go.
Fuzzy indexes for search: Lucene uses a finite state automaton over the term dictionary to find words within an edit distance.
Keep everything in RAM: VoltDB, MemSQL, Oracle TimesTen; Redis and Couchbase offer weaker durability; Memcached is a cache where loss is acceptable.
Durability via special hardware, change logs to disk, periodic snapshots, or replication.
Counter‑intuitively, they’re fast mainly because they avoid the overhead of encoding in‑memory structures into disk formats — not just because they skip disk reads (the OS caches disk blocks anyway).
They can offer data structures hard to build on disk, like Redis’s priority queues and sets.
Anti‑caching: evict least‑recently used data to disk when memory is short and load it back when needed.
OLTP (transaction processing): small numbers of records looked up by key; random‑access, low‑latency writes from user input; current state of data; end users via a web app; GB to TB.
OLAP (analytics): aggregate over huge numbers of records; bulk import (ETL) or event streams; history of events over time; used by analysts for decisions; TB to PB.
Running analytics on the OLTP database hurts its performance, so companies moved analytics to a separate data warehouse.
A warehouse is a read‑only copy of data from many OLTP systems, loaded via Extract‑Transform‑Load (ETL).
Vendors: Teradata, Vertica, SAP HANA, ParAccel/Amazon Redshift; open source SQL‑on‑Hadoop: Hive, Spark SQL, Impala, Presto, Drill.
Star schema (dimensional modeling): a central fact table where each row is an event (e.g. a sale), surrounded by dimension tables (who, what, where, when, how, why) referenced by foreign keys.
Fact tables can be huge and very wide (100+ columns). Snowflake schemas further split dimensions into sub‑dimensions — more normalized, less convenient.
Analytic queries usually touch a few columns out of hundreds, but over billions of rows.
Instead of storing each row together, store all values of each column together (e.g. one file per column). Rows are reassembled by position.
Parquet is a columnar format; this idea also applies to non‑relational data.
Columns compress very well because values repeat: bitmap encoding (one bitmap per distinct value), then run‑length encoding of those bitmaps.
Bitmaps make WHERE … IN and AND/OR filters fast via bitwise operations.
Vectorized processing: tight loops over compressed column chunks that fit in CPU L1 cache, using SIMD instructions.
You can sort the rows (whole rows, across all column files) by chosen columns, e.g. date first then product. The first sort column compresses best (long runs).
Different replicas can be stored in different sort orders, and the query planner picks the best (as in Vertica).
Writes are harder in compressed, sorted column files. Solution: LSM‑style — write to an in‑memory store, then merge into column files in bulk.
Materialized views store precomputed query results; they must be updated when data changes, which makes writes costlier.
A data cube (OLAP cube) is a grid of aggregates by several dimensions: very fast for those queries, but inflexible for others.

qs.q: Why don’t databases index everything by default?
o: Every index slows down writes, so you choose based on your queries
qs.e: Indexes are a deliberate trade‑off between read speed and write cost.

qs.q: In a Bitcask‑style hash index, what’s kept in memory?
o: A map from each key to the byte offset of its latest value
qs.e: One disk seek per read. Downside: all keys must fit in RAM.

qs.q: How are deletes handled in a log‑structured hash store?
o: Append a tombstone record; compaction drops the key later
qs.e: The tombstone tells merging to discard earlier values for that key.

qs.q: What are two limitations of hash indexes?
o: Slow writes and no crash recovery
Keys must fit in memory, and range queries are inefficient
qs.e: That’s what SSTables and LSM‑trees address.

qs.q: What defines an SSTable?
o: Segment sorted by key, each key appearing once per segment
qs.e: Sorting enables efficient merging and a sparse index.

qs.q: Why can an SSTable use a sparse in‑memory index?
o: Because keys are sorted, you can jump to the nearest indexed key and scan
qs.e: One key every few kilobytes is enough.

qs.q: In an LSM‑tree, where does a new write go first?
o: The memtable (in‑memory balanced tree), plus an append‑only log for crash safety
qs.e: When the memtable grows past a threshold, it’s written out as a new SSTable.

qs.q: What does a Bloom filter do in an LSM‑tree?
o: Quickly tells you a key does NOT exist, avoiding many disk reads
qs.e: Lookups for missing keys would otherwise check every segment.

qs.q: A four‑level B‑tree with 4 KB pages and branching factor 500 can store roughly…
qs.e: Branching factor several hundred keeps trees shallow.

qs.q: What happens when you insert into a full B‑tree page?
o: The page splits into two half‑full pages and the parent is updated
The key goes to an overflow log only
qs.e: This keeps the tree balanced with depth O(log n).

qs.q: Why do B‑trees need a write‑ahead log?
o: To recover to a consistent state if the DB crashes mid‑way through overwriting pages
qs.e: Every change is recorded in the WAL before it’s applied to the tree pages.

qs.q: What is write amplification?
o: One write to the DB leading to multiple writes to disk over its lifetime
qs.e: It matters for SSDs (limited write cycles) and write throughput.

qs.q: Which is a known downside of LSM‑trees?
o: Compaction can interfere with ongoing requests, hurting high‑percentile response times
Keys exist in many places so writes are slow
qs.e: And if compaction can’t keep up, unmerged segments grow until disk runs out.

qs.q: Why do B‑trees make transactional semantics easier?
o: Each key exists in exactly one place in the index, so range locks attach directly to the tree
qs.e: In LSM‑trees a key may exist in multiple segments.

qs.q: A clustered index…
o: Stores rows in a separate heap file
Stores the actual row data within the index
qs.e: MySQL InnoDB’s primary key is clustered; secondary indexes point to the primary key.

qs.q: Which index suits ‘restaurants within this latitude AND longitude box’?
o: Multi‑dimensional index such as an R‑tree
qs.e: A concatenated index can only filter efficiently on one range at a time.

qs.q: Why are in‑memory databases fast, according to the book?
o: Mainly because they avoid the overhead of encoding in‑memory data structures for disk
qs.e: The OS caches recently used disk blocks anyway, so disk reads alone don’t explain the speed‑up.

qs.q: Which describes OLAP rather than OLTP?
o: Small lookups by key from users
Aggregations over huge numbers of records, used by analysts
qs.e: OLTP serves end users; OLAP serves analysis and decisions.

qs.q: In a star schema, what’s in the fact table?
o: Individual events (e.g. each sale), with foreign keys to dimension tables
qs.e: Dimensions describe who, what, where, when, how and why.

qs.q: Why is column‑oriented storage good for analytics?
o: Queries read only the few columns they need out of very wide tables
qs.e: It avoids loading hundreds of unused columns from disk.

qs.q: Why do columns compress so well?
o: Values in a column are often repetitive, enabling bitmap and run‑length encoding
qs.e: Especially when the number of distinct values is small compared to the number of rows.

qs.q: In a sorted column store, which column compresses best?
qs.e: Sorting by it creates long runs of identical values.

qs.q: How do column stores usually handle writes?
o: Buffer writes in an in‑memory store (LSM‑style), then merge into column files in bulk
Write each column to a B‑tree
qs.e: In‑place updates in sorted, compressed columns would be very expensive.

qs.q: What’s the trade‑off of a data cube?
o: Very fast for its pre‑aggregated dimensions but inflexible for other queries
qs.e: Warehouses usually keep raw data too, using cubes only as a performance boost.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you track page‑view counters for a moderate number of URLs, updated constantly. What engine design fits best?
o: Bitcask‑style log with in‑memory hash index
qs.e: Many updates per key, keys fit in memory — the hash index’s sweet spot.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you need extremely high write throughput for time‑series sensor data and can tolerate some read variance. B‑tree or LSM?
qs.e: LSM‑trees favour writes with sequential I/O; watch compaction and p99 reads.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your LSM‑based DB’s disk keeps filling up and reads slow down over weeks. What’s likely happening?
o: Compaction can’t keep up with the write rate, so unmerged segments pile up
qs.e: Explicit monitoring of compaction backlog is needed — many engines don’t throttle writes automatically.

qs.q: Boss scenario: analysts run SUM over 3 columns of a 200‑column, billion‑row table and it’s slow in your row store. What fixes it?
o: Move it to a column‑oriented warehouse
qs.e: Column storage reads only the needed columns, compressed, with vectorized processing.

qs.q: Boss scenario: the OLTP database for your shop gets slow whenever the BI team runs reports. Best structural fix?
o: ETL the data into a separate data warehouse optimized for analytics
qs.e: Separate access patterns get separate systems.

terms: Segment file sorted by key, each key once
In‑memory balanced tree buffering LSM writes
Dropping overwritten keys from log segments
Special record marking a key as deleted
Quickly says a key definitely isn’t present
Changes recorded before being applied, for recovery
Number of child references per B‑tree page
One logical write causing many disk writes
Index that stores the full row itself
Index storing enough columns to answer some queries
Central table of events in a star schema
One bit‑vector per distinct column value
Precomputed grid of aggregates by dimension

chapters.title: Encoding and Evolution
chapters.blurb: How data is turned into bytes, and how to change formats over time while old and new code run side by side.

b: Apps change, so data formats change. With rolling upgrades (servers) and users who don’t update (clients), old and new code and data coexist.
Backward compatibility: newer code can read data written by older code (usually easy — you know the old format).
Forward compatibility: older code can read data written by newer code (harder — old code must ignore additions it doesn’t understand).

In memory: objects, lists, hash tables with pointers. On disk/network: a self‑contained byte sequence. Translating is encoding (serialization, marshalling); the reverse is decoding (parsing, deserialization, unmarshalling).
Built‑ins like Java’s java.io.Serializable, Ruby Marshal or Python pickle are tempting but problematic:

They tie you to one language; decoding can instantiate arbitrary classes (a security hole allowing remote code execution); versioning is often an afterthought; and performance can be poor (Java’s is notoriously bloated).
Generally a bad idea except for very transient purposes.
Widely supported, human‑readable, good for data interchange between organisations — but with subtle problems.

Numbers are ambiguous: XML/CSV can’t tell numbers from digit strings; JSON doesn’t distinguish integers from floats or specify precision. Integers above 2^53 lose precision in JavaScript doubles — Twitter returns tweet IDs twice, as a number and as a string.
No binary strings: people Base64‑encode binary, increasing size by about 33%.
Schemas exist (JSON Schema, XML Schema) but are optional and complex; CSV has no schema and vague escaping rules.
Binary JSON variants (MessagePack, BSON, BJSON…) save some space but keep field names in the data, so savings are small (an 81‑byte JSON record became 66 bytes in MessagePack).
Binary encoding libraries (Thrift from Facebook, Protobuf from Google) requiring a schema written in an interface definition language (IDL), with code generation for many languages.
Instead of field names, the encoding uses field tags (numbers like 1, 2, 3) — much more compact.
Same example record: Thrift BinaryProtocol 59 bytes; Thrift CompactProtocol 34 bytes (packs field type and tag together, variable‑length integers); Protocol Buffers 33 bytes.
‘required’ vs ‘optional’ makes no difference to the encoding — required just enables a runtime check.
Field tags are the key: you can rename fields freely but must never change a tag number.
Adding a field: give it a new tag. Old code skips unknown tags (forward compatible). For backward compatibility, new fields must be optional or have a default.
Removing a field: only optional fields, and never reuse its tag number.
Changing datatypes is risky: e.g. 32‑bit to 64‑bit — new code reading old data is fine, but old code reading new data truncates the value.
Protobuf has a ‘repeated’ marker, so an optional single field can safely become repeated. Thrift has a dedicated list type that supports nested lists.
Started in 2009 as a Hadoop subproject. Schema in Avro IDL or JSON. No tag numbers and no type info in the data — just values concatenated. The example record: 32 bytes, the smallest.
To decode, you need the exact schema the writer used (writer’s schema). The reader may expect a different schema (reader’s schema). Avro resolves them side by side, matching fields by name.
Fields in the writer but not the reader are ignored; fields the reader expects but the writer lacks take the reader’s default.
So you may only add or remove fields that have default values. To allow null, use a union type (e.g. union { null, long }) — null can be the default only if it’s in the union.
Changing types is possible if Avro can convert; renaming uses aliases in the reader’s schema (backward compatible, not forward).

cards.t: How does the reader get the writer’s schema?
b: Large file with many records (Avro object container files): include the writer’s schema once at the start of the file.
Database with individually written records: store a schema version number with each record and keep a list of schema versions.
Network connection: negotiate the schema version at connection setup (Avro RPC).
Big win: dynamically generated schemas. Dump a relational DB by generating an Avro schema from table columns; if the DB schema changes, just regenerate — no manual tag numbers.
Code generation is optional — nice for dynamically typed languages and data exploration (e.g. Apache Pig).
Binary formats with schemas are much more compact because they omit field names.
The schema is valuable documentation that can’t drift out of date, since it’s required for decoding.
Keeping a database of schemas lets you check backward and forward compatibility before deploying.
In statically typed languages, generated code enables compile‑time type checking.
Schema evolution gives the same flexibility as schemaless JSON, with better guarantees and tooling.
Writing to a DB is like sending a message to your future self. Backward compatibility is clearly needed.
Forward compatibility too: during a rolling upgrade, a newer version may write a value that an older version later reads.
Trap: old code reads a record containing a new field, decodes it into a model object that drops unknown fields, then writes it back — the new field is lost. Preserve unknown fields.

Data outlives code: five‑year‑old data sits in the old encoding unless migrated. Rewriting everything is expensive, so most DBs allow schema changes like adding a column with null default, filling it in at read time.
Archival snapshots/dumps are usually encoded consistently in the latest schema, e.g. as Avro container files or Parquet.
Clients and servers; a service exposes an application‑specific API. Microservices/service‑oriented architecture aim for teams to deploy independently, so old and new versions must coexist.
REST: a design philosophy built on HTTP principles — simple formats, URLs for resources, HTTP features for caching, auth and content types. OpenAPI/Swagger can describe REST APIs.
SOAP: an XML protocol with a complex set of standards (WS‑*), described with WSDL; heavy reliance on tooling; fell out of favour outside large enterprises.
RPC tries to make a network request look like a local function call (location transparency). That abstraction is fundamentally flawed.

cards.t: Why RPC isn’t a local call
b: A local call is predictable; a network request may be lost or the remote machine slow or unavailable — beyond your control.
A request may time out with no result, and you don’t know whether it was processed.
Retrying might execute the action twice unless you build deduplication (idempotence).
Latency varies wildly.
You can’t pass references/pointers; everything must be encoded into bytes — painful for large objects.
Client and service may be in different languages, so types must be translated (e.g. JavaScript’s numbers above 2^53).
Modern frameworks (gRPC on Protobuf, Finagle on Thrift, Rest.li on JSON) are explicit about remoteness, using futures/promises and streams.

Compatibility: assume servers update before clients, so requests need backward compatibility and responses forward compatibility. Public APIs often run several versions side by side (version in URL or Accept header).
Asynchronous messages go through a message broker (message queue), which stores them temporarily.

Advantages over RPC: buffers when the recipient is overloaded or unavailable; redelivers to a crashed process to avoid loss; the sender needn’t know the recipient’s address (useful in the cloud); one message can go to many recipients; sender and recipient are decoupled.
It’s usually one‑way: the sender doesn’t wait for a response.
Brokers: RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, NATS, Apache Kafka. Producers send to a named queue/topic; consumers subscribe.

Distributed actor frameworks (Akka, Orleans, Erlang OTP): actors communicate by async messages, location transparency works better since messages may be lost anyway. Rolling upgrades still need forward and backward compatible message encodings.

qs.q: Backward compatibility means…
o: Old code can read new data
New code can read data written by old code
qs.e: Usually the easier direction: the new code knows about the old format.

qs.q: Forward compatibility means…
o: New code can read old data
Old code can read data written by newer code
You can roll forward a migration
qs.e: It requires old code to ignore additions it doesn’t understand.

qs.q: What’s a serious security risk of language‑built‑in serialization like Java Serializable?
o: Decoding can instantiate arbitrary classes, enabling remote code execution
qs.e: Plus language lock‑in, poor versioning and poor efficiency.

qs.q: Why does Twitter return tweet IDs both as a number and a string in JSON?
o: IDs above 2^53 lose precision in JavaScript’s double‑precision numbers
qs.e: JSON doesn’t specify integer vs float precision.

qs.q: Base64‑encoding binary data in JSON increases its size by about…
qs.e: A hack forced by JSON/XML lacking binary strings.

qs.q: Why do binary JSON variants like MessagePack save so little space?
o: They still include field names in the encoded data
qs.e: 81 bytes → 66 bytes in the book’s example — modest at best.

qs.q: What replaces field names in Thrift and Protobuf encodings?
qs.e: Tags are compact aliases for fields defined in the IDL.

qs.q: Which encoding produced the smallest result in the book’s example?
qs.e: Avro (32 bytes) < Protobuf (33) < Thrift Compact (34) < Thrift Binary (59) < MessagePack (66) < JSON (81).

qs.q: In Thrift/Protobuf, what can you NEVER change?
o: The order fields appear in the IDL file
qs.e: Changing the tag would make all existing data invalid.

qs.q: Why must newly added fields be optional or have a default (in tag‑based formats)?
o: For backward compatibility — new code reading old data wouldn’t find them
qs.e: Old data won’t contain the new field, so a required check would fail.

qs.q: What happens if old code reads a 64‑bit value where it expects 32 bits?
qs.e: Changing datatypes risks precision loss or truncation.

qs.q: How does Avro match writer’s and reader’s schemas?
o: It doesn’t; they must be identical
qs.e: Fields only in the writer are ignored; fields only in the reader get defaults.

qs.q: In Avro, which fields can you add or remove while keeping full compatibility?
o: Only fields with a default value
qs.e: The default fills the gap whichever side lacks the field.

qs.q: How does Avro allow a field to be null?
o: Use a union type including null
qs.e: Avro has no optional/required markers; unions and defaults do that job.

qs.q: What’s a big advantage of Avro for dumping a relational database?
o: Schemas can be generated dynamically from table columns, with no manual tag management
qs.e: Regenerate the schema whenever the DB schema changes.

qs.q: How might a database of Avro records know which writer’s schema to use?
o: Store a schema version number with each record
qs.e: Files use a header; network connections negotiate at setup.

qs.q: Which is NOT a merit of schemas?
o: Allowing data to be read without any schema at all
qs.e: Schema‑based binary data needs the schema to decode.

qs.q: Old code reads a record with a new field, then writes it back. What’s the risk?
o: The new field gets silently dropped
qs.e: Code should preserve unknown fields when round‑tripping records.

qs.q: Why is ‘data outlives code’ important?
o: Code is stored in the DB
Old data in old encodings remains long after code is redeployed
qs.e: Migrations are expensive, so DBs tolerate several encodings at once.

qs.q: What’s fundamentally wrong with making RPC look like a local function call?
o: Network requests can be lost, time out with unknown outcome, have variable latency and can’t pass pointers
qs.e: Location transparency hides failure modes you must handle.

qs.q: Why does retrying a timed‑out RPC need care?
o: The original request may have succeeded, so retrying can execute it twice unless it’s idempotent
qs.e: Build deduplication/idempotence into the protocol.

qs.q: For RPC compatibility, what’s the usual assumption?
o: Servers update first, so requests need backward compatibility and responses forward compatibility
qs.e: Clients may not upgrade for a long time, especially across organisations.

qs.q: Which is NOT an advantage of a message broker over direct RPC?
o: Buffering when the recipient is down
The sender gets a synchronous response immediately
qs.e: Messaging is usually one‑way and asynchronous.

qs.q: Why does location transparency work better in the actor model than in RPC?
o: The actor model already assumes messages may be lost, even within a process
qs.e: There’s less mismatch between local and remote communication.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your mobile app’s v1 clients will read data produced by your v3 server for months. Which property must your encoding preserve?
o: Forward compatibility, so old clients ignore new fields
qs.e: Old readers, new writers → forward compatibility.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a teammate wants to remove a Protobuf field and reuse its tag number for a new field. What do you say?
o: Never reuse a removed tag — old data with that tag would be misinterpreted
qs.e: Reserve old tags permanently.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you’re exporting a 500‑table relational DB to Hadoop daily, and tables change schema often. Best format?
o: Avro with schemas generated from the DB
qs.e: Avro’s lack of tags makes dynamically generated schemas easy.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a payment RPC times out. The client retries automatically and the customer is charged twice. What’s missing?
o: Idempotence: a unique request ID so the server deduplicates retries
qs.e: A timeout says nothing about whether the request was processed.

qs.q: Boss scenario: an order service must keep working even when the email service is down for an hour. Which dataflow?
qs.e: The broker buffers messages and delivers them when the recipient recovers.

terms: New code reads data written by old code
Old code reads data written by new code
Number identifying a field in Thrift/Protobuf
The schema used when the data was encoded
The schema the decoding app expects
Interface definition language for a schema
Deploying new code to a few nodes at a time
Remote call made to look like a local function
Repeating an operation has the same effect as once
Intermediary that stores and forwards messages
Concurrency via isolated actors exchanging messages
Text encoding of binary that adds about 33%

chapters.title: Replication
chapters.blurb: Keeping copies of the same data on several machines: leaders and followers, replication lag, multi‑leader and leaderless designs, and their conflicts.

b: Keep data geographically close to users (lower latency).
Keep working when some parts fail (higher availability).
Scale out the number of machines serving reads (higher read throughput).
Copying data once is easy; all the difficulty is in handling changes to replicated data.
Three popular approaches: single‑leader, multi‑leader and leaderless.
One replica is the leader (master/primary): all writes go to it. It sends changes to followers (read replicas/slaves/secondaries) as a replication log or change stream.
Clients can read from the leader or any follower; followers apply writes in the same order as the leader.
Built into PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle Data Guard, SQL Server AlwaysOn, MongoDB, RethinkDB, Espresso; also Kafka and RabbitMQ’s highly available queues.
Synchronous: the leader waits for the follower to confirm before reporting success. The follower is guaranteed up to date, but if it doesn’t respond, writes block.
So making all followers synchronous is impractical. Semi‑synchronous: one follower is synchronous, the rest async; if the sync one slows down, an async one is promoted.
Fully asynchronous is common: the leader keeps processing writes even if followers fall behind, but if the leader fails, unreplicated writes are lost — the durability guarantee is weakened.
Chain replication is a variant aiming at good performance without data loss.

New follower: take a consistent snapshot of the leader (ideally without locks), copy it, then request all changes since the snapshot’s exact position in the log (PostgreSQL: log sequence number; MySQL: binlog coordinates), then catch up.
Follower failure: catch‑up recovery — it knows the last transaction processed from its own log and requests what it missed.

Leader failure → failover: (1) detect failure, usually via timeout; (2) choose a new leader, ideally the most up‑to‑date replica, by election or by an appointed controller; (3) reconfigure clients and ensure the old leader becomes a follower when it returns.
With async replication, the new leader may miss writes from the old one. If the old leader comes back, those writes conflict and are usually just discarded — violating durability.

Discarding writes is dangerous if other systems depend on the data. A GitHub incident: an out‑of‑date MySQL follower was promoted and reused auto‑increment primary keys that were also used in Redis, so some private data was disclosed to the wrong users.

Split brain: two nodes both believe they’re leader and accept writes, risking corruption. Systems may shut one down (STONITH — shoot the other node in the head), but a careless mechanism can shut down both.
Choosing the timeout: too long means slow recovery; too short means unnecessary failovers, e.g. during a load spike, making things worse.
Because of these problems, some ops teams prefer manual failover.

Statement‑based: send each INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE. Breaks with nondeterministic functions (NOW(), RAND()), auto‑increment columns or statements depending on existing data (must run in exactly the same order), and side effects (triggers, stored procedures). MySQL used this before 5.1.

Write‑ahead log shipping: send the storage engine’s own WAL. Very low level (which bytes changed in which disk blocks), so replication is tightly coupled to the storage engine — often you can’t run different versions on leader and followers, preventing zero‑downtime upgrades.

Logical (row‑based) log: a separate format describing writes at row granularity. Decoupled from storage internals, so it’s easier to keep backward compatible and for external systems to parse (change data capture). MySQL’s binlog in row mode.
Trigger‑based: application code runs on change and logs it to a separate table read by an external process (Oracle GoldenGate, Databus, Bucardo). Flexible but more overhead and bugs.
Read‑scaling with async followers means reads may be stale. If you stop writing, followers eventually catch up — eventual consistency.
Lag is usually a fraction of a second, but under load or network trouble it can be seconds or minutes.
Three anomalies and the guarantees that fix them follow.

Read‑your‑writes (read‑after‑write) consistency: users always see their own updates. Techniques: read things the user might have modified from the leader (e.g. own profile); read from the leader for a minute after an update; track the timestamp of the user’s last write and use a replica at least that fresh. Cross‑device users need this centralised.

Monotonic reads: a user doesn’t see time go backward (seeing a comment, then refreshing and it’s gone because a staler replica answered). Fix: each user always reads from the same replica, e.g. chosen by hashing user ID.

Consistent prefix reads: if writes happen in a certain order, anyone reading sees them in that order. Violations look like an answer appearing before its question — a problem with partitioned databases. Fix: write causally related data to the same partition, or track causal dependencies.
Pretending replication is synchronous when it isn’t causes problems; transactions exist to give stronger guarantees.
More than one node accepts writes; each leader is also a follower of the others.

Use cases: multi‑datacenter operation (one leader per DC: better local performance, tolerance of DC outages and network problems); clients with offline operation (a calendar app on each device is effectively a leader with its own local DB, e.g. CouchDB); collaborative editing (Google Docs‑style).
Huge downside: the same data may be modified concurrently in two places, so write conflicts must be resolved.
Often retrofitted (MySQL Tungsten, PostgreSQL BDR, Oracle GoldenGate) and has subtle pitfalls with auto‑increment keys, triggers and integrity constraints — considered dangerous territory.
Avoid conflicts: route all writes for a given record through the same leader (e.g. a user’s home datacenter). The simplest and most recommended strategy.

Converge: every replica must reach the same final value. Options: give each write a unique ID and pick the highest (last write wins — LWW, prone to data loss); give replicas IDs and let a higher ID win (also loses data); merge values (e.g. alphabetical concatenation); record the conflict and let app code or the user resolve it later.
Custom resolution: on write (handler runs when a conflict is detected, e.g. Bucardo) or on read (all versions stored and returned to the app, e.g. CouchDB).

Automatic resolution research: CRDTs (conflict‑free replicated datatypes), mergeable persistent data structures (Git‑style three‑way merge), operational transformation (behind Etherpad and Google Docs).
Circular: each node forwards writes to the next. Star: one root forwards to all others. All‑to‑all: every leader sends to every other.
Circular and star: a single node failure can interrupt replication flow; nodes tag writes with IDs they’ve passed through to avoid infinite loops.
All‑to‑all is more fault tolerant, but some links may be faster than others, so messages can arrive out of order (e.g. an update arrives before the insert it depends on).
Timestamps alone don’t fix ordering; version vectors can.
Any replica accepts writes directly from clients (or a coordinator that doesn’t enforce ordering). Popularised by Amazon’s Dynamo; used by Riak, Cassandra, Voldemort (‘Dynamo‑style’).
Writes go to several replicas in parallel; reads also query several and use version numbers to pick the newest. No failover needed.
Catching up stale replicas: read repair (fix stale values seen during reads — good for frequently read data) and an anti‑entropy background process (copies missing data, no ordering, may be slow).
Quorum: with n replicas, a write must be confirmed by w nodes and a read must query r nodes. If w + r > n, at least one read node has the latest value. Common: n odd (3 or 5), w = r = (n + 1) / 2.
Smaller w and r give lower latency and higher availability but more stale reads.

Even with w + r > n, stale values can be returned: with a sloppy quorum; with concurrent writes (unclear order; LWW may lose writes); a read concurrent with a write; a write that succeeded on fewer than w nodes isn’t rolled back on the others; a node holding a new value fails and is restored from an old one.
So Dynamo‑style DBs are optimised for eventual consistency; quorums are not absolute guarantees. Monitoring staleness is harder than in leader‑based systems.

Sloppy quorum: during a network interruption, accept writes on reachable nodes that aren’t among the n ‘home’ nodes; when the network heals, they’re sent home — hinted handoff. Improves write availability, but a read with r nodes may not see the latest value.
Multi‑datacenter: Cassandra and Voldemort count n across all DCs, but wait only for a quorum within the local one.

Last write wins (LWW): attach a timestamp, keep the ‘biggest’. Achieves convergence but silently discards concurrent writes (only Cassandra’s supported conflict resolution). Safe only if keys are written once and never updated, e.g. a UUID per write.
Happens‑before: B depends on A if B knows about A. Two operations are concurrent if neither knows about the other — exact time doesn’t matter.

Version numbers per key: the server increments a version on each write and returns all values the client hasn’t seen; the client must send the last version it read, and merge values (siblings) before writing back.
Merging siblings: union for adds; deletions need a tombstone marker. CRDTs in Riak do this automatically.
With multiple replicas, use a version number per replica per key: the collection is a version vector (Riak uses dotted version vectors).

qs.q: Which is NOT a reason to replicate data?
o: Lower latency by being close to users
Higher write throughput on a single key without conflicts
qs.e: Replication helps reads, latency and availability; write scaling is mostly partitioning’s job.

qs.q: In single‑leader replication, where do writes go?
qs.e: Followers apply the leader’s replication log in the same order.

qs.q: What’s the main downside of fully synchronous replication to all followers?
o: Any one slow or failed follower blocks all writes
qs.e: That’s why semi‑synchronous (one sync follower) is common.

qs.q: What does fully asynchronous replication weaken?
o: Durability — writes acknowledged by the leader can be lost if it fails
qs.e: The leader keeps working even if all followers lag, at the cost of possible loss.

qs.q: How does a new follower get set up without downtime?
o: Take a consistent snapshot, copy it, then replay changes since the snapshot’s log position
qs.e: The log position is the LSN in PostgreSQL or binlog coordinates in MySQL.

qs.q: What happened in the GitHub failover incident?
o: An out‑of‑date follower was promoted and reused primary keys also used in Redis, exposing private data to wrong users
qs.e: Discarding writes is dangerous when other systems depend on the data.

qs.q: What is split brain?
o: Two partitions with the same key
Two nodes both believing they’re leader and accepting writes
A network partition with no leader
qs.e: Without a resolution mechanism, data can be lost or corrupted.

qs.q: Why does statement‑based replication break with NOW() or RAND()?
o: They’re nondeterministic and produce different values on each replica
qs.e: Leaders can substitute fixed return values, but edge cases abound.

qs.q: Why is WAL shipping a problem for zero‑downtime upgrades?
o: It’s tightly coupled to the storage engine’s byte‑level format, so leader and follower versions often must match
qs.e: Logical (row‑based) logs decouple replication from storage internals.

qs.q: What’s a key benefit of logical (row‑based) replication logs?
o: Decoupled from the storage engine, easier to keep compatible and for external systems to parse (change data capture)
qs.e: MySQL’s binlog in row‑based mode is an example.

qs.q: A user updates their profile then sees the old version. Which guarantee is missing?
qs.e: Fix: read the user’s own profile from the leader, or use a replica at least as fresh as their last write.

qs.q: A comment appears, then disappears on refresh. Which guarantee is missing?
qs.e: Fix: route each user to the same replica, e.g. by hashing user ID.

qs.q: An observer sees an answer before the question it responds to. Which guarantee is missing?
qs.e: Common with partitioned DBs where partitions progress independently.

qs.q: Which is a typical use case for multi‑leader replication?
o: Multiple datacenters, offline‑capable clients and collaborative editing
qs.e: Each device or datacenter acts as a leader.

qs.q: The simplest, most recommended way to deal with multi‑leader write conflicts is…
o: Avoid them: route all writes for a record through the same leader
qs.e: E.g. each user has a home datacenter for their writes.

qs.q: What’s the problem with last write wins (LWW)?
qs.e: It’s only safe when keys are written once and never updated.

qs.q: Which technique underlies Google Docs‑style collaborative editing?
qs.e: CRDTs and mergeable persistent data structures are related approaches.

qs.q: In an all‑to‑all multi‑leader topology, what can go wrong?
o: A single node failure stops everything
Messages can arrive out of order, e.g. an update before its insert
qs.e: Version vectors help order these correctly.

qs.q: With n=3, w=2, r=2, why are reads expected to be up to date?
o: Because w + r > n, so read and write sets overlap in at least one node
qs.e: The overlap guarantees at least one read node has the latest write — in theory.

qs.q: Read repair works best for…
qs.e: Rarely read values rely on anti‑entropy, which may be slow.

qs.q: What is hinted handoff?
o: Writes accepted by non‑home nodes during an outage are later sent to the right home nodes
qs.e: Part of sloppy quorums — improves write availability but weakens read guarantees.

qs.q: Two operations are concurrent when…
o: They happen at the same millisecond
Neither knows about (or depends on) the other
qs.e: Physical time doesn’t matter; causal knowledge does.

qs.q: What is a version vector?
o: The collection of version numbers from all replicas for a key
qs.e: It lets replicas tell overwrites from concurrent writes. Riak uses dotted version vectors.

qs.q: Why do deletes need tombstones when merging siblings?
o: A plain removal would reappear when merged with a sibling that still has the item
qs.e: A tombstone marks that the item was removed.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your async leader dies. The newest follower is promoted, then the old leader comes back with writes the new leader never saw. Default outcome?
qs.e: Which is why async failover can violate durability — and why other systems must not depend on those IDs.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a global calendar app must let each office edit offline and sync later. Which replication style fits?
o: Multi‑leader (each device/DC a leader) with conflict resolution
qs.e: Offline clients are effectively leaders; conflicts must be designed for.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a shopping cart in a Dynamo‑style store loses an item after two concurrent adds from different tabs. What’s the likely cause and fix?
o: LWW discarded a concurrent write; track versions and merge siblings (union)
qs.e: Detect concurrency with version vectors and merge — or use a CRDT.

qs.q: Boss scenario: users complain that after posting a reply, it vanishes on refresh then returns. You use random read replicas. Cheapest fix?
o: Pin each user to the same replica (monotonic reads) and read own writes from the leader briefly
qs.e: Targeted session guarantees fix this without global synchronous replication.

qs.q: Boss scenario: during a network blip your Cassandra cluster keeps accepting writes but reads with r=2 sometimes miss them. Why?
o: Sloppy quorum: writes landed on non‑home nodes, which the read didn’t contact; hinted handoff fixes it later
qs.e: Sloppy quorums trade read guarantees for write availability.
