Two nodes both acting as leader
Delay before a follower reflects a write
Users always see their own updates
A user never sees time go backward
Writes are seen in the order they happened
w + r > n so reads overlap writes
Fixing stale replicas found during reads
Returning temporarily stored writes to home nodes
Keep the value with the biggest timestamp
Per‑replica version numbers for a key
Data type that merges concurrent edits automatically

chapters.title: Partitioning
chapters.blurb: Splitting a large dataset across machines: how to divide keys, avoid hot spots, index secondary attributes, rebalance and route requests.

b: Each record belongs to exactly one partition (called a shard in MongoDB/Elasticsearch, region in HBase, tablet in Bigtable, vnode in Cassandra/Riak, vBucket in Couchbase).
Main reason: scalability — spread data and query load across many disks and processors.
Usually combined with replication: each partition has copies on several nodes; one node may lead some partitions and follow others.
Goal: spread data and load evenly. Unfair distribution is skew; a partition with disproportionately high load is a hot spot.
Assign each partition a continuous range of keys, like volumes of an encyclopedia. Boundaries adapt to the data, chosen manually or automatically.
Keys within a partition can be kept sorted, so range scans are efficient.
Used by Bigtable, HBase, RethinkDB and MongoDB before 2.4.
Risk: certain access patterns create hot spots. If the key is a timestamp, all of today’s writes hit one partition.
Fix: prefix the key with something else, e.g. sensor name then timestamp — load spreads, but a time range across all sensors needs one query per sensor.
A good hash function makes skewed data uniformly distributed. Cassandra and MongoDB use MD5; Voldemort uses Fowler–Noll–Vo.
It needn’t be cryptographically strong, but must be consistent: Java’s Object.hashCode and Ruby’s Object#hash can differ across processes.
Each partition gets a range of hashes. You lose efficient range queries — adjacent keys are scattered.

Cassandra’s compromise: a compound primary key where only the first part is hashed, and the other columns are sorted inside the partition, e.g. (user_id, update_timestamp) gives all of one user’s updates in time order.
‘Consistent hashing’ originally meant a specific technique for CDN caches; the term is confusing for databases — just say hash partitioning.
Hashing can’t help if everyone reads and writes the same key — a celebrity on social media causing a storm of activity.
Most systems don’t compensate automatically, so the app must. Trick: append a random two‑digit number to the hot key, splitting writes across 100 keys and partitions.
Cost: reads must fetch all 100 keys and combine them, and you need bookkeeping to know which keys were split. Only worth it for the few hot keys.
Secondary indexes don’t map neatly to partitions. Two approaches.
Document‑based (local index): each partition keeps its own index covering only its documents. Writes only touch one partition.
Reads must query all partitions and combine results — scatter/gather — which is expensive and prone to tail latency amplification.
Widely used: MongoDB, Riak, Cassandra, Elasticsearch, SolrCloud, VoltDB. Vendors suggest structuring partitioning so secondary queries can hit one partition where possible.
Global index covering data in all partitions, itself partitioned — but differently from the primary key, e.g. colours a–r on one partition, s–z on another. The term determines the partition.
Partitioning by the term itself allows range scans; by a hash of the term gives more even load.
Reads are efficient: one partition holds all matches for a term.
Writes are slower and more complex: one document write may update several index partitions, requiring a distributed transaction to keep the index instantly in sync.
In practice updates are often asynchronous, e.g. DynamoDB’s global secondary indexes usually update within a fraction of a second.
Rebalancing = moving load between nodes as data grows, query throughput rises or machines fail.
Requirements: load shared fairly afterwards; the DB keeps serving reads and writes during it; move no more data than necessary.
Don’t use hash mod N: when the number of nodes N changes, most keys must move — very expensive.

Fixed number of partitions: create many more partitions than nodes (e.g. 1,000 for 10 nodes). A new node steals a few partitions from each existing node; only whole partitions move. Used by Riak, Elasticsearch, Couchbase and Voldemort. Choosing the count is hard: too big wastes overhead, too small makes rebalancing and recovery expensive.

Dynamic partitioning: split a partition when it grows beyond a size (HBase default: 10 GB) and merge when it shrinks. The number adapts to data volume. An empty DB starts with one partition, so pre‑splitting helps. Used by HBase, RethinkDB; MongoDB supports both key‑range and hash.
Partitioning proportionally to nodes: a fixed number of partitions per node (Cassandra: 256 by default). New nodes split random existing partitions and take half. Requires hash partitioning.
Fully automatic rebalancing is convenient but unpredictable: it’s expensive (moves lots of data), and combined with automatic failure detection it can be dangerous.
Example: an overloaded node responds slowly; others decide it’s dead and rebalance away from it, adding load to it and the network — possibly a cascading failure.
Having a human in the loop to approve rebalancing is slower but can prevent operational surprises (Couchbase, Riak and Voldemort suggest assignments that an admin commits).
A form of service discovery: how does a client know which node holds key X — especially as partitions move?
Option 1: clients contact any node (e.g. via round‑robin load balancer); it handles the request or forwards it.
Option 2: a partition‑aware routing tier forwards requests.
Option 3: clients themselves know the partition assignment and connect directly.

Many systems use a coordination service like ZooKeeper to track the authoritative mapping; routing tiers subscribe to changes (Espresso uses Helix; HBase, SolrCloud and Kafka use ZooKeeper; MongoDB uses its config servers and mongos routers).
Cassandra and Riak use a gossip protocol among nodes instead, avoiding an external coordination service.
DNS is usually enough to find node IP addresses, which change slowly.
Massively parallel processing (MPP) analytic DBs split complex queries into stages and partitions to run in parallel.

qs.q: What’s the main reason for partitioning?
o: Scalability — spreading data and query load across many machines
qs.e: Replication handles redundancy; partitioning handles scale.

qs.q: What is a hot spot?
o: A partition with disproportionately high load
qs.e: Skew makes partitioning less effective; in the extreme, all load lands on one partition.

qs.q: Key‑range partitioning by timestamp often leads to…
o: All current writes landing on one partition (hot spot)
qs.e: Prefix the key, e.g. with sensor name, to spread writes.

qs.q: What’s the main advantage of key‑range partitioning?
o: Efficient range scans, since keys are sorted within ranges
qs.e: Used by Bigtable and HBase.

qs.q: What does hash partitioning sacrifice?
qs.e: Adjacent keys get scattered across partitions.

qs.q: Why can’t you use Java’s Object.hashCode for partitioning?
o: It may return different values for the same key in different processes
qs.e: The hash must be consistent across processes and machines.

qs.q: In Cassandra, with a primary key (user_id, update_timestamp)…
o: user_id is hashed to choose the partition; updates are sorted by timestamp within it
qs.e: A neat compromise: hash for distribution, sort for range scans within one user.

qs.q: How can an app handle one extremely hot key?
o: Append a random number (e.g. two digits) to split it across up to 100 keys, then combine on read
qs.e: Only worth it for a few hot keys, since reads become more expensive.

qs.q: Document‑partitioned (local) secondary indexes make reads…
o: Scatter/gather across all partitions, which is expensive
qs.e: Writes are cheap though — only one partition is touched.

qs.q: A term‑partitioned (global) secondary index makes…
o: Reads efficient, writes slower and more complex
qs.e: A single write may affect several index partitions.

qs.q: How are global secondary indexes often updated in practice?
o: Asynchronously, e.g. DynamoDB updates usually within a fraction of a second
qs.e: Instant consistency would need distributed transactions across partitions.

qs.q: Why is hash mod N a bad partitioning scheme?
o: Changing N moves most keys to different nodes
qs.e: Rebalancing should move only the necessary data.

qs.q: With a fixed number of partitions, what moves when a node is added?
o: Whole partitions stolen from existing nodes
qs.e: Key‑to‑partition assignment never changes; only partition‑to‑node does.

qs.q: What’s tricky about choosing a fixed number of partitions?
o: Too many adds overhead; too few makes rebalancing and recovery expensive as data grows
qs.e: It’s set at setup time and hard to change later.

qs.q: Dynamic partitioning means…
o: Partitions split when too big and merge when too small
qs.e: HBase splits at 10 GB by default.

qs.q: Why pre‑split a dynamically partitioned DB?
o: An empty DB starts with one partition, so all initial writes hit one node
qs.e: Pre‑splitting needs you to know what the key distribution will look like.

qs.q: Cassandra’s default rebalancing approach is…
o: A fixed number of partitions per node (256 by default)
qs.e: Partition count grows proportionally to the number of nodes.

qs.q: Why can fully automatic rebalancing be dangerous?
o: Combined with automatic failure detection, it can shift load onto a merely slow node and cause cascading failure
qs.e: A human in the loop is slower but safer.

qs.q: Which uses a gossip protocol for routing instead of ZooKeeper?
qs.e: Gossip spreads cluster state changes among nodes.

qs.q: What role does ZooKeeper typically play in routing?
o: Keeps the authoritative mapping of partitions to nodes; routers subscribe to changes
qs.e: A separate coordination service tracking cluster metadata.

qs.q: Boss scenario: an IoT system stores readings keyed by timestamp in HBase and one region server melts down each day. Fix?
o: Prefix keys with device ID (or similar) so writes spread across ranges
qs.e: Classic timestamp hot spot; trade‑off is per‑device queries for time ranges.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a used‑car site needs ‘find all red cars’ fast across 50 partitions, and writes are less frequent. Which index style?
qs.e: Global indexes make reads hit one partition; writes pay the cost.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a celebrity’s posts make one partition hot even with hash partitioning. What can you do?
o: Split that key by appending a random suffix and combine on read
qs.e: Hashing can’t distribute a single key; the app must.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you’re designing a store expected to grow from 1 TB to 500 TB, unsure how. Fixed partitions or dynamic?
o: Dynamic partitioning (or proportional to nodes), so partitions adapt to volume
qs.e: Fixed counts work best when total size is predictable.

qs.q: Boss scenario: during a load spike, your cluster’s auto‑rebalancer moved partitions off a slow node and the whole cluster collapsed. Lesson?
o: Keep a human in the loop for rebalancing decisions
qs.e: Automatic rebalancing plus failure detection can cause cascading failures.

Uneven distribution of data or load
Continuous ranges of keys per partition
Partition by a hash of the key
Secondary index per partition, scatter/gather reads
Querying all partitions and combining results
Split when big, merge when small
Nodes spread cluster state to each other
Creating initial partitions in an empty DB

chapters.title: Transactions
chapters.blurb: Grouping reads and writes into one unit that fully succeeds or fails, and the isolation levels that decide which concurrency bugs you’re protected from.

b: Many things go wrong: software or hardware failing mid‑write, the app crashing, network interruptions, concurrent writes overwriting each other, reading partial updates, race conditions.
A transaction groups several reads and writes into one logical unit: it either succeeds (commit) or fails (abort, rollback) entirely. If it fails, the app can safely retry.
Transactions simplify the programming model by letting the DB handle certain errors and concurrency issues (safety guarantees).
They’re not free: some apps don’t need them and can get higher performance or availability by weakening or dropping them.
Atomicity: not about concurrency — it’s abortability. If a fault occurs mid‑transaction, all writes are discarded, so retrying is safe.
Consistency: invariants about your data (e.g. credits and debits balance) — a property of the application, not really the database. The C was arguably added to make the acronym work.
Isolation: concurrently executing transactions don’t interfere. The textbook ideal is serializability (as if run one at a time); in practice weaker levels are common.
Durability: committed data isn’t forgotten — written to non‑volatile storage and/or replicated. Perfect durability doesn’t exist (disks fail, SSDs corrupt, data center fires).
ACID implementations differ widely; systems that don’t meet it are sometimes called BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency), which is even vaguer.

Single‑object writes: storage engines almost always provide atomicity and isolation for one object (via a log for crash recovery and a lock per object). Atomic increment and compare‑and‑set help too — but these aren’t transactions in the usual sense.
Multi‑object transactions are needed when several pieces of data must stay in sync: foreign key references, denormalized data in documents, and secondary indexes.
Many distributed datastores abandoned multi‑object transactions because they’re hard across partitions and can hurt performance or availability.
Retrying is simple but not perfect.
The transaction may have succeeded but the network failed while acknowledging — a retry runs it twice unless deduplicated.
If the error was due to overload, retrying makes it worse; use exponential backoff and limit retries.
Only retry transient errors (deadlock, isolation violation, temporary network issue), not permanent ones (constraint violation).
Side effects outside the DB (e.g. sending an email) may happen even if the transaction aborts; two‑phase commit can help coordinate across systems.
If the client process fails while retrying, the data it was trying to write is lost.
The most basic isolation level, default in many DBs (Oracle 11g, PostgreSQL, SQL Server 2012, MemSQL).
No dirty reads: you only see data that has been committed — no partially updated state, no data that may be rolled back.
No dirty writes: you only overwrite committed data. Prevents e.g. a used‑car sale going to one buyer while the invoice goes to another.

Implementation: row‑level locks for writes, held until commit. For reads, the DB remembers the old committed value and serves it until the new one commits (read locks would make reads wait for long writes).

Read committed still allows read skew (nonrepeatable read): Alice has $500 in each of two accounts; mid‑transfer she reads one before and one after, and sees $900 total. Temporary — but unacceptable for backups (inconsistencies become permanent if restored), analytic queries and integrity checks.
Snapshot isolation: each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot — all data committed at the moment it started.
Readers never block writers and writers never block readers.

Implemented with multi‑version concurrency control (MVCC): the DB keeps several committed versions of each object. Each row has created_by and deleted_by transaction IDs; updates become delete + create.
Visibility rules: ignore writes by transactions in progress when you started, by aborted ones, and by any with a later transaction ID; everything else is visible.
Naming is confusing: Oracle calls it ‘serializable’; PostgreSQL and MySQL call it ‘repeatable read’.
Lost update: two transactions read‑modify‑write the same value concurrently (e.g. incrementing a counter, editing a JSON document, two users editing a wiki page) and one change is clobbered.
Atomic write operations: e.g. UPDATE counters SET value = value + 1 — the best solution when expressible. ORMs can accidentally bypass them.
Explicit locking: SELECT … FOR UPDATE to lock rows you’ll modify. Easy to forget.

Automatic detection: let transactions run in parallel and abort the one that would lose an update. PostgreSQL repeatable read, Oracle serializable and SQL Server snapshot isolation do this; MySQL/InnoDB’s repeatable read does not.
Compare‑and‑set: update only if the value hasn’t changed since you read it.

With replication (multi‑leader/leaderless), locks and CAS don’t work; allow concurrent writes to create siblings and merge, or use commutative atomic operations. LWW, the default in many replicated DBs, is prone to lost updates.
Write skew: two transactions read the same objects, then update different objects, based on what they read — violating an invariant neither alone would break.
Example: two doctors on call, both feel ill, each checks that ‘at least two are on call’ and goes off call — now nobody is on call.
Other examples: double‑booking a meeting room, multiplayer game moves, claiming a username, double‑spending a balance.
Pattern: a SELECT checks a condition, the app decides, then a write changes the result of that SELECT.
A phantom is when a write in one transaction changes the result of a search query in another. Snapshot isolation prevents phantoms for read‑only queries, but not in read‑write cases like write skew.
Locking rows doesn’t help when the check is for the absence of rows. Materializing conflicts (e.g. a table of time slots to lock) works but is ugly — serializable isolation is usually better.
Serializable isolation: the strongest — the outcome is as if transactions ran one at a time. Three ways to implement it.

Actually run them serially on a single thread. Became viable around 2007 because RAM got cheap enough to hold whole active datasets, and OLTP transactions are short. Used by VoltDB/H‑Store, Redis, Datomic.
Requires stored procedures: no interactive multi‑round‑trip transactions — the whole transaction code is submitted ahead of time.

Constraints: transactions must be small and fast; the active dataset should fit in memory; write throughput must fit one CPU core, or be partitioned so each transaction touches one partition (cross‑partition transactions are much slower).
Was the only widely used serializability algorithm for about 30 years. Not to be confused with two‑phase commit.
Writers block both other writers and readers; readers block writers (stronger than snapshot isolation’s rule).
Shared locks for reading (many holders); exclusive lock for writing (one holder, no shared). Locks held until the end of the transaction: acquire during, release at end — the two phases.
Deadlocks happen; the DB detects and aborts one transaction, which the app must retry.
Performance is significantly worse; latency is unstable and high percentiles can be very slow, since one slow transaction can stall many.
Phantoms are handled by predicate locks (lock all objects matching a condition, even non‑existent ones) or, more practically, index‑range (next‑key) locks that lock a broader range.
Newer (first described in 2008): full serializability with only a small performance penalty over snapshot isolation. Used in PostgreSQL since 9.1 and FoundationDB.
Optimistic: instead of blocking, transactions run on a snapshot; at commit time the DB checks whether isolation was violated and aborts if so.

Pessimistic (2PL) assumes anything may go wrong and waits; optimistic hopes things are fine and checks at the end. Optimistic performs badly under high contention (many aborts) but well when there’s spare capacity and low contention.
Detection 1: reads of stale MVCC versions — a write by another transaction was ignored at read time but committed before you commit.
Detection 2: writes that affect prior reads — the DB tracks which transactions read data (e.g. via index ranges) and notifies them if another transaction writes to it.
Read‑only queries never block and need no locks, making SSI attractive for read‑heavy workloads.

qs.q: In ACID, atomicity is best described as…
o: Abortability: on a fault, all of a transaction’s writes are discarded
qs.e: It’s about faults mid‑transaction, not concurrent access.

qs.q: Why is ACID ‘consistency’ really an application property?
o: It refers to app‑defined invariants; the DB can’t stop you writing bad data that satisfies constraints
qs.e: The app relies on A, I and D to achieve C.

qs.q: Ideal ‘isolation’ in the textbook sense is…
qs.e: In practice weaker levels are common for performance.

qs.q: When should you NOT retry an aborted transaction?
qs.e: Retrying a permanent error just fails again.

qs.q: Read committed prevents…
qs.e: You only see and overwrite committed data.

qs.q: How does read committed typically avoid dirty reads without read locks?
o: Remember the old committed value and return it until the new one commits
qs.e: Read locks would make reads wait for long‑running writes.

qs.q: Alice sees $900 instead of $1,000 during a transfer. What anomaly is this?
qs.e: Snapshot isolation prevents it.

qs.q: Why is read skew a problem for backups?
o: Inconsistent parts captured during writes would become permanent if restored
qs.e: Long‑running read queries need a consistent snapshot.

qs.q: What’s the key promise of snapshot isolation?
o: Each transaction sees a consistent snapshot as of when it started; readers and writers don’t block each other
qs.e: Implemented with MVCC.

qs.q: What do PostgreSQL and MySQL call snapshot isolation?
qs.e: Oracle calls it serializable — naming is a mess.

qs.q: Best fix for a lost update on a counter?
o: An atomic operation like UPDATE … SET value = value + 1
qs.e: Use atomic ops whenever the change can be expressed that way.

qs.q: Which does NOT automatically detect lost updates at its snapshot level?
qs.e: Automatic detection is a nice feature that InnoDB lacks.

qs.q: Two on‑call doctors both go off call, leaving nobody. What’s this?
qs.e: Both read the same data, then updated different rows.

qs.q: Why doesn’t SELECT … FOR UPDATE fix a ‘no row exists yet’ check, like booking an empty room?
o: There are no rows to lock — the conflict is a phantom
qs.e: Phantoms need predicate/index‑range locks or serializable isolation.

qs.q: What made single‑threaded serial execution viable around 2007?
o: RAM became cheap enough to hold active datasets, and OLTP transactions are short
qs.e: Used by VoltDB/H‑Store, Redis and Datomic.

qs.q: Serial execution systems require transactions to be submitted as…
qs.e: No waiting on network round trips within a transaction.

qs.q: In two‑phase locking, what can a reader block?
o: Writers to the objects it read
qs.e: Writers block readers and writers; readers block writers.

qs.q: What’s the main downside of 2PL?
o: Poor and unstable performance, with frequent deadlocks and long waits
qs.e: One slow transaction can stall many others.

qs.q: Index‑range (next‑key) locks are…
o: A practical approximation of predicate locks that lock a broader range
qs.e: They lock more than necessary but have much lower overhead.

qs.q: SSI is called ‘optimistic’ because…
o: Transactions proceed without blocking and the DB checks for conflicts at commit
qs.e: It performs badly under high contention.

qs.q: Which DB uses SSI?
qs.e: FoundationDB also uses a similar approach.

qs.q: Two‑phase locking vs two‑phase commit:
o: 2PL is for isolation; 2PC is for atomic commit across nodes
qs.e: Completely different concepts with confusingly similar names.

qs.q: Boss scenario: two users book the last seat simultaneously. Your DB runs snapshot isolation. What happens and what fixes it?
o: Write skew could double‑book; use serializable isolation or materialize the conflict
qs.e: SI checks against a snapshot that doesn’t see the other booking.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your nightly analytics query runs 2 hours on the OLTP DB and returns inconsistent totals. Which isolation level helps without blocking writers?
qs.e: A consistent snapshot, with readers never blocking writers.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a wiki loses edits when two people save the same page. The ORM reads, edits, and writes back. Quick fix?
o: Compare‑and‑set or explicit locking on save (or atomic operations)
qs.e: Classic lost update from read‑modify‑write cycles.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a high‑contention inventory system on SSI shows huge abort rates. What might perform better?
o: Pessimistic locking (2PL) or restructuring to reduce contention
qs.e: Optimistic control suffers when many transactions conflict.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a transaction sends a welcome email, then aborts and retries — the user gets two emails. Why?
o: Side effects outside the DB happen even if the transaction aborts
qs.e: Coordinate side effects (e.g. outbox pattern, idempotence or 2PC).

terms: Seeing parts of the DB at different points in time
Keeping multiple committed versions of objects
Decisions on stale reads break an invariant
A write changes another transaction’s search results
Result as if transactions ran one at a time
Optimistic serializable isolation with commit checks
Update only if the value is unchanged
Whole transaction code submitted ahead of time

chapters.title: The Trouble with Distributed Systems
chapters.blurb: Everything that can go wrong once you have more than one machine: lost packets, unreliable clocks, process pauses, and deciding what’s true.

b: On a single computer, things tend to work or fail completely; the hardware is designed to be deterministic.
In distributed systems, partial failures happen: some parts break in unpredictable ways while others work. They’re nondeterministic — you may not even know whether something succeeded.
Supercomputers (HPC) treat a failure like a single‑node crash: stop everything, restore from a checkpoint.

Cloud internet services must be online at all times, run on commodity hardware with higher failure rates, use IP/Ethernet networks, and span geography — so fault tolerance must be built into software.
You can build a more reliable system from unreliable parts (error‑correcting codes, TCP over IP), but there’s always a limit.
Most distributed systems use asynchronous packet networks: no guarantee when or whether a message arrives.

When you send a request and get no response, many things could have happened: request lost; request queued; remote node crashed; remote node paused (e.g. GC); request processed but response lost; response delayed.
The sender can’t tell which. The usual approach: a timeout — after which you still don’t know if the request was processed.
Network faults are surprisingly common, even in controlled data centers: misconfigured switches, network partitions, even sharks biting undersea cables.
You don’t necessarily need to tolerate them, but you must know how your software reacts. Testing by deliberately triggering faults (chaos testing) is wise.
Sometimes you get explicit feedback: a TCP RST/FIN if the port is closed, a script notifying others when a process crashes, a switch reporting a link down.
But in general you can’t rely on it; even acknowledgements and retries can fail.

Timeout trade‑off: long timeouts mean waiting long to declare a node dead; short ones detect faults faster but risk falsely declaring a node dead during a temporary slowdown — then work moves to others, possibly causing cascading failure and actions executing twice.
A theoretical network with max delay d and handling time r would allow a timeout of 2d + r. Real networks have unbounded delays.
Network switch queues: several nodes sending to the same destination fill the switch queue; packets wait or are dropped when it overflows.
OS queues: if all CPU cores are busy, incoming requests wait for the application.
Virtualisation: a VM may pause for tens of milliseconds while another uses the CPU, buffering incoming data.
TCP flow control (congestion avoidance) limits sending rate; and TCP retransmission of lost packets adds delay visible to the app.
Noisy neighbours in shared data centers make it worse.

Choose timeouts experimentally by measuring round‑trip distributions; better still, adjust automatically based on observed response time and jitter (Phi Accrual failure detector, used in Akka and Cassandra). UDP is a choice for latency‑sensitive apps (videoconferencing) where late data is useless.
The telephone network allocates a circuit with fixed, guaranteed bandwidth for each call: bounded delay, no queueing (synchronous).
Data center networks and the internet use packet switching because traffic is bursty: a fixed circuit wastes bandwidth when idle and slows transfers when it’s too small. TCP adapts dynamically.
Variable delays are the result of a cost/benefit trade‑off: dynamic resource partitioning gives better utilisation (cheaper) at the cost of variable delay.
Quality of service and admission control can emulate circuits, but this isn’t enabled in multi‑tenant data centers or the public internet.
Each machine has its own quartz clock, not perfectly accurate. Network Time Protocol (NTP) syncs clocks with servers that use more accurate sources (GPS).
Time‑of‑day clocks return wall‑clock time (e.g. clock_gettime(CLOCK_REALTIME)). Synced with NTP, they may jump backward, so they’re unsuitable for measuring elapsed time.
Monotonic clocks (CLOCK_MONOTONIC, System.nanoTime) always move forward — good for measuring durations, but their absolute value is meaningless and can’t be compared across machines.
NTP may adjust the monotonic clock’s frequency (slewing) but never jumps it.
Quartz drift: Google assumes up to 200 ppm, i.e. about 6 ms drift for a clock resynced every 30 seconds, or 17 seconds for a clock resynced once a day.
If a clock differs too much from NTP, it may refuse to sync or be forcibly reset, jumping backward or forward.
A node accidentally firewalled off from NTP can drift unnoticed for a while.
NTP sync is only as good as network delay; over congested networks, errors can be large. Some NTP servers are misconfigured and wrong by hours.
Leap seconds have broken many large systems; smearing them over a day helps.
VMs: virtualised hardware clocks can jump when a VM is paused.
On devices you don’t control, users may set wrong times on purpose.
Very precise sync is possible (PTP, GPS receivers, monitoring — e.g. MiFID II requirements for trading) but needs significant effort.
Problems with clocks are silent: the system keeps working with subtly wrong data rather than crashing. Monitor clock offsets and remove nodes that drift too far.

Ordering events across nodes with timestamps is dangerous. With last write wins, a write from a node whose clock is slightly fast can silently override a causally later write from another node. A database writes can mysteriously disappear.
‘Recent’ depends on a local clock; NTP can’t make ordering perfect when drift is comparable to network delay.
Logical clocks (incrementing counters) are safer for ordering events: they capture relative order, not elapsed time.
Clock readings have a confidence interval: e.g. 95% confidence the time is between 10.3 and 10.5 seconds past the minute. Most APIs hide this.

Google Spanner’s TrueTime API explicitly returns [earliest, latest]. For transaction ordering, Spanner waits for the length of the interval before committing, so intervals don’t overlap. Google puts GPS receivers or atomic clocks in each data center to keep the uncertainty around 7 ms.
A thread can be paused for a long time at any point, then continue without knowing it was paused.

Causes: stop‑the‑world garbage collection (sometimes minutes!); VM suspension and live migration; laptop lid closing; OS context switches or a hypervisor running other VMs (steal time); synchronous disk I/O (even class loading in Java); swapping to disk (thrashing); a Unix SIGSTOP (e.g. Ctrl‑Z).
Lease example: a node checks its lease is valid for 10 more seconds, then pauses 15 seconds, then processes a request believing it still holds the lease — while another node has taken over.
Hard real‑time systems (aircraft, airbags) guarantee response deadlines but need special OSes, libraries and lots of testing — too expensive for most data systems.
Mitigations: treat GC pauses as planned brief node outages (warn the system, stop routing requests to that node); or use GC only for short‑lived objects and restart processes periodically.

cards.t: Truth is defined by the majority
b: A node can’t trust its own judgement: it might think it’s alive while others have declared it dead (e.g. it can receive but its outgoing messages are dropped, or it was paused by GC).
So decisions require a quorum — votes from a majority of nodes. That removes dependence on any one node.
The leader and the lock: a system may require only one leader, one lock holder, or one user per username. A node that believes it’s ‘the chosen one’ may be wrong if the majority has moved on.
Real bug: HBase had a problem where a client whose lock lease had expired during a pause kept writing, corrupting a file.
When granting a lock or lease, the lock service also returns a fencing token — a number that increases every time a lock is granted.
Every write to storage includes the token. Storage rejects writes with a token lower than one it has already processed.
So a client that was paused and lost its lease can’t corrupt data: its old token is refused.
ZooKeeper’s zxid or the znode version (cversion) can serve as fencing tokens.
Requires the storage service to check tokens actively; it protects against mistaken, not malicious, nodes.
A Byzantine fault is a node behaving arbitrarily — lying, sending corrupted or contradictory messages (the Byzantine Generals Problem).
Byzantine fault tolerance matters in aerospace (radiation corrupting memory/CPU) and in systems with mutually untrusting parties, like peer‑to‑peer networks and blockchains.

In typical data center systems, we assume nodes are unreliable but honest; Byzantine‑tolerant protocols are complicated and costly. They also don’t protect against bugs replicated in all nodes, or attackers who compromise many nodes.
Cheap protection against ‘weak lying’: checksums at the application level, input sanitization, and using multiple NTP servers to discard outliers.

Timing models: synchronous (bounded delay, pauses and drift — unrealistic); partially synchronous (behaves synchronously most of the time but sometimes exceeds bounds — the realistic model); asynchronous (no timing assumptions, not even clocks — very restrictive).

Node failure models: crash‑stop (a node dies and never returns); crash‑recovery (nodes crash and may restart; stable storage survives, memory is lost — the most useful model); Byzantine (arbitrary faults).
Correctness is defined by properties. Safety: nothing bad happens (e.g. uniqueness of fencing tokens). If violated, there’s a specific point in time when it broke, and it can’t be undone.
Liveness: something good eventually happens (e.g. a request eventually gets a response). It may not hold now but there’s hope it will. Often contains ‘eventually’.
Typically, safety must always hold, even if all nodes crash; liveness may have caveats (e.g. only if a majority is up).
Models simplify reality; real implementations still need to handle the ‘impossible’ cases (e.g. lost stable storage).

qs.q: What makes distributed systems fundamentally harder than a single computer?
qs.e: Some parts fail while others work, and you may not know whether something succeeded.

qs.q: You send a request and get no response. What can you conclude?
o: Nothing definitive — it may have been lost, queued, processed with a lost reply, or the node paused
qs.e: The sender can’t distinguish these cases.

qs.q: Why can’t you choose a perfect timeout in typical networks?
o: Network delays and processing times are unbounded
qs.e: The 2d + r formula only works with guaranteed maximum delays.

qs.q: What’s the risk of a too‑short timeout?
o: Falsely declaring a slow node dead, shifting load and possibly executing actions twice or causing cascading failure
qs.e: Especially harmful when the slowness is caused by overload.

qs.q: Which is NOT a source of network delay variability?
o: Bounded circuits in the telephone network
qs.e: Circuit switching gives bounded delay; packet networks queue.

qs.q: What does the Phi Accrual failure detector do?
o: Adjusts suspicion of failure based on observed response time distribution
qs.e: Used in Akka and Cassandra.

qs.q: Why do data center networks use packet switching rather than circuits?
o: Traffic is bursty; dynamic sharing gives better utilisation and lower cost at the price of variable delay
qs.e: Variable delay is a trade‑off, not a law of nature.

qs.q: Which clock should you use to measure elapsed time?
qs.e: Time‑of‑day clocks can jump backward when synced.

qs.q: Can you compare monotonic clock values across machines?
o: No — their absolute values are meaningless
qs.e: They’re only useful for durations on one machine.

qs.q: With 200 ppm drift and daily resyncs, roughly how far can a clock drift?
qs.e: About 6 ms if resynced every 30 seconds.

qs.q: Why is last write wins with timestamps dangerous across nodes?
o: A node with a fast clock can silently override causally later writes, so data disappears
qs.e: Logical clocks are safer for ordering events.

qs.q: What does Spanner’s TrueTime API return?
qs.e: Spanner waits out the uncertainty before committing.

qs.q: Which is NOT a cause of process pauses?
qs.e: Also laptop sleep, context switches, synchronous I/O and SIGSTOP.

qs.q: A node checks its lease is valid for 10 s, then pauses for 15 s. What’s the danger?
o: It may act as lease holder after another node has taken over
qs.e: Code can be paused between any two lines.

qs.q: How do distributed systems decide whether a node is dead?
qs.e: No single node can trust its own judgement.

qs.q: What is a fencing token?
o: A number that increases each time a lock is granted; storage rejects older tokens
qs.e: It stops a paused former lock holder from corrupting data.

qs.q: What is a Byzantine fault?
o: A node behaving arbitrarily, including lying or sending corrupted messages
qs.e: Relevant to aerospace and blockchains; usually not assumed in data centers.

qs.q: Which system model is most realistic for typical data systems?
qs.e: Mostly bounded, occasionally not; nodes crash and come back with stable storage.

qs.q: ‘Fencing tokens are unique’ is an example of…
qs.e: Safety violations happen at a specific point in time and can’t be undone.

qs.q: ‘Every request eventually gets a response’ is…
qs.e: Liveness properties often contain ‘eventually’.

qs.q: Which cheap measure protects against ‘weak forms of lying’?
o: Checksums, input sanitization and multiple NTP servers
qs.e: Practical and inexpensive.

qs.q: Boss scenario: two app servers both believe they hold the lock on a file after one had a 20‑second GC pause; the file gets corrupted. What prevents this?
o: Fencing tokens checked by the storage service
qs.e: The paused client’s stale token gets rejected.

qs.q: Boss scenario: Cassandra writes mysteriously vanish; one node’s clock is 300 ms ahead. Why?
o: LWW used timestamps from the fast clock, so its writes beat later ones
qs.e: Silent data loss from clock skew is a classic LWW hazard.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your monitoring measures request duration using the system wall clock and sometimes reports negative durations. Fix?
o: Use a monotonic clock for elapsed time
qs.e: Wall clocks can jump backward when synchronized.

qs.q: Boss scenario: during a traffic spike, your failure detector declares busy nodes dead, shifts their load, and the cluster collapses. Better approach?
o: Adaptive timeouts based on observed latency distributions (e.g. Phi Accrual) and care with automatic failover
qs.e: Premature declarations of death can cause cascading failures.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a node can receive messages but its outgoing messages are dropped. It still thinks it’s the leader. What should happen?
o: The majority declares it dead and elects a new leader; its own belief doesn’t count
qs.e: Truth is defined by the majority — and fencing guards against its stale actions.

Waiting limit after which a node is presumed dead
Part of the network cut off from the rest
Always moves forward; good for durations
Protocol for syncing clocks with time servers
Quartz clocks running fast or slow
A thread stopped, e.g. by GC, unaware it paused
Majority vote used to decide what’s true
Increasing number rejecting stale lock holders
Arbitrary or lying behaviour by a node
Spanner’s clock API returning an uncertainty interval

chapters.title: Consistency and Consensus
chapters.blurb: Strong guarantees that let a distributed system behave like a single copy: linearizability, ordering and causality, atomic commit, and consensus.

b: Most replicated DBs provide at least eventual consistency (better called convergence): stop writing and replicas eventually agree. It’s a very weak guarantee and tricky for app developers.
Stronger models are easier to use correctly but may cost performance or fault tolerance.

The best approach to fault tolerance: find general abstractions with useful guarantees (like transactions), implement them once, and let apps rely on them. Consensus — getting all nodes to agree — is one of the most important.
Also called atomic consistency, strong consistency, immediate consistency or external consistency.
Idea: make the system appear as if there were only one copy of the data, with all operations atomic.

It’s a recency guarantee: once a write completes, all subsequent reads see it. Once any read has returned the new value, all later reads (by any client) must return it too, even if the write is still in progress.
Example: Alice sees the final score of a match on a refreshed page; Bob, refreshing later, sees the old score from a lagging replica — a linearizability violation.

Linearizability ≠ serializability. Serializability is about transactions (groups of objects) behaving as if run in some serial order. Linearizability is a recency guarantee on reads and writes of a single object. Strict serializability combines both (2PL and actual serial execution typically provide it; SSI does not).
Locking and leader election: all nodes must agree who holds the lock. Coordination services like ZooKeeper and etcd use consensus to implement linearizable operations for this.

Uniqueness constraints: unique usernames or emails, no negative bank balance, no overselling stock or double‑booked seats — all need a single up‑to‑date value everyone agrees on (like a lock or compare‑and‑set).

Cross‑channel timing dependencies: e.g. a web server stores a full‑size photo in file storage and sends a message to a resizer via a queue. If the queue is faster than storage replication, the resizer may see an old or missing image. Two communication channels create a race.
Single‑leader replication: potentially linearizable if you read from the leader or synchronous followers (and the node really is the leader — snapshot isolation or a delusional leader breaks it).
Consensus algorithms (ZooKeeper, etcd): linearizable — they prevent split brain and stale replicas.
Multi‑leader replication: not linearizable — concurrent writes on multiple nodes, async replication.

Leaderless (Dynamo‑style): probably not. LWW based on clocks isn’t, sloppy quorums aren’t, and even strict quorums can be non‑linearizable with variable network delays. You can make it linearizable at a performance cost: synchronous read repair before returning, and writers reading a quorum first. Even then, linearizable compare‑and‑set needs consensus.

If a network interruption separates replicas: a linearizable system must make disconnected replicas unavailable (wait or error); a system that doesn’t need linearizability can stay available on each side.

That’s the CAP theorem: better phrased as ‘either consistent or available when partitioned’, since partitions aren’t optional. Its formal version is very narrow (one model, one fault) and it has little practical value for system design today.
Few systems are actually linearizable. Even RAM on a multi‑core CPU isn’t: each core has its own cache, written back asynchronously.

The main reason to drop linearizability is performance, not fault tolerance. It has been proven that linearizable response time must be at least proportional to the uncertainty of network delays — so it’s inherently slow in variable networks.
Ordering keeps coming up: leaders order writes, serializability orders transactions, timestamps and clocks try to order events.
Causality imposes order: a question comes before its answer; a row is created before it’s updated; a consistent snapshot means consistent with causality.
Causal order is a partial order: some operations are ordered, others are concurrent (incomparable). Linearizability gives a total order — every operation in one timeline.
Linearizability implies causality. Causal consistency is the strongest model that doesn’t slow down due to network delays and stays available during network failures.
Tracking causality: nodes need to know which version of the data a read saw (like version vectors generalised across the whole DB, or SSI’s tracking of read versions).
Instead of tracking all causal dependencies, use sequence numbers or timestamps (from a logical clock) to order events consistently with causality.
With a single leader, its replication log’s order is a total order consistent with causality.
Without a single leader, approaches like odd/even counters per node, physical timestamps or preallocated blocks aren’t consistent with causality.

Lamport timestamps: each node has a counter and an ID; a timestamp is the pair (counter, node ID). Every node and client tracks the maximum counter seen and includes it in every request; on receiving a larger value, a node increases its own counter to that. Gives a total order consistent with causality.
Unlike version vectors, Lamport timestamps can’t tell whether two operations are concurrent.

Limit: the total order only emerges after the fact. To enforce uniqueness of a username right now, a node must know no other node is concurrently claiming it — you need to know when the order is finalised. That leads to total order broadcast.

A protocol for exchanging messages with two safety properties: reliable delivery (if a message is delivered to one node, it’s delivered to all) and totally ordered delivery (every node gets messages in the same order).
Used by ZooKeeper and etcd. It’s exactly what state machine replication needs: if every replica processes the same writes in the same order, they stay consistent.
It’s like an append‑only log that every node reads in the same order; the order is fixed at delivery time.

Implementing linearizable storage on it: to claim a username, append a message claiming it, read the log until your message comes back, and if the first claim for that name is yours, commit; otherwise abort. Reads can also be made linearizable by sequencing them through the log, or by waiting until all prior entries are seen (sync() in ZooKeeper).
Linearizable compare‑and‑set (or increment‑and‑get) can implement total order broadcast, and vice versa. Both are equivalent to consensus.
Consensus situations: leader election (avoid split brain) and atomic commit (all nodes in a distributed transaction must agree to commit or all abort).

FLP result: no algorithm can always reach consensus if there’s any risk of a node crashing — in the asynchronous model without clocks or timeouts. With timeouts or random numbers, consensus becomes solvable.

Two‑phase commit (2PC) uses a coordinator (transaction manager). Phase 1: it asks each participant to prepare; each votes yes only if it can definitely commit (written to disk, constraints checked). Phase 2: if all say yes, the coordinator writes the decision to its log (the commit point) then tells everyone to commit; if any says no, all abort.
Two points of no return: a participant that votes yes surrenders the right to abort; once the coordinator decides, the decision is irrevocable.
If the coordinator crashes after participants vote yes, they’re stuck ‘in doubt’ (uncertain) until it recovers — 2PC is a blocking protocol.
Three‑phase commit (3PC) is non‑blocking in theory but assumes bounded network delays and response times — not realistic.
Database‑internal distributed transactions (all nodes run the same software) can work quite well.
Heterogeneous ones span different technologies (e.g. a DB and a message broker) — e.g. process a message only if the DB transaction commits — achieving exactly‑once message processing.

XA (X/Open eXtended Architecture) is a standard C API for 2PC across heterogeneous systems; the coordinator is often a library in the app process, so if the app server dies, so does the coordinator’s log.
In‑doubt transactions hold locks (e.g. row locks) until resolved, potentially blocking other transactions for a long time — the DB is effectively unavailable for that data.

Orphaned in‑doubt transactions (coordinator log lost) need manual resolution by an administrator; XA has heuristic decisions that let a participant decide unilaterally — a euphemism for probably breaking atomicity.
Distributed transactions amplify failures, conflicting with building fault‑tolerant systems.

Properties: uniform agreement (no two nodes decide differently); integrity (no node decides twice); validity (the decided value was proposed by some node); termination (every node that doesn’t crash eventually decides).
Agreement, integrity and validity are safety properties; termination is liveness. It requires a majority of nodes to be working.
Best‑known algorithms: Viewstamped Replication, Paxos, Raft and Zab. They actually decide a sequence of values — they implement total order broadcast.
Epoch numbering: each election increments an epoch (ballot, view or term number); within an epoch the leader is unique. Higher epochs win.
Two rounds of voting: first to choose a leader, then to approve proposals. The quorums must overlap, so a vote on a proposal checks no higher‑epoch leader exists.

Limitations: voting is like synchronous replication (performance cost); requires a strict majority; most assume a fixed set of nodes; rely on timeouts, so variable delays cause frequent spurious elections; Raft has edge cases with unreliable links.
ZooKeeper and etcd are ‘distributed key‑value stores’ — really coordination services holding small amounts of data that fit in memory, replicated with fault‑tolerant total order broadcast.

Features: linearizable atomic operations (e.g. compare‑and‑set for locks), total ordering of operations (zxid as a fencing token), failure detection (sessions with heartbeats; ephemeral nodes deleted when a session times out), and change notifications (clients watch for changes).
Uses: choosing a leader among nodes of a service; allocating work, e.g. partitions to nodes, and rebalancing when nodes join or fail; service discovery (finding the IP for a service).
Membership services decide which nodes are currently alive and part of the cluster — combining failure detection with consensus so nodes agree.
Most apps don’t talk to consensus directly but rely on tools like ZooKeeper, which outsources coordination for HBase, Kafka, Hadoop YARN and others.

qs.q: Eventual consistency is better described as…
o: Convergence: replicas eventually agree if writes stop
qs.e: It says nothing about when replicas converge.

qs.q: What is linearizability, in one phrase?
o: The system behaves as if there’s a single copy of the data with atomic operations
qs.e: It’s a recency guarantee on reads and writes.

qs.q: Once a read returns a new value in a linearizable system…
o: Others may still see old values
All subsequent reads must return that value or newer
qs.e: Even if the write operation hasn’t completed yet.

qs.q: Linearizability vs serializability:
o: Linearizability is a recency guarantee on single objects; serializability is about transactions behaving as if serial
qs.e: Combining both is strict serializability.

qs.q: Does SSI provide linearizability?
o: No — reads come from a consistent snapshot that may not include more recent writes
qs.e: 2PL and actual serial execution typically are linearizable.

qs.q: Which is a use case requiring linearizability?
qs.e: Also leader election, locks and cross‑channel timing dependencies.

qs.q: Why does the image resizer example break without linearizability?
o: The message queue may be faster than file storage replication, so the resizer reads an old or missing image
qs.e: Two communication channels create a race.

qs.q: Which replication approach is NOT linearizable?
qs.e: Concurrent writes on multiple nodes with async replication.

qs.q: The more useful reading of the CAP theorem is…
o: Either consistent (linearizable) or available when partitioned
qs.e: Network partitions aren’t a choice; they happen.

qs.q: What’s the main reason many systems drop linearizability?
o: Performance — response time is inherently tied to network delay uncertainty
qs.e: Even multi‑core RAM isn’t linearizable, for performance.

qs.q: Causal order is…
o: A partial order — some operations are concurrent and incomparable
Always the same as wall‑clock order
qs.e: Linearizability gives a total order.

qs.q: Which is the strongest consistency model that doesn’t slow down due to network delays?
qs.e: It also remains available in the face of network failures.

qs.q: A Lamport timestamp is…
o: A pair (counter, node ID), where nodes adopt the maximum counter they see
qs.e: It gives a total order consistent with causality.

qs.q: What can’t Lamport timestamps do?
o: Tell whether two operations are concurrent
qs.e: Version vectors can; Lamport timestamps are more compact.

qs.q: Why aren’t Lamport timestamps enough to enforce unique usernames immediately?
o: You only know the total order after collecting all operations — you can’t know right now that nobody else is claiming it
qs.e: You need to know when the order is finalised — total order broadcast.

qs.q: The two properties of total order broadcast are…
o: Reliable delivery and totally ordered delivery
qs.e: Every node gets the same messages in the same order.

qs.q: Total order broadcast is equivalent to…
qs.e: These problems are deeply connected.

qs.q: The FLP result says consensus is impossible…
o: In the asynchronous model, without clocks or timeouts, if a node may crash
qs.e: Timeouts or randomness make it solvable in practice.

qs.q: In 2PC, what is the commit point?
o: When the coordinator writes its commit decision to its log
qs.e: After that, the decision is irrevocable.

qs.q: Why is 2PC called a blocking protocol?
o: If the coordinator crashes after participants vote yes, they must wait in doubt until it recovers
qs.e: Participants can’t safely abort or commit on their own.

qs.q: What’s the operational danger of in‑doubt transactions?
o: They hold locks until resolved, blocking other transactions on that data
qs.e: Orphaned ones may need manual resolution.

qs.q: XA ‘heuristic decisions’ are…
o: A participant unilaterally deciding an in‑doubt transaction, likely breaking atomicity
qs.e: A polite name for an emergency escape hatch.

qs.q: Which consensus property is a liveness property?
qs.e: Termination requires a majority of nodes to be working.

qs.q: What do Raft, Paxos, Zab and Viewstamped Replication really decide?
o: A sequence of values — they implement total order broadcast
qs.e: Each decision appends to a log.

qs.q: What’s the role of epoch (term/ballot) numbers?
o: Within each epoch the leader is unique; higher epochs win conflicts
qs.e: Overlapping quorums ensure no higher‑epoch leader is missed.

qs.q: What does ZooKeeper use ephemeral nodes for?
o: Failure detection: they’re deleted when a client’s session times out
qs.e: Combined with watches for change notifications.

qs.q: Which is a typical use of a coordination service?
o: Leader election, partition assignment and service discovery
qs.e: Small amounts of data that change slowly and fit in memory.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your signup service runs on a multi‑leader DB across 3 regions and duplicate usernames keep appearing. What fixes it?
o: Route username claims through a linearizable store or consensus (e.g. ZooKeeper/etcd, or a single leader per name)
qs.e: Uniqueness constraints need linearizability.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you must atomically commit to Postgres and publish to a message broker. 2PC via XA is proposed. Main operational risk?
o: A coordinator crash leaves in‑doubt transactions holding locks, possibly needing manual fixes
qs.e: Distributed transactions amplify failures; log‑based alternatives exist (see later chapters).

qs.q: Boss scenario: during a network partition, your bank requires reads to reflect all prior writes. What must the minority side do?
qs.e: Consistent or available when partitioned — not both.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your Raft cluster on a flaky network keeps holding elections and throughput tanks. Why?
o: Timeouts trigger spurious leader elections under variable network delay
qs.e: Consensus relies on timeouts to detect failure.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you need a 5‑node cluster to keep making progress if nodes fail. How many can fail?
qs.e: Consensus needs a strict majority: 3 of 5 must be up.

chapters.title: Batch Processing
chapters.blurb: Processing large bounded datasets: Unix tools, MapReduce and distributed filesystems, joins at scale, and the dataflow engines that followed.

b: Services (online): wait for requests, respond quickly; measured by response time and availability.
Batch processing (offline): take a large fixed input, run a job, produce output; often scheduled periodically; measured by throughput.
Stream processing (near‑real‑time): between the two — consumes inputs and produces outputs shortly after events happen, with lower latency than batch.
Batch processing is an old idea — punch‑card tabulating machines (Hollerith, 1890 US census) did aggregation in batches.
Example: find the five most popular pages in a web server log with a pipeline: read the file, extract the URL field (awk), sort, count duplicates (uniq -c), sort by count, take the top five (head).
Surprisingly powerful: processes gigabytes in seconds and is easy to adapt.

Versus an in‑memory hash table in a script: fine if the working set (distinct URLs) fits in memory. If not, sorting wins: GNU sort automatically spills to disk and parallelises across cores, so it handles datasets bigger than memory.
Mergesort’s sequential access patterns perform well on disks.

Make each program do one thing well. Expect the output of every program to be the input of another, as yet unknown, program. Design and build to be tried early. Use tools to lighten programming tasks.
A uniform interface: files (file descriptors) as an ordered sequence of bytes, often ASCII text with one record per line — any program can connect to any other.
Separation of logic and wiring: programs read stdin and write stdout, so the shell user wires them together (loose coupling, a kind of inversion of control).
Transparency and experimentation: inputs are immutable, you can inspect intermediate output with less, write it to a file and restart later.
Biggest limitation: Unix tools run on a single machine. That’s where Hadoop comes in.
MapReduce is like Unix tools distributed across thousands of machines. Its jobs read and write files on a distributed filesystem — Hadoop’s HDFS (an open source take on the Google File System).
HDFS is shared‑nothing: a daemon on each machine serves its local disk, and a central NameNode tracks which blocks live where.
Data is replicated across machines, or protected with erasure coding (like Reed–Solomon), which survives failures with less storage overhead than full replication.
Scales to tens of thousands of machines and petabytes, using cheap commodity hardware.

Four steps: (1) read input files and split into records; (2) the mapper extracts a key and value from each record; (3) sort all key‑value pairs by key; (4) the reducer iterates over sorted pairs, processing all values for each key together.
You write only the mapper and reducer — the framework does the sorting. Mapper: called once per record, stateless. Reducer: gets a key and an iterator over all its values.

Parallelism comes from partitioning: input is split into blocks, and the scheduler runs each mapper on a machine holding a replica of its input — ‘putting the computation near the data’ to save network transfer.
Mapper output is partitioned by hash of key, sorted, and written to local disk. Reducers fetch their partition from each mapper — the shuffle.

A single job is limited; jobs are chained into workflows, where one job’s output directory is the next job’s input. Schedulers: Oozie, Azkaban, Luigi, Airflow, Pinball. Higher‑level tools (Pig, Hive, Cascading, Crunch, FlumeJava) set up multi‑stage workflows automatically.
Batch jobs process whole datasets, so a ‘join’ means resolving all occurrences of an association, not looking up one record. Random‑access lookups over the network per record would be far too slow.
Example: join user activity events with a user database. Copy the user DB (e.g. from a backup via ETL) into HDFS alongside the events.

Sort‑merge join: one mapper set emits (user ID, event); another emits (user ID, profile). Sorting brings all records for each user together; secondary sort can arrange for the user record to come first, so the reducer needs little memory.
Key insight: MapReduce separates the network communication (bringing related data to the same place, by key) from the application logic. Partial failures are handled by retrying tasks transparently.
GROUP BY works the same way: use the grouping key as the mapper’s output key. Also used for sessionization (collating all events for a user session).
A hot key (e.g. a celebrity with millions of followers) sends a huge amount of data to one reducer — a straggler that holds up the whole job, since the job only finishes when all tasks are done.
Pig’s skewed join first runs a sampling job to find hot keys, then sends their records to one of several random reducers, and replicates the other side of the join to all of them.
Crunch’s sharded join is similar but requires hot keys to be specified explicitly. Hive’s skewed join stores hot keys in separate files (declared in metadata) and uses a map‑side join for them.
Grouping with hot keys can use two stages: first aggregate on random partitions to compact, then a second job combines the per‑reducer results.
Reduce‑side joins are general but costly (sorting, copying to reducers, merging). If you know something about the data, map‑side joins skip the reduce phase.

Broadcast hash join: one input is small enough to fit in memory; each mapper loads it into a hash table and streams the large input, looking up each record. Supported by Pig (‘replicated join’), Hive (‘MapJoin’), Cascading, Crunch, and Impala.

Partitioned hash join: if both inputs are partitioned the same way (same key, same hash function, same number of partitions), each mapper loads only one partition’s hash table. Hive calls it bucketed map join.
Map‑side merge join: if inputs are also sorted by the key, the mapper can merge them like a reducer would, without fitting either in memory.
Map‑side joins require knowing the physical layout of the data, so metadata (e.g. Hive’s metastore/HCatalog) matters.
Batch output usually isn’t a report — it’s some other structure.

Building search indexes: Google’s original use of MapReduce. Mappers partition documents, reducers build index files per partition. Indexes are written once and then read‑only; rebuild periodically or incrementally.

Key‑value stores as output: e.g. classifiers or recommendation data that a web app queries. Don’t write directly from each mapper/reducer to a production DB: network round trips per record are slow, many tasks in parallel can overwhelm the DB, and partial job failures leave partial output visible.

Better: build a brand‑new database file inside the job, write it to HDFS, then bulk‑load it into servers that serve it read‑only (Voldemort, Terrapin, ElephantDB, HBase bulk loading). Switching to the new files is atomic, and old files remain for rollback.

Immutable inputs and outputs give human fault tolerance: if buggy code produces bad output, roll back to the previous code version and rerun — not possible with a DB that was overwritten. This enables faster feature development, and it’s good for minimising irreversibility.
Massively parallel processing (MPP) databases had parallel joins and processing a decade before MapReduce. Differences:

Diversity of storage: MPP DBs require careful upfront modelling. Hadoop lets you dump any data into HDFS first and figure out how to process it later — the ‘data lake’ or ‘enterprise data hub’. ‘Raw data is better’ is sometimes called the sushi principle.
Diversity of processing models: MPP DBs are monolithic with SQL; Hadoop runs arbitrary code — SQL engines (Hive, Impala), ML, full‑text indexing, image analysis — on the same cluster and files.
Designing for frequent faults: MPP DBs abort the whole query on a node failure; MapReduce retries individual tasks and writes eagerly to disk for fault tolerance.

Why MapReduce is so failure‑tolerant: at Google, batch tasks run at low priority in shared clusters and can be killed (preempted) by higher‑priority processes — around a 5% chance per hour for a task. Long jobs would rarely finish without task‑level retries.
MapReduce fully materializes intermediate state: every job writes its output to HDFS before the next job reads it.

Downsides: a job can only start when all tasks of the previous one finish (stragglers slow everything); mappers often just re‑read files written by reducers (redundant); intermediate files are replicated across nodes, which is overkill for temporary data.

Dataflow engines (Spark, Tez, Flink) model the entire workflow as one job, a graph of operators. Sorting only happens where needed; no unnecessary map tasks; locality optimizations; intermediate state kept in memory or local disk; operators can start as soon as input is ready (pipelining); JVM processes are reused.

Fault tolerance without materialization: recompute lost data from earlier stages. Spark tracks ancestry via resilient distributed datasets (RDDs); Flink checkpoints operator state. Recomputation requires deterministic operators (watch out for hash‑table iteration order, random numbers, system clocks).
Final results are still usually written to durable storage.
Graph algorithms (e.g. PageRank) are iterative: repeat until done. MapReduce reads the whole input on each iteration — inefficient.

Pregel model / bulk synchronous parallel (BSP): a vertex sends messages to other vertices along edges; in each iteration a function is called for every vertex with its incoming messages. Vertices remember state between iterations. Implemented in Giraph, Spark GraphX and Flink Gelly.

Fault tolerance via periodic checkpointing of all vertex state. Graph partitioning across machines causes lots of cross‑machine messaging; single‑machine graph tools (e.g. GraphChi) can even be faster.

High‑level languages/APIs (Hive, Pig, Cascading, Crunch, Spark and Flink APIs) are easier to use and can be partly declarative: a query optimizer picks join algorithms; some use columnar storage and vectorized execution.
Batch processing is becoming more like MPP databases while keeping the flexibility to run arbitrary code and read arbitrary formats — plus specialised domains like ML and statistics (Mahout, MADlib).

qs.q: Batch processing systems are primarily measured by…
qs.e: How long a job over a large input takes.

qs.q: Why can GNU sort handle data larger than memory?
o: It automatically spills to disk and merges, using sequential access patterns
qs.e: Sorting beats an in‑memory hash table when the working set is too large.

qs.q: Which is part of the Unix philosophy?
o: The output of every program should be usable as input to another
qs.e: Plus a uniform interface (files) and separating logic from wiring.

qs.q: What’s the main limitation of Unix tools for big data?
o: They run on a single machine
qs.e: MapReduce distributes the same ideas across many machines.

qs.q: What does HDFS’s NameNode do?
o: Tracks which file blocks are stored on which machines
qs.e: Data blocks are replicated or erasure‑coded across machines.

qs.q: What advantage does erasure coding have over replication?
o: Survives failures with less storage overhead
qs.e: Reed–Solomon codes are a common example.

qs.q: In MapReduce, what does the framework do that you don’t write?
qs.e: The sort step is implicit.

qs.q: ‘Putting the computation near the data’ means…
o: Running each mapper on a machine that holds a replica of its input
qs.e: Saves copying input over the network.

qs.q: What is the shuffle?
o: Reducers fetching their partitions of sorted mapper output from each mapper
qs.e: Mapper output is partitioned by key hash, sorted, and fetched by reducers.

qs.q: Why not do a batch join by querying a remote database per record?
o: Network round trips per record would be very slow and could overwhelm the DB, and results would be nondeterministic
qs.e: Instead, copy the DB into the distributed filesystem and join locally.

qs.q: What makes sort‑merge (reduce‑side) joins work?
o: Mappers emit the join key, so sorting brings all related records to the same reducer
qs.e: Secondary sort can put the user record first.

qs.q: What’s a straggler caused by skew?
o: One reducer with far more data (a hot key) holding up the whole job
qs.e: Jobs finish only when all tasks are done.

qs.q: How does Pig’s skewed join handle hot keys?
o: Samples to find hot keys, spreads their records over several reducers, and replicates the other input to them
qs.e: Parallelises work on hot keys at the cost of replicating the smaller side.

qs.q: When can you use a broadcast hash join?
o: One input is small enough to fit in memory in every mapper
qs.e: Each mapper loads the small input into a hash table.

qs.q: A partitioned hash join (bucketed map join) requires…
o: Both inputs partitioned the same way by the join key
qs.e: Same key, hash function and number of partitions.

qs.q: Why shouldn’t mappers write directly to a production database?
o: Per‑record network writes are slow, many parallel tasks can overwhelm the DB, and partial failures leave partial results visible
qs.e: Build new DB files inside the job and bulk‑load them instead.

qs.q: What does immutable input/output give batch jobs?
o: Human fault tolerance — buggy output can be fixed by rolling back code and rerunning
qs.e: A database overwritten by buggy code can’t be recovered this easily.

qs.q: The ‘sushi principle’ says…
o: Raw data is better — store it first, figure out processing later
qs.e: Hadoop’s data lake approach, versus MPP’s upfront modelling.

qs.q: Why is MapReduce so tolerant of task failures?
o: At Google, low‑priority batch tasks are frequently preempted, so task‑level retries are essential
qs.e: About a 5% chance per hour that a task is killed.

qs.q: Which is a downside of MapReduce’s full materialization of intermediate state?
o: Jobs wait for all previous tasks; redundant mappers; replicating temporary data is overkill
qs.e: Dataflow engines fix this.

qs.q: How does Spark recover lost intermediate data?
o: Recomputing it from ancestry tracked via RDDs
qs.e: Recomputation requires deterministic operators.

qs.q: Why must operators be deterministic for recomputation‑based fault tolerance?
o: Recomputed data must match what downstream operators already consumed
qs.e: Watch out for random numbers, clocks and unordered hash iteration.

qs.q: What is the Pregel / BSP model for?
o: Iterative graph processing where vertices exchange messages each iteration
qs.e: Implemented by Giraph, GraphX and Flink Gelly.

qs.q: Which of these is NOT a dataflow engine?
qs.e: HDFS is the distributed filesystem.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a nightly job joins a 5 TB clickstream with a 50 MB country lookup table. Best join?
qs.e: The small table fits in each mapper’s memory.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a recommendation job writes directly to the production DB from 2,000 tasks, and the site slows down every night. Better approach?
o: Build DB files in the job, write to HDFS, and bulk‑load them atomically into read‑only servers
qs.e: Also gives atomic switching and easy rollback.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a bug in yesterday’s batch code produced wrong recommendations. What’s the recovery?
o: Roll back to the previous code and rerun on the immutable input
qs.e: Immutable inputs make batch jobs easy to rerun.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a 10‑stage MapReduce workflow is slow, mostly writing and re‑reading intermediate files. What helps most?
o: Move it to a dataflow engine like Spark or Flink
qs.e: Pipelining and in‑memory intermediate state avoid repeated materialization.

qs.q: Boss scenario: one reducer takes 6 hours while others finish in 10 minutes, due to one celebrity user. Fix?
o: A skewed join: sample hot keys and spread them across reducers (or two‑stage aggregation)
qs.e: Hot keys cause stragglers.
