chapters.title: Stream Processing
chapters.blurb: Processing unbounded data as it arrives: messaging systems, log‑based brokers, change data capture, event sourcing, time windows, joins, and fault tolerance.

b: Batch processing assumes a bounded input. In reality data arrives continuously; stream processing handles unbounded data incrementally as it happens.
An event is a small, self‑contained, immutable record of something that happened at a point in time, often with a timestamp.
A producer (publisher/sender) generates an event once; many consumers (subscribers/recipients) can process it. Related events are grouped into a topic or stream.
Polling a database for new events is expensive at low latency; it’s better for consumers to be notified when new events appear.

What happens if producers send faster than consumers can process? Three options: drop messages, buffer them in a queue (what if it outgrows memory?), or apply backpressure/flow control (block the producer, as Unix pipes and TCP do).
What happens if nodes crash or go offline — are messages lost? Durability costs (disk writes, replication); some apps can tolerate loss (e.g. periodic sensor readings).

Direct messaging without intermediaries: UDP multicast (financial feeds), brokerless libraries like ZeroMQ, StatsD over UDP for metrics, webhooks. Requires the app to handle loss; producers and consumers must be online.
A broker (message queue) is a server that producers and consumers connect to; it centralises durability and handles clients coming and going.
Consumers are generally asynchronous: the producer only waits for the broker to confirm buffering.

Traditional brokers (JMS / AMQP standards: RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ, HornetQ, Qpid, TIBCO, IBM MQ, Azure Service Bus, Google Cloud Pub/Sub) delete a message once it’s delivered and acknowledged — not suitable for long‑term storage. Queues are assumed short.
Multiple consumers: load balancing (each message to one consumer — share the work) or fan‑out (each message to all consumers). Combine with consumer groups.
Acknowledgements: a client must ack processing; if the connection closes without ack, the broker redelivers. Combined with load balancing, redelivery can reorder messages.
Combine durable storage with low‑latency notification: a producer appends to the end of a log; a consumer reads it sequentially and waits for new messages (like tail -f).
Scale by partitioning the log across machines; within a partition, every message has a monotonically increasing offset; there’s no ordering across partitions. A topic is a group of partitions.
Examples: Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis Streams, Twitter’s DistributedLog. Throughput of millions of messages per second through partitioning and replication.
Fan‑out is trivial: consumers read independently without deleting. Load balancing assigns whole partitions to consumers within a group.
Downsides: the number of consumers sharing a topic is at most the number of partitions; a slow message holds up its partition (head‑of‑line blocking).

Guideline: use JMS/AMQP style when messages are expensive to process, order doesn’t matter, and you want per‑message parallelism. Use log‑based when throughput is high, each message is fast to process and ordering matters.
Since partitions are read sequentially, the broker only needs each consumer’s current offset (similar to a replication log sequence number). Messages below it are processed.
If a consumer fails, another takes over from the last recorded offset; messages processed after that but before the offset was saved will be seen twice.
The log is divided into segments; old segments are deleted or archived — it’s effectively a large bounded buffer on disk (a circular buffer).
Back‑of‑envelope: a 6 TB disk written at 150 MB/s fills in about 11 hours, so a log typically holds several days or weeks of messages.
Throughput is constant regardless of history, since every message is written to disk anyway.
If a consumer falls behind beyond retention, it misses messages — but that only affects that consumer, so monitor lag.
Replaying old messages is easy: reading is non‑destructive, so you can reprocess from an earlier offset — great for experimentation and recovery, like batch processing.

cards.t: Databases and streams: keeping systems in sync
b: Apps often combine an OLTP DB, cache, search index and warehouse, each needing its own copy of the data.

Dual writes (app code writes to each system) have problems: race conditions can leave two systems permanently inconsistent (writes interleave in different orders); one write may succeed and the other fail (an atomic commit problem).
Better: make one system the leader and others followers of its change log.
CDC observes all data changes written to a database and extracts them in a form other systems can replicate — making the DB the leader and derived systems (search index, cache, warehouse) followers.

Implementations: database triggers (fragile, overhead) or parsing the replication log. Examples: LinkedIn’s Databus, Facebook’s Wormhole, Yahoo’s Sherpa, Bottled Water (PostgreSQL), Maxwell and Debezium (MySQL binlog), Mongoriver (MongoDB), Oracle GoldenGate.
CDC is usually asynchronous: the DB doesn’t wait for consumers, so lag issues apply.
Initial snapshot: a new derived system needs a full copy first, corresponding to a known position in the change log.
Log compaction: keep only the latest value per key (with tombstones for deletes). Then the log contains a full copy of the DB and a new consumer can start at offset 0. Kafka supports this.
Some DBs now offer change streams as a first‑class API (RethinkDB, Firebase, CouchDB, Meteor, VoltDB). Kafka Connect integrates CDC tools with Kafka.
Developed in the domain‑driven design community. Store all changes to application state as a log of immutable events, at the level of the application (not the DB’s low‑level changes).
Events reflect intentions (‘student cancelled course enrolment’) rather than mechanics (‘row deleted from enrolments’). Makes evolving the app, debugging and guarding against bugs easier.
To serve reads, derive the current state from the event log. Log compaction isn’t possible in the same way, since later events don’t override earlier ones; snapshots help performance.
Commands vs events: a user request is a command that may fail validation. Once validated and accepted, it becomes an event — a durable, immutable fact. Consumers can’t reject an event.
Event sourcing is similar to the chronicle data model and fact tables in star schemas.
Mutable state and an append‑only log of immutable events don’t contradict each other: the state is the integral of the event stream over time; the change stream is the derivative of the state.
As the saying goes: the log is the truth; the database is a cache of a subset of the log.
Accountants have used this for centuries: a ledger appends transactions; mistakes are corrected by adding a compensating entry, not erasing.
Advantages: easier recovery from buggy code; more information captured (e.g. a customer adding then removing an item from their cart — useful for analytics).

Command query responsibility segregation (CQRS): separate how data is written (the event log) from how it’s read (multiple read‑optimised views derived from it). Normalization debates become moot — you can denormalize views freely.
Concurrency control becomes simpler: one event encapsulates a user action, and events for a partition can be processed serially.

Limitations: datasets with high churn may grow huge; sometimes data must truly be deleted for legal reasons (privacy regulations) — ‘excision’ (Datomic) or ‘shunning’ (Fossil), which is hard because copies live in many places.
Write events to a DB/cache/search index; push them to users (alerts, dashboards); or process input streams into output streams (pipelines of operators/jobs).
Complex event processing (CEP): search for patterns of events using a high‑level declarative query — queries are stored long‑term and events flow past them (Esper, IBM InfoSphere Streams, Apama).

Stream analytics: aggregations and statistics over windows — rates, rolling averages, trend comparisons. Probabilistic algorithms (Bloom filters, HyperLogLog, percentile estimators) save memory. Frameworks: Storm, Spark Streaming, Flink, Concord, Samza, Kafka Streams; hosted Google Cloud Dataflow, Azure Stream Analytics.
Maintaining materialized views: keeping derived data (caches, indexes, warehouses) up to date — may need all events over all time, not just a window.
Search on streams: store queries and match each document as it arrives (e.g. alerts for new property listings; Elasticsearch’s percolator).
Message passing and RPC (actor frameworks) are similar but mostly for concurrency management rather than data management.
Batch jobs use the event timestamps in the data. Many stream frameworks use the local system clock (processing time) — fine only if the delay between event and processing is negligible.

Event time vs processing time: delays from queueing, network faults, consumer restarts or reprocessing can make them diverge. A restarted processor may then see a spike in request rate that never happened.
Stragglers: you can never be sure all events for a window have arrived. Either ignore them (and monitor how many are dropped) or publish a correction later.

Whose clock? A mobile device may buffer events offline for hours, and its clock may be wrong. Fix: log three timestamps — when the event occurred (device clock), when it was sent (device clock), and when the server received it (server clock). The difference between the last two estimates the device clock offset.
Tumbling window: fixed length, every event belongs to exactly one window (e.g. each minute).
Hopping window: fixed length but windows overlap to give smoothing (e.g. 5‑minute windows with a 1‑minute hop).
Sliding window: contains all events within some interval of each other (e.g. any events within 5 minutes), implemented by keeping a sorted buffer and removing expired events.
Session window: no fixed duration; groups all events from the same user that occur close together, ending when the user is inactive for a while (e.g. 30 minutes) — common in website analytics.

Stream‑stream join (window join): e.g. match searches with clicks on results within an hour, to compute click‑through rates. The processor maintains state of recent events indexed by session ID and emits a ‘clicked’ or ‘not clicked’ event when the window expires.

Stream‑table join (stream enrichment): enrich activity events with user profile info. Rather than querying a remote DB per event, load a local copy of the DB into the processor and keep it updated via change data capture.

Table‑table join (materialized view maintenance): e.g. keep a Twitter home timeline cache up to date from streams of tweets and follow/unfollow events — equivalent to continuously maintaining a join query.

Time dependence: if state changes over time (e.g. tax rates), which version do you join with? Ordering across streams is nondeterministic. In warehouses this is a slowly changing dimension (SCD), often solved with a unique ID for each version of the record.
Batch jobs can retry failed tasks with exactly‑once semantics for output. Streams never finish, so it’s harder.
Microbatching: break the stream into small blocks (~1 second, as in Spark Streaming) and treat each like a batch. Tumbling windows by processing time are implicit.
Checkpointing: Flink periodically generates rolling checkpoints of state, triggered by barriers in the message stream; on crash, restart from the latest checkpoint.
Both give exactly‑once within the framework, but output that leaves the processor (DB writes, emails) may happen twice on retry.

Atomic commit: make all outputs and side effects happen only if processing succeeds — used internally in Google Cloud Dataflow, VoltDB, and Kafka’s transaction support. Kept within the system, not heterogeneous XA.

Idempotence: design operations so applying them multiple times has the same effect, e.g. store the message offset alongside the written value to detect duplicates. Requires deterministic replay, same message order, and fencing against zombie nodes.

Rebuilding state after failure: keep state in a remote datastore (slow), local state replicated (Flink snapshots to durable storage; Samza and Kafka Streams send changes to a dedicated Kafka topic with log compaction), or rebuild from input streams.

qs.q: What’s an event in stream processing?
o: A small, self‑contained, immutable record of something that happened
qs.e: Usually with a timestamp.

qs.q: Which is NOT an option when producers outpace consumers?
qs.e: Unix pipes and TCP use backpressure.

qs.q: Traditional JMS/AMQP brokers typically…
o: Delete messages once delivered and acknowledged
qs.e: They aren’t meant for long‑term storage.

qs.q: Load balancing vs fan‑out:
o: Load balancing sends each message to one consumer; fan‑out sends each to all
qs.e: Consumer groups combine the two.

qs.q: Why can redelivery reorder messages in a traditional broker?
o: With load balancing, an unacknowledged message is redelivered to another consumer after later messages were processed
qs.e: Use a separate queue per consumer to avoid it.

qs.q: In a log‑based broker like Kafka, what defines order?
o: Offsets within a partition; no ordering across partitions
qs.e: A topic is a group of partitions.

qs.q: What’s a downside of log‑based brokers for load balancing?
o: Consumers sharing a topic can’t exceed the number of partitions, and a slow message blocks its partition
qs.e: Head‑of‑line blocking within a partition.

qs.q: When is a log‑based broker the better choice?
o: Messages are expensive to process and order doesn’t matter
High throughput, fast per‑message processing, and ordering matters
qs.e: JMS/AMQP fits expensive, order‑insensitive work.

qs.q: What does the broker track per consumer in a log‑based system?
qs.e: Like a replication log sequence number.

qs.q: Roughly how long would a 6 TB disk last at 150 MB/s?
qs.e: In practice logs often keep days or weeks of messages since writes aren’t always at full bandwidth.

qs.q: Why is replaying messages easy in log‑based brokers?
o: Reading doesn’t delete messages; you can restart from an earlier offset
qs.e: Great for experiments and recovering from bugs.

qs.q: What’s wrong with dual writes to a DB and a search index?
o: Race conditions can permanently desynchronise them, and one write can fail while the other succeeds
qs.e: Better: derive the index from the DB’s change log.

qs.q: Change data capture makes the database…
o: The leader, with derived systems as followers of its change stream
qs.e: Typically by parsing the replication log.

qs.q: What does log compaction keep?
o: The latest value for each key (with tombstones for deletes)
qs.e: So the log becomes a full copy of the database.

qs.q: Event sourcing stores…
o: Application‑level immutable events reflecting user intent
qs.e: E.g. ‘student cancelled enrolment’ rather than ‘row deleted’.

qs.q: A command differs from an event because…
o: A command may still be rejected by validation; an event is an accepted, immutable fact
qs.e: Consumers can’t reject events.

qs.q: ‘State is the integral of the event stream’ means…
o: State is computed from accumulating all events over time
Events are derived from state only
qs.e: And the change stream is the derivative of state.

qs.q: What does CQRS separate?
o: The form in which data is written from the forms in which it’s read
qs.e: Many read‑optimised views can be derived from one event log.

qs.q: What’s a limitation of immutable event logs?
o: Some data must be truly deleted for legal/privacy reasons, which is hard
qs.e: Datomic calls it excision; Fossil calls it shunning.

qs.q: Complex event processing (CEP) stores…
o: Queries long‑term, with events flowing past them to match patterns
qs.e: The reverse of a normal database.

qs.q: Why can using processing time cause a fake spike in request rate?
o: A restarted processor catches up on a backlog, so many old events look like they happened now
qs.e: Use event time when it matters.

qs.q: How do you estimate a mobile device’s clock offset?
o: Compare the device’s send time with the server’s receive time
qs.e: Log occurred, sent and received timestamps.

qs.q: Which window type groups a user’s events until they’re inactive for a while?
qs.e: Common in website analytics.

qs.q: 5‑minute windows that advance every 1 minute are…
qs.e: Tumbling windows don’t overlap.

qs.q: Matching searches with later clicks is a…
qs.e: State is kept for a time window, indexed by session ID.

qs.q: Best way to enrich events with user profile data in a stream processor?
o: Query the remote DB per event
Keep a local copy of the profile DB updated via change data capture
qs.e: Avoids network round trips per event.

qs.q: How does Flink achieve fault tolerance?
o: Periodic checkpoints triggered by barriers in the stream
qs.e: Spark Streaming uses microbatching instead.

qs.q: How can a stream processor make writes to an external DB safe on retry?
o: Make them idempotent, e.g. store the message offset with the write to detect duplicates
qs.e: Requires deterministic replay and fencing against zombies.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your search index sometimes shows a product’s old price forever, because the app writes to the DB and Elasticsearch separately. Fix?
o: Feed Elasticsearch from the DB’s change data capture stream
qs.e: One leader, ordered changes, followers derived from it.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you need to rebuild a new recommendation view from all historical data in Kafka. What makes this possible?
o: A log‑based broker with long retention or log compaction, so you can replay from offset 0
qs.e: Reading is non‑destructive in log‑based brokers.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a fraud system processing transactions in strict order, at 1M msgs/s, each processed in microseconds. JMS‑style or log‑based broker?
qs.e: High throughput and per‑key ordering are log‑based strengths.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a mobile game’s per‑minute event counts are wrong because phones upload events hours late. What’s the fix?
o: Window by event time, adjust device clock offsets, and handle stragglers with corrections
qs.e: Log occurred, sent and received times; decide how to handle late events.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your stream job crashes and on restart emails some customers twice. Why, and what helps?
o: Side effects outside the framework were repeated on replay; use idempotent sends (dedup by ID) or atomic commit of outputs
qs.e: Exactly‑once inside the framework doesn’t cover external effects.

chapters.title: The Future of Data Systems
chapters.blurb: Putting it all together: integrating systems through dataflow, unbundling databases, building correct systems end to end, and the ethics of data.

b: For any given problem there are several solutions with different trade‑offs, and no single tool fits every access pattern. Complex apps combine several.
Figure out the dataflows: where data is written first and which representations are derived from where.
If all writes go through a single system of record and other representations derive from it via change data capture in the same order, they stay consistent. Event sourcing works similarly.

Derived data vs distributed transactions: both keep systems in sync. Transactions offer linearizability (read your writes) but are hard to make fault‑tolerant across heterogeneous systems; log‑based derived data is asynchronous but more robust and better at integrating diverse systems.

Limits of total ordering: a single leader for the log can’t scale indefinitely; multiple datacenters and microservices lack one total order; offline clients and widely distributed events make it impossible. Causality can still be captured with techniques like logical timestamps.
Both produce derived datasets from inputs (search indexes, recommendation systems, analytics). The lines are blurring: Spark does streams via microbatches; Flink does batch on a streaming engine.
Reprocessing existing data to maintain a system as it evolves — batch can reprocess historical data, streams handle new changes.

Schema migrations can be gradual: maintain old and new schemas side by side as two independently derived views, shift users gradually, and roll back at any time — like the old railway gauge conversions where dual‑gauge track allowed both trains.

Lambda architecture: record immutable events and run batch (e.g. Hadoop) and stream (e.g. Storm) systems in parallel — the stream gives a quick approximate view, the batch a later correct one. Problems: maintaining the same logic twice, merging outputs, and expensive full reprocessing.
Unifying them (sometimes called kappa architecture) needs: replaying historical events through the same stream engine, exactly‑once semantics, and windowing by event time rather than processing time.

Unix and relational databases tackled information management with different philosophies: Unix gives low‑level abstractions (files, pipes); databases give high‑level ones (SQL, transactions) that hide complexity.

Database features like secondary indexes, materialized views, replication logs and full‑text search indexes are similar to what we build with batch and stream processors when we derive data across systems.

Composing storage technologies: two approaches. Federated databases (unifying reads, ‘polystore’): one query interface over many storage engines. Unbundled databases (unifying writes): reliably plugging systems together via change data capture and event logs — like Unix pipes for data.
Asynchronous event logs with idempotent writes are more robust than distributed transactions across heterogeneous systems: failures stay local, and teams can work independently.
Unbundling isn’t about beating single databases on performance — it’s about breadth: combining several tools for diverse workloads. If one tool does everything you need, use it.
‘Database inside‑out’: think of an app as a set of derivation functions that transform data — like a spreadsheet, where changing one cell recalculates everything depending on it.
Derivation functions: secondary indexes, full‑text indexes, ML models, caches — some generic and built into DBs, others application‑specific code.

Separation of application code and state: keep stateless app code (easy to deploy and scale) separate from state in databases, as is common — but instead of a DB as a passive variable that apps poll, subscribe to changes (observers).

Stream processors and services: an order service needing currency conversion could query an exchange‑rate service synchronously, or subscribe to a stream of rate updates and keep a local copy — replacing a network request with a local lookup. Faster and more robust to the other service failing.
Time‑dependence matters: when reprocessing, decide whether to use the rate at purchase time.

cards.t: Observing derived state: write path & read path
b: Write path: the part of the dataflow precomputed eagerly when data comes in (e.g. updating a search index). Read path: work done lazily only when someone asks (searching the index).
A derived dataset is where the two paths meet — a trade‑off between work at write time and at read time. Indexes, caches and materialized views shift the boundary.
Twitter timelines again: fan‑out on write for most users, read‑time merges for celebrities — moving the boundary per user.
Stateful, offline‑capable clients: a device’s on‑screen state is a cache/materialized view of server state.

Pushing state changes to clients: instead of polling, server‑sent events or WebSockets let the server push updates, extending the write path all the way to the end user. Clients reconnecting after offline catch up from their last offset.
Reads are events too: logging read requests as events gives better tracking of causal dependencies (what the user saw when making a decision) at storage cost.
We want applications that are reliable and correct even with faults. Transactions have been the traditional tool, but they’re not the only way, and they don’t cover everything.
Immutable, append‑only data makes it easier to recover from mistakes like bugs that delete data.
Exactly‑once (effectively‑once) processing: an operation retried after a fault should have the same final effect as if no fault occurred — idempotence is the key tool.
Duplicate suppression at one layer (e.g. TCP, or a DB transaction) doesn’t prevent duplicates across the whole chain: a user may click submit twice, or a client may retry after a timeout.
Fix: generate a unique operation ID (e.g. a UUID in the client form) and pass it end to end; the DB enforces a uniqueness constraint on that ID, so duplicates are rejected.

End‑to‑end argument (Saltzer, Reed and Clark, 1984): some functions can only be implemented correctly with the knowledge of the endpoints. Low‑level reliability features help performance but aren’t sufficient — the app needs its own end‑to‑end checks (e.g. end‑to‑end encryption, checksums).

Uniqueness constraints need consensus — but a log can provide it: partition the log by the value that must be unique (e.g. username hash). A single‑threaded processor per partition decides which request came first and accepts or rejects it.
This scales by increasing partitions and is the same idea as total order broadcast.

Multi‑partition operations without atomic commit: e.g. a money transfer touching payer account, payee account and request ID. Append the request (with a unique ID) to one log partition; a processor emits debit and credit instructions to the relevant partitions, deduplicated by request ID. If it crashes, it reprocesses from its checkpoint, emitting the same deterministic instructions.
Splitting a transaction into stages with a durable log achieves correctness without distributed transactions.
‘Consistency’ conflates two requirements.
Timeliness: users observe the system in an up‑to‑date state. Violations are temporary — wait and retry (eventual consistency). Linearizability is a strong way to get it.
Integrity: no corruption, no contradictory or false data; derived data is accurate. Violations are permanent and need explicit repair.
In most applications integrity matters far more: a slow credit card transaction showing up later is fine; a wrong balance or vanishing money is not.
Event‑based dataflow systems decouple the two: they provide integrity (via immutable events, deterministic derivations, idempotence and end‑to‑end request IDs) without requiring timeliness.

Many real apps accept temporary constraint violations and fix them with apologies: overbooked flights, out‑of‑stock items, double‑booked rooms are already handled by compensating transactions (refunds, vouchers, apologies) because real life involves human error anyway.
So strict synchronous constraint checking isn’t always required; check optimistically and fix later.

Coordination‑avoiding data systems: preserve integrity without atomic commit or linearizability, so they can run across datacenters with asynchronous multi‑leader replication and better performance and availability.
Synchronous coordination can still be used where needed, at a smaller scope than distributing transactions everywhere.

System models assume certain things don’t happen (e.g. data on disk isn’t corrupted). In reality, hardware and software both fail in unlikely ways: random bit flips, rowhammer (memory access patterns flipping bits in adjacent rows), and bugs even in mature databases (MySQL failed to correctly maintain uniqueness constraints; PostgreSQL’s serializable isolation had write‑skew anomalies).
Application code is even buggier. Weak isolation and misuse of transactions are common.

Don’t just blindly trust that what you’re promised works: audit. Check data integrity regularly (e.g. HDFS and Amazon S3 read back and compare replicas in the background; test backups by restoring them).
Design for auditability: event logs make provenance clear, and deterministic derivations can be rerun to verify.
End‑to‑end integrity checks across the whole pipeline give confidence, and help you move faster.
Cryptographic tools: Merkle trees and certificate transparency allow tamper‑evident verifiable logs; blockchain ideas exist, though costly.

cards.t: Doing the right thing: predictive analytics
b: Every system is built for a purpose with consequences beyond its intended use. Data is about people — their behaviour, interests and identity. Treat it with humanity and respect.

Predictive analytics decides about loans, insurance, hiring and policing. Algorithms can systematically exclude people from jobs, flights, insurance or property — an ‘algorithmic prison’ with no due process.

Bias and discrimination: algorithms learn patterns from biased data and can amplify them; even if protected traits are excluded, correlated proxies (e.g. postcode) leak them. Predictive analytics extrapolates from the past; if the past was discriminatory, it codifies that.
Responsibility and accountability: who’s responsible when an algorithm makes a mistake? Decisions should be explainable and appealable.
Feedback loops: e.g. a bad credit score leads to worse jobs, which leads to worse scores — a downward spiral. Use systems thinking to understand how a system interacts with society.

When users enter data deliberately, the system serves them. When it tracks behaviour as a side effect, the relationship changes — especially when funded by advertising, where users are no longer the customer.
Thought experiment: replace the word ‘data’ with ‘surveillance’ and see how phrases sound (‘surveillance‑driven organisation’, ‘real‑time surveillance streams’).

Consent and freedom of choice: users rarely understand what data they give or how it’s used; privacy policies obscure more than they reveal; for widely used services, opting out isn’t a realistic choice (social cost).
Privacy doesn’t mean keeping everything secret — it’s the freedom to choose what to reveal to whom. Surveillance transfers that right from individuals to companies.
Data as assets and power: data is valuable, which creates incentives to collect more and risks of leaks, insider abuse or misuse by future regimes. Some call it a toxic asset or hazardous material.

Like the Industrial Revolution’s pollution and labour abuses, which took regulation to fix, the information age needs better norms. Build with a culture of respect: purge data when no longer needed, collect only what’s required, and consider legislation and self‑regulation.
We engineers should build a world worth living in — treating people as humans, not metrics to optimise.

qs.q: What’s the most robust way to keep a DB, cache and search index consistent?
o: A single system of record with others derived via its ordered change log
qs.e: Same order of writes means consistent derived views.

qs.q: Distributed transactions vs log‑based derived data:
o: Transactions give linearizable reads but are fragile across heterogeneous systems; logs are async but more robust
qs.e: The author leans toward logs for integrating diverse systems.

qs.q: Why can’t you always have a single total order of events?
o: A single leader can’t scale indefinitely; multi‑datacenter, microservices and offline clients break it
qs.e: Capturing causality is the more achievable goal.

qs.q: What’s the railway‑gauge analogy about?
o: Gradual schema migrations: run old and new derived views side by side and migrate users gradually
qs.e: Every stage is reversible.

qs.q: What’s a key problem with the lambda architecture?
o: Maintaining the same logic in two systems and merging their outputs
qs.e: Unifying batch and stream in one engine addresses this.

qs.q: Which is NOT required to unify batch and stream processing?
o: Replaying historical events through the same engine
qs.e: Event time is needed for correct reprocessing of history.

qs.q: Federated databases unify ___; unbundled databases unify ___.
qs.e: Federation offers one query interface; unbundling plugs systems together via logs.

qs.q: Why are async event logs with idempotent writes more robust than distributed transactions?
o: Failures stay local instead of spreading, and teams can work independently
qs.e: Loose coupling at the system level.

qs.q: ‘Database inside‑out’ means thinking of an app as…
o: Derivation functions over data, like a spreadsheet recalculating dependent cells
qs.e: Subscribe to changes rather than poll.

qs.q: Why subscribe to an exchange‑rate stream rather than query a rate service?
o: It turns a network request into a local lookup — faster and resilient if the rate service fails
qs.e: Dataflow replaces synchronous dependencies.

qs.q: What’s the write path vs read path?
o: Work done eagerly when data arrives vs lazily when someone queries
qs.e: Indexes, caches and views shift the boundary.

qs.q: Pushing updates to clients via WebSockets does what?
o: Extends the write path all the way to the end user’s device
qs.e: The client’s state is a materialized view of server state.

qs.q: Why doesn’t TCP’s duplicate suppression make an app exactly‑once?
o: Duplicates can occur at other layers, e.g. a user double‑clicking or a client retrying after timeout
qs.e: Only end‑to‑end request IDs suppress duplicates across the whole chain.

qs.q: The end‑to‑end argument says…
o: Some functions can only be done correctly with knowledge at the endpoints; low‑level features help but aren’t sufficient
qs.e: From Saltzer, Reed and Clark (1984).

qs.q: How can a log enforce unique usernames without distributed transactions?
o: Partition by username hash; a single‑threaded processor per partition accepts the first claim and rejects later ones
qs.e: Equivalent to total order broadcast per partition.

qs.q: How does a money transfer work across partitions without atomic commit?
o: Append the request with a unique ID to a log; a processor emits deterministic debit/credit instructions deduplicated by that ID
qs.e: Splitting into stages with durable logs gives correctness.

qs.q: Timeliness violations are ___; integrity violations are ___.
qs.e: That’s why integrity matters much more in most apps.

qs.q: Which matters more for a bank?
o: Integrity: balances must never be wrong
qs.e: A pending transaction appearing later is fine; money vanishing isn’t.

qs.q: What are ‘apologies’ in the context of constraints?
o: Compensating actions (refunds, vouchers) when a constraint is temporarily violated
qs.e: Overbooking is already handled this way in real business.

qs.q: Coordination‑avoiding systems aim to…
o: Preserve integrity without atomic commit or linearizability, gaining performance and availability
qs.e: Synchronous coordination is used only where truly needed.

qs.q: What is rowhammer?
o: Memory access patterns flipping bits in adjacent DRAM rows
qs.e: An example of why you should verify, not blindly trust, data.

qs.q: ‘Trust, but verify’ in data systems means…
o: Regularly audit data integrity, e.g. reading back replicas and test‑restoring backups
qs.e: Event logs and deterministic derivations make audits easier.

qs.q: What’s the risk of predictive analytics trained on past data?
o: It can codify and amplify past discrimination, even via proxy variables
qs.e: Excluding protected traits isn’t enough when proxies leak them.

qs.q: What’s an ‘algorithmic prison’?
o: Being systematically excluded from jobs, insurance or services by algorithms, with no recourse
qs.e: Decisions should be explainable and appealable.

qs.q: Replacing ‘data’ with ‘surveillance’ in phrases is meant to…
o: Highlight how pervasive tracking looks from the user’s perspective
qs.e: A thought experiment about the relationship between services and users.

qs.q: Privacy is best described as…
o: The freedom to choose what to reveal, and to whom
qs.e: Surveillance transfers that choice from individuals to companies.

qs.q: Boss scenario: an e‑commerce site sometimes creates two orders when users double‑click ‘Buy’ on a slow network. Robust fix?
o: Generate a unique request ID in the client and enforce uniqueness on it in the DB
qs.e: Disabling the button helps UX, but only an end‑to‑end ID suppresses all duplicates.

qs.q: Boss scenario: you must migrate a huge table to a new schema with zero risk. Dataflow‑style approach?
o: One big migration over a weekend
Derive a new view from the same event log alongside the old one, shift traffic gradually, and keep rollback
qs.e: Gradual, reversible migration through derived views.

qs.q: Boss scenario: a hotel booking system across regions occasionally double‑books, and a manager proposes global 2PC. Alternative?
o: Accept and add apologies/compensation for rare cases, or route each room’s bookings through one log partition
qs.e: Integrity can be preserved with partitioned logs; rare conflicts can be compensated.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your team builds a hiring model that excludes candidates by postcode. What’s the ethical problem?
o: Postcode can be a proxy for race or class, encoding discrimination
qs.e: Consider bias, accountability, and feedback loops.

qs.q: Boss scenario: your app stores detailed location history ‘just in case’. What does the book recommend?
o: Collect only what’s needed, purge it when no longer needed, and treat it as a hazardous asset
qs.e: Data can leak, be misused internally, or fall into the hands of future regimes.

chapters.title: MongoDB SDE3 interview track
chapters.blurb: Every DDIA idea mapped to how MongoDB actually implements it, pitched at a mid‑level (SDE3) loop: explain the mechanism clearly, name the trade‑off, and know what happens when it fails.

b: SDE3 is mid‑level: you’re expected to explain mechanisms precisely and reason about trade‑offs, not set company‑wide strategy.
Strong answers link the book concept to the MongoDB feature: “a replica set is single‑leader replication; w:majority is a quorum write.”
Always say what you gain, what you pay, and one failure mode. Example: secondary reads scale reads but can return stale data.
Know your own debugging path: explain(), checking indexes, reading the logs, measuring p99 client‑side.
Version details change; MongoDB 9.0 shipped in September 2026. Skim current docs before the interview rather than memorising numbers.
MongoDB bets on locality: data read together is stored together in one BSON document (16 MB max).
Embedding fits one‑to‑many trees loaded together. Referencing fits shared or unbounded data (many‑to‑one, many‑to‑many).
$lookup gives left‑outer joins in aggregation; $graphLookup does recursive traversal like a graph query.
Schema is on‑read by default; $jsonSchema validation adds schema‑on‑write per collection (validationLevel strict/moderate, validationAction error/warn).
Rule of thumb: model for how the app reads, then check write cost, growth and consistency needs.
Subset: embed the recent N items, keep the rest elsewhere — bounded documents, smaller working set.
Bucket: one document per time period of events — fewer index entries, better compression (time series collections automate it).
Extended reference: copy a few hot fields from a referenced document to avoid a join (selective denormalization).
Outlier: handle the rare huge document separately — the document version of a hot key.
Computed: precompute aggregates at write time — moving work from the read path to the write path.
Schema versioning: a version field plus lazy migration — data outlives code.
Default engine: a B‑tree engine. Each collection and each index is its own B‑tree table.
MVCC: keeps multiple versions in cache so readers get a snapshot without blocking writers.
Document‑level concurrency: writers to the same document conflict; a WriteConflict is retried internally outside transactions.
Cache defaults to roughly 50% of (RAM − 1 GB). If eviction falls behind, app threads help evict — visible as p99 latency spikes.
Durability: journal (write‑ahead log) plus checkpoints about every 60 s; recovery = last checkpoint + journal replay.
Compression: snappy by default for data (zstd/zlib optional), prefix compression for indexes.
Why B‑tree not LSM: read‑heavy point and range lookups, predictable latency, each key in one place.
Types: single, compound, multikey (one entry per array element), unique, partial, sparse, TTL, hashed, 2dsphere, text, wildcard; Atlas Search and Vector Search run separately.
ESR rule for compound indexes: Equality fields first, then Sort, then Range. It follows from B‑tree ordering: equality narrows to a contiguous run, sort comes free, range scans inside it.
Every index slows every write (write amplification) and uses cache.
Diagnose with explain("executionStats"): compare keys examined, docs examined and docs returned; look for COLLSCAN and in‑memory SORT.
Covered query: all needed fields are in the index, so documents aren’t fetched.
BSON = typed binary JSON: int32, int64, double, Decimal128, Date, ObjectId, binary. Fixes JSON’s number and binary problems, but stores field names in every document.
ObjectId (12 bytes) starts with a timestamp, so it’s roughly increasing — a hot spot as a ranged shard key.
Rolling upgrades: secondaries first, step down the primary, upgrade it. Feature compatibility version (FCV) holds back new on‑disk formats until all nodes are upgraded, so you can still downgrade.
Stable API lets apps pin an API version so server upgrades don’t break them.
Prefer update operators ($set) over full‑document replace so old app versions don’t drop fields they don’t know.
Single‑leader: one primary takes writes; secondaries replicate. Up to 50 members, at most 7 voting.
Member options: priority 0, hidden, delayed, arbiter (votes, no data — discouraged).
Oplog (local.oplog.rs): a capped collection holding a logical log. Entries are idempotent — an $inc is stored as the resulting $set — so re‑applying is safe.
Secondaries pull oplog batches from a sync source (chaining allowed) and apply them in parallel while keeping per‑document order.
Initial sync = copy all data + apply oplog from the start point (snapshot + log position).
Oplog window: if a secondary falls behind the oldest entry, it must fully resync. Size the oplog for your longest maintenance window.
Heartbeats every 2 s; if the primary is unreachable for electionTimeoutMillis (10 s default), a secondary calls an election.
Raft‑style: each election increments a term; voters only vote for candidates whose oplog is at least as current as theirs.
A primary that can’t see a majority steps down by itself.
Rollback: writes on an old primary that never reached a majority are undone when it rejoins (recover to the majority point; data saved to rollback files).
Key line for interviews: w:"majority" writes are never rolled back; w:1 writes can be.
A two‑node set can’t fail over: losing either node loses the majority.
w:0 — no acknowledgement. w:1 — primary applied it (can be rolled back).
w:"majority" — a majority of voting members have it; journaled by default. The default for most deployments since 5.0.
w:<n> or tag sets — e.g. require one copy per region.
j:true — wait for the on‑disk journal.
wtimeout — stop waiting; the write may still succeed later. A timeout is an unknown outcome, not a failure.
Primary‑secondary‑arbiter sets: if the secondary is down, majority writes can’t be acknowledged.
local — this node’s latest data, may be rolled back. available — similar, fastest on sharded clusters, may include orphans.
majority — only majority‑committed data. Durable, but a lagging secondary can still return older data.
linearizable — primary only, confirms it’s still primary via a majority round trip; slow; single‑document reads.
snapshot — a consistent point‑in‑time view (used in transactions).
Read preference: primary, primaryPreferred, secondary, secondaryPreferred, nearest; tag sets; maxStalenessSeconds to bound lag.
Secondary reads bring back DDIA’s lag anomalies; causally consistent sessions fix them per client.
Components: shards (each a replica set), mongos routers, and a config server replica set holding the routing table.
Ranged sharding keeps adjacent keys together (good range queries, hot‑spot risk). Hashed sharding spreads monotonic keys (no range queries on that key).
Targeted queries include the shard key and hit one or few shards. Without it, mongos scatters to all shards and waits for the slowest (tail latency amplification).
Secondary indexes are local to each shard (document‑partitioned). So a unique index must be prefixed by the shard key.
Zones pin key ranges to specific shards, e.g. EU users on EU hardware.
High cardinality: many distinct values so data can split finely.
Low frequency: no single value owns a big share of documents (else jumbo chunks).
Non‑monotonic, or hashed: otherwise all inserts hit the top range.
Matches the main queries so most of them target one shard.
Common good choice: compound like {tenantId: 1, orderId: 1}; or hashed on a high‑cardinality ID when you don’t need range scans on it.
Fixes later: refine the key by adding suffix fields, or reshard live to a new key.
Data is split into contiguous key ranges (chunks), default target 128 MB in recent versions — DDIA’s dynamic partitioning.
The balancer moves ranges between shards; recent versions balance by data size. Balancing windows keep migrations out of peak hours.
Migration: copy documents, stream ongoing changes, brief critical section blocking writes to that range, commit new owner on the config server, delete old copy later.
Leftover copies are orphan documents — why ‘available’ read concern can return them.
mongos caches routing info with a version; a shard with a newer version rejects the request, mongos refreshes and retries — versioned metadata acting like a fencing token.
Jumbo chunk: too many documents share one shard key value, so it can’t split or move. Fix by adding cardinality to the key.
Single‑document writes are always atomic; operators like $inc, $push and findAndModify avoid most lost updates.
Multi‑document transactions: replica sets since 4.0, sharded clusters since 4.2.
Isolation is snapshot isolation: no dirty reads, no read skew, same‑document conflicts abort one writer — but write skew is possible.
Prevent write skew by making both transactions write a shared document (materialize the conflict) or by a unique index.
TransientTransactionError → retry the whole transaction. UnknownTransactionCommitResult → retry commit (it’s idempotent). withTransaction() does both.
Cross‑shard transactions use two‑phase commit; the coordinator’s decision is stored in its replica set, so one machine failing doesn’t leave others stuck.
Default lifetime 60 s. Long transactions pin old versions in cache and hurt everyone — keep them short.
Election timeout trade‑off: lower = faster failover but more false elections under jitter or load.
Two nodes may briefly both think they’re primary; only the newer term can get majority acknowledgements, so majority writes stay safe.
Election terms act as fencing tokens: messages from older terms are rejected.
MongoDB doesn’t order operations by wall clocks; it uses cluster time, a hybrid logical clock (wall time + counter, take the max seen).
mongod is C++ (no GC pauses), but OS stalls, disk stalls, eviction stalls and VM migration still pause it.
A network error after sending a write = unknown outcome. Retryable writes resend with the same session and transaction number so the server applies it once.
Replication protocol is a Raft variant: terms, voting rules, majority commit point. Differences: secondaries pull the oplog, chaining allowed, priorities, a catch‑up phase for new primaries.
The oplog is total order broadcast: every secondary applies the same operations in the same order.
Majority commit point: the latest oplog position known to be on a majority.

Causally consistent sessions carry operationTime and clusterTime; a secondary waits until it has caught up before answering. With majority concerns you get read‑your‑writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes and writes‑follow‑reads.
No ZooKeeper: consensus is built into each replica set; the config server replica set holds sharding metadata.

CP or AP? With majority writes, the minority side can’t accept writes during a partition (consistency). Clients can trade toward availability per operation with w:1 and secondary reads. CAP is too coarse — describe the settings.
Change streams expose the oplog as a CDC API for a collection, database or cluster, in replication order.
Only majority‑committed changes are emitted, so consumers never act on rolled‑back data.
Resume tokens are consumer offsets. If the oplog has moved past a token, you can’t resume and must re‑snapshot.
On sharded clusters mongos merges per‑shard streams in cluster‑time order.
Feeding search, caches or Kafka from change streams beats dual writes, which can drift permanently.
Aggregation pipeline = declarative dataflow ($match, $group, $lookup, $merge…). The optimizer reorders stages; sharded pipelines split into shard and merge parts. Map‑reduce is deprecated.
$merge into a collection gives incrementally maintained materialized views.
1) Requirements and load parameters (reads/s, writes/s, data size, growth, read/write ratio).
2) Data model: embed vs reference, patterns, document size limits.
3) Indexes: ESR, which queries are covered.
4) Replication and consistency: write concern, read concern, read preference, sessions.
5) Sharding: shard key, targeted vs scatter queries, hot keys.
6) Failure modes: failover, rollback, retries, idempotency keys.
7) Observability: p50/p99 measured client‑side, replication lag, cache eviction, oplog window.
Typical prompts: multi‑tenant SaaS, chat/feed, IoT telemetry with time series, order/payment service with idempotency.

qs.q: A replica set is which DDIA replication style?
qs.e: One primary takes writes; secondaries pull the oplog.

qs.q: How is an $inc recorded in the oplog?
o: As a $set of the resulting value, so re‑applying is safe
qs.e: Oplog entries are made idempotent.

qs.q: What happens to a w:1 write if the primary fails before replicating it?
o: It may be rolled back when the old primary rejoins
qs.e: Classic async‑failover lost write from DDIA ch. 5.

qs.q: Which writes are guaranteed never to be rolled back?
qs.e: Once on a majority, any electable primary has them.

qs.q: A w:"majority" write with wtimeout times out. What do you know?
o: Nothing definitive — it may still replicate; treat as unknown and keep it idempotent
qs.e: A timeout isn’t a failure signal.

qs.q: Since which version is majority the implicit default write concern for most deployments?
qs.e: Safer defaults; arbiter setups are an exception to watch.

qs.q: Why are arbiters discouraged?
o: In a primary‑secondary‑arbiter set, losing the secondary blocks majority writes
qs.e: The arbiter votes but holds no data to acknowledge writes.

qs.q: Default electionTimeoutMillis?
qs.e: Heartbeats are every 2 s.

qs.q: Which candidate can win a MongoDB election?
o: One whose oplog is at least as up to date as the voters’
qs.e: Raft’s election restriction, so majority‑committed writes aren’t lost.

qs.q: What plays the role of a fencing token in replica sets?
qs.e: Messages from older terms are rejected.

qs.q: A secondary falls behind the oldest oplog entry. What must happen?
qs.e: Size the oplog window for maintenance and outages.

qs.q: Can readConcern: majority return stale data?

qs.q: How is readConcern: linearizable made safe?
o: The primary confirms it’s still primary via a majority round trip before returning

qs.q: What do causally consistent sessions give you (with majority concerns)?
o: Read‑your‑writes, monotonic reads, monotonic writes, writes‑follow‑reads
qs.e: The session carries operationTime and clusterTime.

qs.q: Cluster time is a…
o: Hybrid logical clock: wall time plus a counter, advancing to the max seen

qs.q: Is MongoDB CP or AP — best answer?
o: With majority writes it favours consistency during partitions; clients can trade toward availability per operation; CAP is too coarse
qs.e: Describe the actual settings.

qs.q: WiredTiger’s main data structure is…
qs.e: Each collection and index is a B‑tree table.

qs.q: Why does WiredTiger use MVCC?
o: So readers see a snapshot without blocking writers
qs.e: Snapshot isolation at the engine level.

qs.q: Roughly how often does WiredTiger checkpoint?
qs.e: The journal covers changes between checkpoints.

qs.q: Latency spikes appear when WiredTiger…
o: Can’t evict dirty cache fast enough, so app threads help evict
qs.e: A common source of p99 problems.

qs.q: ESR rule order for a compound index?
qs.e: Follows from how B‑tree keys are ordered.

qs.q: In explain output, docs examined ≫ docs returned suggests…
o: A poorly selective or missing index
qs.e: Aim for keys examined ≈ docs returned.

qs.q: What’s a multikey index?
o: One index entry per array element
qs.e: Large arrays mean many entries and slower writes.

qs.q: Why is a ranged ObjectId shard key a bad idea?
o: ObjectIds increase over time, so all inserts hit the top range
qs.e: Monotonic key → hot spot. Hash it instead.

qs.q: Why must a unique index on a sharded collection include the shard key prefix?
o: Indexes are local per shard, so no shard can check global uniqueness alone
qs.e: Document‑partitioned secondary indexes (DDIA ch. 6).

qs.q: A query without the shard key on a 40‑shard cluster…
o: Is scattered to all shards; latency set by the slowest
qs.e: Tail latency amplification.

qs.q: What causes a jumbo chunk?
o: Too many documents sharing one shard key value, so the range can’t split
qs.e: Refine the shard key to add cardinality.

qs.q: How does mongos learn its routing table is stale?
o: The shard rejects the request’s older version; mongos refreshes and retries
qs.e: Versioned metadata acts like fencing.

qs.q: What are orphan documents?
o: Leftover copies on a shard after a range migrated away, before cleanup
qs.e: ‘available’ read concern can return them.

qs.q: Default target chunk size in recent versions?
qs.e: Check current docs; it has changed over versions.

qs.q: What isolation do MongoDB transactions provide?
qs.e: Write skew is still possible.

qs.q: How do you prevent write skew in MongoDB?
o: Make both transactions write a shared document, or use a unique index
qs.e: Materializing the conflict.

qs.q: On TransientTransactionError you should…
qs.e: withTransaction() does this for you.

qs.q: On UnknownTransactionCommitResult you should…
qs.e: The commit may have already succeeded.

qs.q: Why keep transactions short?
o: Long transactions pin old versions in cache, raising pressure for everyone; default limit is 60 s
qs.e: Model for single‑document atomicity first.

qs.q: How do cross‑shard transactions avoid 2PC’s coordinator blocking problem?
o: The coordinator’s decision is replicated in its replica set, so a new primary can finish it
qs.e: 2PC backed by consensus.

qs.q: What do retryable writes rely on?
o: A session ID plus transaction number so the server applies a retried write once
qs.e: Idempotence built into the driver protocol.

qs.q: What’s a change stream resume token?
o: A consumer offset into the oplog
qs.e: Store it to resume after a crash.

qs.q: Why do change streams only emit majority‑committed changes?
o: So consumers never act on data that gets rolled back
qs.e: Safety for downstream systems.

qs.q: What does FCV protect?
o: The ability to downgrade during a rolling upgrade, by holding back new formats
qs.e: Forward compatibility made explicit.

qs.q: Why prefer $set over replacing the whole document?
o: Old app versions won’t drop fields they don’t know about
qs.e: The unknown‑field round‑trip trap from ch. 4.

qs.q: Which pattern bounds a growing array of comments?
qs.e: Keeps documents small and the working set in RAM.

qs.q: Why does a two‑member replica set not fail over automatically?
o: Losing either member leaves no majority to elect a primary
qs.e: Use at least three voting members.

qs.q: Boss: a payment API retries after a network error and sometimes charges twice. What’s your fix on MongoDB?
o: An idempotency key stored with a unique index (plus retryable writes)
qs.e: End‑to‑end request IDs from DDIA ch. 12.

qs.q: Boss: users post a comment, refresh, and it’s missing. Reads go to secondaries. Smallest fix?
o: Use a causally consistent session (or read own data from the primary)
qs.e: Read‑your‑writes via sessions.

qs.q: Boss: multi‑tenant SaaS, one tenant is 70% of traffic and the shard key is {tenantId: 1}. What breaks and how do you fix it?
o: That tenant’s ranges become a hot shard; use a compound key like {tenantId, orderId} or hashed suffix, possibly a dedicated zone
qs.e: Hot key handling from ch. 6.

qs.q: Boss: an inventory transaction checks ‘stock ≥ 1’ then inserts an order; two run at once and stock goes negative. Why, and fix?
o: Write skew under snapshot isolation; have both update the same stock document (e.g. $inc with a filter)
qs.e: An atomic conditional update on the stock document is simplest.

qs.q: Boss: IoT devices send 200k readings/s; queries are ‘last 24 h for device X’. Design?
o: One doc per reading, ranged ObjectId shard key
Time series collection (bucketing), shard on device ID plus time, TTL for retention
qs.e: Bucket pattern, avoiding monotonic hot spots.

qs.q: Boss: your search index drifts from MongoDB because the app writes to both. Fix?
o: Feed the search index from change streams with stored resume tokens
qs.e: CDC instead of dual writes.

qs.q: Boss: p99 on a dashboard query jumped after the cluster grew from 4 to 32 shards. Likely cause?
o: The query lacks the shard key and scatters to all shards; tail latency amplification
qs.e: Add the shard key to the filter or redesign the key.

qs.q: Boss: the primary freezes for 30 s, wakes up and keeps accepting w:1 writes. What happens to them?
o: A new primary in a higher term exists; the old one steps down and its unreplicated writes are rolled back
qs.e: Majority writes would never have been acknowledged there.

chapters.title: Deep dive: replication & failover internals
chapters.blurb: The parts of replica sets that separate good answers from great ones: optimes, pre‑vote, catch‑up, safe reconfig, flow control, and how drivers find the primary.

b: Each oplog entry has a timestamp (ts) and the election term (t). Together they form an optime that orders every write in the set.
Each member tracks its last applied optime and last durable (journaled) optime and reports them to others via heartbeats and replication progress updates.
The primary computes the majority commit point: the newest optime that a majority of voting members have durably written. It is gossiped to secondaries.
Majority reads are served from a storage snapshot at the commit point, using WiredTiger timestamps.
Idle sets still advance: the primary writes periodic no‑op oplog entries so optimes, lag metrics and the commit point keep moving.

Dry‑run (pre‑vote) election: a candidate first asks whether it would win without bumping the term. This avoids term inflation from a node that’s partitioned and keeps timing out — the same idea as Raft’s PreVote.
A voter grants a vote only if it hasn’t voted in that term, the candidate’s config is current, and the candidate’s last applied optime is at least as new as the voter’s.
Priority takeover: a caught‑up secondary with higher priority than the primary calls an election to take over.
Catch‑up takeover: a secondary that is further ahead than a new primary can take over if the primary fails to catch up.
New primary catch‑up: before accepting writes, a newly elected primary may fetch entries it lacks from other members, reducing rollbacks.
Planned stepdown (replSetStepDown) waits for an electable secondary to catch up first, so planned maintenance doesn’t lose w:1 writes.
Secondaries fetch batches from a sync source, chosen by ping time and freshness; chaining through other secondaries is allowed unless disabled.
Batches are applied in parallel by writer threads, partitioned by document, so operations on the same document keep their order.
Readers on a secondary read from the last fully applied batch boundary (a storage snapshot), so they never see half a batch.
Flow control (since 4.2) throttles writes on the primary when majority‑committed lag grows past a target (about 10 s), protecting the cache and the oplog window.
Delayed members apply the oplog with a fixed lag (e.g. 1 hour) to give a recovery window from human error. They should be hidden and priority 0.
Safe reconfig (4.4+): change at most one voting member per reconfig and wait for the previous config to be committed by a majority. This prevents two disjoint majorities across configs.
Hidden members are invisible to drivers but replicate and can vote — handy for backups and analytics.
Drivers follow the Server Discovery and Monitoring spec: monitor each member with hello, track topology, and pick a server by read preference and a latency window (localThresholdMS, 15 ms default).
Retryable reads and writes retry once on a network error or ‘not primary’ error after re‑selecting a server.
Index builds replicate too: since 4.4 they run simultaneously on members and commit when a commit quorum of members is ready.

qs.e: Timestamp plus election term orders writes across elections.

qs.q: Why does an idle primary write periodic no‑op oplog entries?
o: So optimes, lag and the commit point keep advancing even without user writes
qs.e: Otherwise lag metrics and majority waits would stall.

qs.q: The majority commit point is…
o: The newest optime durably written on a majority of voting members
qs.e: Majority reads and writes are defined relative to it.

qs.q: What problem does the dry‑run (pre‑vote) election solve?
o: A partitioned node repeatedly bumping the term and disrupting a healthy primary when it rejoins
qs.e: Same purpose as Raft’s PreVote extension.

qs.q: A voter will NOT vote for a candidate whose…
o: Last applied optime is older than the voter’s
qs.e: The election restriction protects committed writes.

qs.q: What is a priority takeover?
o: A caught‑up secondary with higher priority triggers an election to become primary
qs.e: Lets you prefer a primary in a specific data center.

qs.q: Why does a newly elected primary run a catch‑up phase?
o: To fetch oplog entries it lacks from other members, reducing rollback
qs.e: Writes on other members that the new primary hasn’t seen would otherwise be rolled back.

qs.q: replSetStepDown waits for what before stepping down?
o: An electable secondary to catch up
qs.e: So planned stepdowns don’t lose recent w:1 writes.

qs.q: How are oplog entries applied in parallel without breaking correctness?
o: Entries are partitioned by document so each document’s ops stay in order
qs.e: Ordering only matters per document for idempotent logical ops.

qs.q: Why don’t readers on a secondary see half‑applied batches?
o: They read from a storage snapshot at the last fully applied batch boundary
qs.e: WiredTiger timestamps make this cheap.

qs.q: What does flow control limit?
o: The primary’s write rate when majority‑committed lag gets too large
qs.e: Protects cache pressure and the oplog window.

qs.q: Why configure a delayed member?
o: To recover from human errors like an accidental drop within the delay window
qs.e: DDIA ch. 1: design for human error. Make it hidden and priority 0.

qs.q: What does safe reconfig enforce?
o: Any number of changes at once
At most one voting member change per reconfig, after the previous config is majority‑committed
qs.e: Prevents two overlapping configs from each having an independent majority.

qs.q: Hidden members…
o: Replicate and can vote but are invisible to drivers
qs.e: Good for backups and analytics without serving app reads.

qs.q: How does a driver find the primary?
o: Monitors each member with hello per the SDAM spec and tracks topology
qs.e: Server selection then uses read preference.

qs.q: What does localThresholdMS control?
o: The latency window for picking among eligible servers (15 ms default)
qs.e: Servers within fastest + threshold are candidates.

qs.q: Retryable writes retry how many times by default?
qs.e: After re‑selecting a server, e.g. the new primary.

qs.q: Since 4.4, how do index builds replicate?
o: Primary first, then each secondary after
Simultaneously on members, committing when a commit quorum is ready
qs.e: Avoids secondaries lagging behind a long index build.

qs.q: writeConcernMajorityJournalDefault = true means…
o: Majority acknowledgement waits for journaled writes on the majority
qs.e: Durable on disk, not just in memory.

qs.q: A secondary’s sync source is usually chosen by…
o: Ping time and being sufficiently up to date
qs.e: Chaining can be disabled to force syncing from the primary.

qs.q: When does a primary step down on its own?
o: When it can’t see a majority of voting members for about the election timeout
qs.e: Limits the time a partitioned node acts as primary.

qs.q: Where does rolled‑back data go?
o: Written to rollback files for manual review
qs.e: Operators can inspect and reapply if needed.

qs.q: Since 4.0, rollback works by…
o: Recovering the storage engine to a stable (majority) timestamp, then resyncing from the sync source
qs.e: Recover‑to‑timestamp, built on WiredTiger timestamps.

qs.q: What does an election increment?
qs.e: Terms order leadership like epochs in DDIA ch. 9.

qs.q: Max voting members in a replica set?
qs.e: Up to 50 members, 7 voting.

qs.q: Why should delayed members be priority 0?
o: They must never become primary because their data is intentionally old
qs.e: Also hidden so apps don’t read stale data.

qs.q: What causes a secondary to enter RECOVERING or require resync after a long outage?
o: Its last optime fell off the sync source’s oplog window
qs.e: Size oplog (or minimum retention hours) for worst‑case outages.

qs.q: Majority reads on a secondary come from…
o: A snapshot at that node’s view of the commit point
qs.e: Durable but possibly behind the primary.

qs.q: Boss: after a network flap, a healthy primary keeps getting deposed by a node that was isolated. Which mechanism should prevent this, and what do you check?
o: Dry‑run elections; check versions/config and that the isolated node isn’t still calling real elections
qs.e: Pre‑vote stops disruptive term bumps.

qs.q: Boss: you want the primary in us‑east unless it fails, then us‑west. How?
o: Higher priority on us‑east members; priority takeover returns leadership after recovery
qs.e: Priorities shape elections.

qs.q: Boss: a teammate dropped a production collection. You have a 1‑hour delayed member. Plan?
o: Restore from it before its delay window passes, stopping it from applying the drop
qs.e: That’s exactly the delayed member’s purpose.

qs.q: Boss: replication lag spikes and primary latency rises during a bulk load. What’s happening?
o: Flow control throttling the primary because majority lag exceeded its target
qs.e: Spread the load or scale secondaries; check cache pressure.

qs.q: Boss: you must replace 2 of 3 voting members. Safe procedure?
o: Add/remove one voting member per reconfig, waiting for each to commit
qs.e: Safe reconfig rule.

qs.q: Boss: planned maintenance on the primary. How do you avoid losing w:1 writes?
o: Use replSetStepDown so an electable secondary catches up first
qs.e: Graceful stepdown.
