chapters.title: Deep dive: sharding internals
chapters.blurb: How sharded clusters really route, migrate, filter orphans, run sorted and aggregated queries, and change shard keys online.

b: The config server replica set stores which ranges each shard owns (the routing table) per sharded collection.
Each collection has a version (with an epoch/UUID that changes if the collection is dropped or resharded); each shard owns a shard version.
Routers attach the version they believe; a shard that knows a newer one returns a stale config error; the router refreshes from the config servers and retries.
Shards also cache their own filtering metadata and refresh when needed. This two‑sided versioning is what lets ranges move while queries run.
Donor shard clones documents in the range to the recipient while recording ongoing changes, which are then transferred.
A short critical section blocks writes to the range, the final changes are applied, and the config servers commit the new owner.
The donor deletes its old copy later in the background (range deletion). Until then those copies are orphans.
Queries with shard versioning include a SHARDING_FILTER stage that drops documents the shard doesn’t own, so orphans don’t appear in results.
Retryable‑write history and session data for the range migrate too, so retries after a migration still deduplicate correctly.
Targeted: the filter includes the shard key (equality or range), so mongos sends it only to owning shards.
Broadcast: no shard key in the filter, so every shard runs it.
Sorted queries: each shard sorts its results and mongos merge‑sorts the streams — like DDIA’s sort‑merge.
limit and skip: each shard returns up to skip + limit documents; mongos applies the final skip and limit, so deep pagination with skip is expensive.
Aggregation splits at the first stage that needs all data (like $group or $sort): the shard part runs in parallel, and a merging part runs on mongos or a chosen shard.
Unsharded collections in a database live on that database’s primary shard.
Shard key values in a document can be updated (since 4.2), as a retryable write or inside a transaction, because the document may move shards.
refineCollectionShardKey (4.4) adds suffix fields to an existing key — cheap, no data movement, fixes jumbo chunks.

reshardCollection (5.0) rewrites the collection to a new key online: it copies data, applies ongoing changes, then blocks writes for a short critical section (about 2 s by default) before switching. Needs spare disk and I/O.
Recent versions add moving an unsharded collection between shards and unsharding a collection.
Hashed sharding of an empty collection can pre‑create initial chunks spread over shards, avoiding the ‘one partition at start’ problem from DDIA.

qs.q: What changes a collection’s epoch/UUID in routing metadata?
o: Dropping and recreating or resharding the collection
qs.e: So routers can’t confuse an old collection’s ranges with a new one’s.

qs.q: Who returns a stale config error?
o: The shard, when the router’s version is older than the shard’s
qs.e: Then mongos refreshes and retries.

qs.q: What does the SHARDING_FILTER stage do?
o: Removes documents the shard doesn’t own (orphans) from results
qs.e: Seen in explain output on sharded queries.

qs.q: When are orphan documents deleted?
o: Later, by background range deletion on the donor
qs.e: Until then, the filter hides them.

qs.q: During the critical section of a migration…
o: Reads and writes are blocked cluster‑wide
Writes to that range are briefly blocked while the last changes move and ownership commits
qs.e: Kept short to limit impact.

qs.q: Why must retryable‑write history move with a range?
o: So a retry that lands on the new owner is still recognised as a duplicate
qs.e: Otherwise migrations could break exactly‑once retries.

qs.q: How does mongos handle a sorted scatter query?
o: Each shard sorts; mongos merge‑sorts the streams
qs.e: Sort‑merge pattern.

qs.q: Why is deep pagination with skip expensive on sharded clusters?
o: Each shard must return skip + limit documents for mongos to merge
qs.e: Use range‑based (keyset) pagination instead.

qs.q: Where does an aggregation pipeline split on a sharded collection?
o: At the first stage needing all data, like $group or $sort; shard part runs in parallel, merge part after
qs.e: Like map and reduce phases.

qs.q: Where do unsharded collections live?
qs.e: Can become a hot spot if many big unsharded collections share one primary shard.

qs.q: Since 4.2, updating a document’s shard key value requires…
o: A retryable write or transaction, since the document may move shards
qs.e: It’s a delete on one shard plus insert on another.

qs.q: What does refineCollectionShardKey do?
o: Adds suffix fields to the existing key without moving data
qs.e: Great for fixing jumbo chunks.

qs.q: Roughly how long is resharding’s final write‑blocking window by default?
qs.e: Copy and catch‑up happen online before it.

qs.q: What does resharding need?
o: Spare disk space and I/O to hold the new copy while catching up
qs.e: Plan capacity before running it.

qs.q: Why pre‑split chunks for a hashed key on an empty collection?
o: So inserts are spread from the start instead of hitting one partition
qs.e: DDIA’s dynamic partitioning cold‑start problem.

qs.q: An updateOne with no shard key on a sharded collection historically…
o: Required the shard key or _id in the filter (relaxed in newer versions)
qs.e: Newer versions allow it with extra coordination; targeting is still cheaper.

qs.q: Which metric reveals poor query targeting on a cluster?
o: Ratio of documents/keys scanned to returned, and broadcast query counts
qs.e: Atlas surfaces query targeting alerts.

qs.q: Which is a valid reason to choose a compound hashed shard key?
o: To get range queries on the hashed field
To spread a monotonic field while keeping a prefix for targeting or zones
qs.e: Compound hashed keys arrived in 4.4.

qs.q: Zones are most useful for…
o: Pinning ranges to shards in specific regions or hardware tiers
qs.e: Data residency and locality.

qs.q: The balancer runs on…
qs.e: Centralised decisions, distributed execution.

qs.q: What happens to a long‑running cursor on a shard when its range migrates away?
o: It keeps reading a consistent view; orphans are filtered by its metadata version
qs.e: Range deletion waits for queries that may still need the data.

qs.q: Why is $lookup into a sharded collection more expensive?
o: Each lookup may need to query several shards for matches
qs.e: Supported in newer versions, but plan for fan‑out.

qs.q: Why might a single huge unsharded collection hurt a sharded cluster?
o: All its load stays on one primary shard
qs.e: Move or shard it.

qs.q: What’s the main risk of a low‑cardinality shard key?
o: Ranges can’t split below one value, creating jumbo chunks and imbalance
qs.e: Cardinality caps how many partitions you can have.

qs.q: Key‑set pagination on a sharded collection means…
o: Filtering by the last seen sort key (e.g. _id > last) with a limit
qs.e: Each shard returns only limit docs.

qs.q: Why can broadcast writes be risky?
o: They touch every shard, raising latency and the chance of partial failure
qs.e: Use multi:true carefully; prefer targeted writes.

qs.q: Boss: a collection sharded on {customerId} has a jumbo chunk for one giant customer. Least disruptive fix?
o: Refine the key to {customerId, orderId} so the range can split
qs.e: No data movement needed to refine.

qs.q: Boss: product wants infinite scroll on a feed across 20 shards using skip. Page 500 is slow. Fix?
o: Key‑set pagination on an indexed sort key
qs.e: Avoid skip + limit fan‑out.

qs.q: Boss: EU regulations require EU customer data to stay in EU regions. Design?
o: Shard key prefixed with region, zones mapping EU ranges to EU shards
qs.e: Zone sharding / global clusters.

qs.q: Boss: you picked {createdAt: 1} as a ranged shard key last year; one shard takes all inserts. Plan?
o: Reshard online to a hashed or compound key, after checking disk headroom and query patterns
qs.e: Monotonic keys cause hot spots.

qs.q: Boss: explain shows SHARDING_FILTER removing many documents. What does that indicate?
o: Lots of orphans awaiting range deletion (e.g. after heavy migrations)
qs.e: Range deletion may be backlogged; usually transient.

qs.q: Boss: a $group pipeline on a sharded collection is slow at the merge step. Ideas?
o: $match early with the shard key, reduce data before $group, and check which node merges
qs.e: Filter and project early so shard‑side work shrinks the data.

terms: Config server map of ranges to shards
Ownership version checked on each request
Error prompting a router refresh and retry
Brief write block when committing a migration
Home of a database’s unsharded collections
Add suffix fields to a shard key
Online rewrite to a new shard key
Page by last seen key, not skip

drills.p: Walk through a range migration end to end, including what protects running queries.
a: Balancer picks donor, recipient and range
Donor records and transfers ongoing changes
Short critical section blocks writes to the range
Config servers commit new ownership and version bump
Routers get stale config and refresh
Donor deletes orphans later; SHARDING_FILTER hides them meanwhile

drills.p: Design the shard key for a multi‑tenant SaaS with one tenant at 60% of traffic.
a: Prefix with tenantId for targeting and isolation
Add a high‑cardinality suffix so big tenants split
Consider hashed suffix for monotonic IDs
Zones to place the whale tenant on dedicated shards

drills.p: Explain how a sorted, limited query runs on a 10‑shard cluster and how you’d make it cheaper.
a: Each shard sorts using an index and returns up to skip + limit
Cost grows with shard count and skip

drills.p: When would you NOT shard a collection?
a: Data and throughput fit one replica set with headroom
Vertical scaling and indexes not exhausted
Queries can’t include a good shard key

chapters.title: Deep dive: storage, indexes & query planning
chapters.blurb: WiredTiger timestamps and the history store, cache eviction, copy‑on‑write checkpoints, index builds, and how the query planner picks and caches plans.

b: Every storage transaction gets a commit timestamp matching its oplog timestamp. Storage history and the oplog share one timeline.
The stable timestamp tracks the majority commit point. Checkpoints only persist data up to it, so after a crash or rollback the node recovers to a majority‑consistent state, then replays the oplog.
Reads can ask for data ‘as of’ a timestamp: majority reads, snapshot reads at a cluster time, and consistent secondary batch reads all use this.
Older versions needed for those reads live first in cache and then in the on‑disk history store; how far back you can read is bounded (by default about 5 minutes for snapshot reads).
Pages in cache are in an in‑memory format; writing them to disk (reconciliation) converts them to the compressed on‑disk format.
Eviction threads start working at around 80% cache use (or ~5% dirty). Around 95% use (or ~20% dirty), application threads are forced to help — the classic latency cliff.
Checkpoints are copy‑on‑write: new versions of pages are written to new blocks and the root swaps atomically; old blocks are freed afterwards. Nothing is overwritten in place.
The journal is a write‑ahead log with group commit (around 100 ms by default; j:true forces an immediate flush). It covers changes since the last checkpoint.
Updates don’t modify documents in place on disk; large documents changed often cost CPU and I/O for reconciliation and cache pressure.
For a new query shape, the planner lists candidate plans (index scans, collection scan) and runs them in a short trial race; the first to produce enough results wins.
The winner is stored in the plan cache keyed by query shape. If its performance later degrades badly, it’s evicted and the planner re‑plans.
explain() modes: queryPlanner (chosen plan), executionStats (keys examined, docs examined, returned, time), allPlansExecution (trial results for rejected plans).
Blocking sorts without a supporting index are limited in memory (100 MB) and spill to disk when allowed.
Index hints force a plan; useful for diagnosis, risky long term.
A compound multikey index can include at most one array field per document (‘parallel arrays’ can’t be indexed).
Multikey indexes can’t cover queries on the array field itself, since an entry holds one element, not the array.
Partial indexes are only used when the query predicate guarantees a match with the index filter.
Collation must match for an index to support string comparisons and sorts.
The TTL monitor runs about every 60 s, so expired documents are removed with a delay; deletes go through the oplog like any write.
Index builds: modern builds take strong locks only briefly at the start and end, and replicated builds commit when a commit quorum is ready.

qs.q: What links WiredTiger’s storage history to the oplog?
o: Commit timestamps equal to oplog timestamps
qs.e: One shared timeline enables majority reads and rollback.

qs.q: The stable timestamp follows…
qs.e: Checkpoints persist only up to it.

qs.q: Why do checkpoints stop at the stable timestamp?
o: So recovery never restores data that might be rolled back
qs.e: After a crash, recover to stable then replay oplog.

qs.q: Where do older versions live when they don’t fit in cache?
qs.e: Lets long or point‑in‑time reads see old versions.

qs.q: Snapshot reads at a past cluster time are limited by…
o: The history window (about 5 minutes by default)
qs.e: Configurable, at a cost in cache and history store size.

qs.q: At roughly what cache usage are application threads forced to help evict?
qs.e: Eviction workers start around 80%; app threads join around 95% (or ~20% dirty).

qs.q: WiredTiger checkpoints are…
o: Copy‑on‑write: new blocks written, root swapped, old blocks freed
qs.e: Like LMDB’s approach in DDIA ch. 3.

qs.q: Default journal group commit interval?
qs.e: j:true flushes immediately for that write.

qs.q: What is reconciliation?
o: Converting in‑memory pages to the on‑disk format when writing them out
qs.e: Where compression happens.

qs.q: How does the planner choose among candidate plans?
o: A trial race; the first to return enough results wins
qs.e: Empirical rather than purely cost‑based.

qs.q: What’s the plan cache keyed by?
qs.e: Different values with the same shape reuse the plan.

qs.q: Which explain mode shows rejected plans’ trial stats?
qs.e: Useful when the planner picks a surprising index.

qs.q: A blocking in‑memory sort without an index is limited to…
qs.e: Add an index that supports the sort.

qs.q: Why can’t you index two array fields together in one compound index?
o: Entries would be the cross product of both arrays (‘parallel arrays’)
qs.e: MongoDB rejects inserts that would need it.

qs.q: Why can’t a multikey index cover a query on the array field?
o: Each entry holds a single element, not the whole array
qs.e: The document must be fetched.

qs.q: When is a partial index used?
o: Only when the query predicate guarantees matching the index’s filter expression
qs.e: Otherwise results could be incomplete.

qs.q: How quickly does a TTL index remove expired docs?
o: With delay; the TTL monitor runs about every 60 s
qs.e: Deletes replicate through the oplog.

qs.q: Why can a frequently updated large document be costly?
o: Each change rewrites in‑memory structures and later reconciles whole pages, increasing CPU, cache and oplog churn
qs.e: Keep hot fields in small documents.

qs.q: keysExamined 50,000, docsExamined 50,000, nReturned 20. What’s likely wrong?
o: The index isn’t selective for this filter; consider a better compound index
qs.e: Aim for keys ≈ returned.

qs.q: What does a FETCH stage after IXSCAN mean?
o: The documents must be loaded to filter or return fields
qs.e: A covered query avoids FETCH.

qs.q: Collation mismatch between query and index causes…
o: The index can’t be used for string comparisons/sorts
qs.e: Specify consistent collation.

qs.q: What’s a risk of index hints in application code?
o: The data distribution changes and the forced plan becomes slow
qs.e: Better to fix indexes or query shape.

qs.q: Time series collections store measurements…
o: In buckets by metadata and time, with columnar compression inside buckets
qs.e: Bucket pattern plus column storage ideas.

qs.q: Why might snappy vs zstd matter?
o: Zstd compresses better at more CPU cost — DDIA’s space vs CPU trade‑off
qs.e: Choose by storage cost vs CPU budget.

qs.q: Why does read‑heavy workload favour WiredTiger’s B‑tree over an LSM?
o: Point and range reads hit one location with predictable latency, no multi‑level merge on read
qs.e: LSMs win on write throughput.

qs.q: An index build on a busy primary in 4.4+…
o: Takes brief exclusive locks only at start and end and commits across members with a commit quorum
qs.e: Still uses I/O and cache; schedule carefully.

qs.q: Boss: p99 jumps every few minutes with ‘app threads evicting’ in metrics. Fix ideas?
o: Reduce cache pressure: bigger cache/RAM, fewer/smaller indexes, shorter transactions, smoother write bursts
qs.e: Classic eviction cliff.

qs.q: Boss: a query got 50× slower after a data change though no index changed. Likely cause?
o: A cached plan that’s now bad for the new data distribution; check allPlansExecution and plan cache
qs.e: Re‑planning, better indexes, or clearing the cached plan.

qs.q: Boss: design an index for find({status:"open", region:"EU", createdAt:{$gte:t}}).sort({priority:-1}).
qs.e: ESR: equality fields, then sort, then range.

qs.q: Boss: long analytics snapshot reads fail with ‘snapshot too old’. Options?
o: Shorten queries, run them on analytics nodes, or raise the history window knowing the cache cost
qs.e: History is bounded to protect cache.

qs.q: Boss: an IoT collection’s disk keeps growing despite deleting old data with a job. Better approach?
o: TTL index or time series expireAfterSeconds, with bucketed storage
qs.e: And consider compact for reclaiming space.

qs.q: Boss: interviewer asks ‘is WiredTiger a WAL + in‑place B‑tree like Postgres?’ Best answer?
o: Partly: it has a WAL (journal) but checkpoints are copy‑on‑write, and history is tied to oplog timestamps
qs.e: Shows you know the internals.

terms: Majority point that checkpoints persist up to
On‑disk older versions for snapshot reads
Writing in‑memory pages in disk format
Removing pages from cache to make room
New blocks written, root swapped atomically
Winning plans saved per query shape
Two array fields in one compound index
Structure of a query without literal values

drills.p: Explain how MongoDB recovers after an unclean shutdown.
a: Checkpoint holds data up to the stable (majority) timestamp
Replay oplog from stable point to rebuild later writes
Rejoin set and sync any missing entries

drills.p: Walk through the query planner for a new query shape and how you’d debug a bad plan.
a: Fix with better compound index (ESR) rather than hints

drills.p: Why does WiredTiger performance fall off a cliff when cache fills, and how do you prevent it?
a: App threads forced to evict at high usage/dirty thresholds
Mitigate: right‑size RAM, fewer/smaller indexes, avoid long transactions, smooth bursts, monitor dirty ratio

drills.p: Design indexes for a ‘my open tickets sorted by priority, last 30 days’ screen and justify each field order.
a: Consider partial index on status open

chapters.title: Deep dive: transactions, consistency & drivers
chapters.blurb: Prepared transactions, cluster‑time snapshots across shards, retryable‑write bookkeeping, lock timeouts, and the exact guarantees each client setting buys.

b: A transaction lives in a logical session (lsid) with a transaction number. Writes are buffered in a storage transaction and become visible together at commit.
Reads use a snapshot. On a sharded cluster, the router picks one cluster time so every shard reads at the same point — a consistent global snapshot built on shared timestamps.
Write conflicts abort the transaction immediately (TransientTransactionError) rather than waiting, so apps must retry.
Transactions take intent locks. If a lock isn’t available quickly (default 5 ms) the transaction aborts rather than queuing behind DDL.
Default lifetime: 60 s. The commit is written to the oplog (large transactions span several entries).
If only one shard was written, commit is a single‑shard commit — no 2PC needed.
With several write shards, a coordinator (one participant shard) sends prepare to all. Each writes a prepare oplog entry and votes with a prepare timestamp.
The commit timestamp is the max prepare timestamp. The decision is made durable in the coordinator’s replica set, then commit goes to all participants.
Read‑only participants can skip the second phase.
While a document is prepared, readers that need it wait (a prepare conflict) — the in‑doubt window from DDIA, kept short.
Each retryable write carries lsid + txnNumber. The server records executed statements in a session table (config.transactions) alongside the oplog.
If the same lsid + txnNumber arrives again, the server returns the original result instead of re‑executing.
This survives failover because the session record replicates, and survives migrations because it moves with the range.
Only single‑document operations (and bulk writes made of them) are retryable; multi:true updates are not.
Retryable reads also retry once on transient errors.
Durable: w:majority (journaled by default). Not rolled back: w:majority. Fast but risky: w:1.
Never see rolled‑back data: readConcern majority. See the latest committed: read from primary with majority, or linearizable for single docs.
Read your own writes: causally consistent session plus majority concerns (or read from primary).
Consistent multi‑document view: transaction with snapshot read concern, or a snapshot read outside a transaction at a cluster time.
Exactly‑once effect of a retried write: retryable writes for single docs; idempotency keys for business operations.

qs.q: What identifies a transaction?
o: Logical session ID (lsid) plus transaction number
qs.e: Also used by retryable writes.

qs.q: How does a sharded transaction get a consistent snapshot across shards?
o: The router picks one cluster time and all shards read at that timestamp
qs.e: Possible because storage and oplog share cluster‑time timestamps.

qs.q: What happens when a transaction hits a write conflict?
qs.e: The client retries the whole transaction.

qs.q: Default maximum wait for a transaction to acquire a lock?
qs.e: Avoids transactions queuing behind DDL and stalling.

qs.q: When does a multi‑shard transaction NOT use 2PC?
o: When only one shard was written (single‑shard commit)
qs.e: An important optimisation.

qs.q: How is the commit timestamp chosen in 2PC?
o: The maximum of the participants’ prepare timestamps
qs.e: Ensures commit is after every prepare.

qs.q: What is a prepare conflict?
o: A read waits because the document it needs is in a prepared, undecided transaction
qs.e: The in‑doubt window, kept brief.

qs.q: Why doesn’t a coordinator crash block participants forever?
o: The commit decision is stored durably in the coordinator shard’s replica set, so a new primary finishes it
qs.e: 2PC on top of consensus.

qs.q: Where are executed retryable‑write statements recorded?
qs.e: So retries after failover return the original result.

qs.q: Which operation is NOT retryable?
qs.e: Multi‑document updates can’t be safely deduplicated this way.

qs.q: Why does retryable‑write history move with chunk migrations?
o: A retry routed to the new owner must still be recognised as already executed
qs.e: Exactly‑once across topology changes.

qs.q: Large transactions (>16 MB of oplog data) are…
o: Written as multiple oplog entries since 4.2
qs.e: Still costly — keep them small.

qs.q: Why can long‑running transactions hurt the whole node?
o: They pin old versions in cache, raising eviction pressure for everyone
qs.e: Hence the 60 s default limit.

qs.q: Snapshot reads outside a transaction let you…
o: Read a consistent view at a chosen cluster time across multiple queries
qs.e: Bounded by the history window.

qs.q: Which combination gives read‑your‑writes on secondaries?
o: Causally consistent session + majority write and read concerns
qs.e: The secondary waits until it reaches the session’s time.

qs.q: Which setting guarantees you’ll never read data that later disappears?
qs.e: Majority‑committed data can’t be rolled back.

qs.q: Why is $clusterTime signed?
o: So clients can’t push the cluster clock forward maliciously
qs.e: Signed with keys stored on the cluster.

qs.q: What should client code do with a network error during commitTransaction?
o: Assume failure and redo the whole txn
Retry commitTransaction (it’s retryable), since the commit may already have happened
qs.e: Handled by withTransaction().

qs.q: Why put an idempotency key in the business document even with retryable writes?
o: Retryable writes only cover the driver’s single retry; user double‑clicks and app restarts need end‑to‑end IDs
qs.e: DDIA’s end‑to‑end argument.

qs.q: Two transactions both decrement the same stock document. What happens?
o: One gets a write conflict and must retry
qs.e: Same‑document conflicts are detected.

qs.q: Can a transaction span a primary election?
o: No — it aborts, and the client retries
qs.e: Transaction state isn’t carried over mid‑flight.

qs.q: What’s the cheapest correct way to decrement stock only if available?
o: A single updateOne with filter {stock: {$gte: 1}} and $inc: -1
qs.e: Single‑document atomic conditional update.

qs.q: Boss: a transfer transaction across two shards stalls readers of one account for seconds. Why?
o: Readers hit prepare conflicts while the 2PC decision is pending (slow participant or coordinator)
qs.e: Keep transactions tiny; investigate slow participants.

qs.q: Boss: you need a nightly report that’s consistent across 6 collections without blocking writes. Approach?
o: Snapshot reads at one cluster time (or a read‑only transaction), on an analytics node if possible
qs.e: Mind the history window; keep it short or chunk it.

qs.q: Boss: users are occasionally charged twice even with retryable writes on. Why?
o: Retries originate above the driver (user re‑click, app restart), so a new lsid/txnNumber is used; add an idempotency key with a unique index
qs.e: End‑to‑end deduplication.

qs.q: Boss: transactions abort with lock timeouts during an index build. What’s going on?
o: DDL holds locks briefly; transactions give up after ~5 ms rather than wait
qs.e: Schedule DDL off‑peak or retry transactions.

qs.q: Boss: interviewer asks ‘are MongoDB transactions serializable?’ Best answer?
o: No, snapshot isolation; write skew is possible, and here’s how to prevent it in this schema
qs.e: Precise and practical.

terms: Logical session ID for retries and transactions
Read waiting on an undecided prepared doc
Skip 2PC when one shard was written
Read at a chosen cluster time
Label meaning retry the whole transaction

drills.p: Walk through a two‑shard transaction from startTransaction to commit, including failure cases.
a: Prepare on participants with prepare timestamps
Decision durable in coordinator replica set
Coordinator failover resumes from durable state
Client retries commit on unknown result

drills.p: Explain how retryable writes guarantee a single effect across a failover.
a: Driver tags write with lsid + txnNumber
Server records result in session table
New primary sees duplicate on retry

drills.p: A product manager asks for ‘strong consistency everywhere’. How do you respond?
a: Majority/primary reads or causal sessions for freshness

drills.p: Show how write skew can happen in a MongoDB booking system and fix it.
a: Two txns read ‘room free’ from snapshot
Or both update a shared room‑slot doc to force conflict

chapters.title: Deep dive: data modelling & design drills
chapters.blurb: Interview‑style design problems on MongoDB: modelling choices, failure handling, and the numbers to sanity‑check a design.

b: Max document size 16 MB; aim far below for hot documents.
Default chunk target ~128 MB in recent versions; a shard key value can’t split below one value.
Up to 50 replica set members, 7 voting; heartbeats 2 s; election timeout 10 s.
Transaction lifetime 60 s; lock acquisition wait 5 ms; snapshot history ~5 minutes by default.
WiredTiger cache ~50% of (RAM − 1 GB); checkpoints ~60 s; journal group commit ~100 ms.
Treat these as approximate and verify against current docs (MongoDB 9.0 shipped September 2026).
Clarify: users, read/write rates, data size and growth, latency targets (p99), consistency needs, regions.
Model: list access patterns first, then embed/reference decisions and patterns (bucket, subset, extended reference, computed).
Index: one index per major query, ESR ordering, check covered queries and write cost.
Scale: when one replica set stops fitting, choose a shard key from the access patterns.
Consistency: choose write concern, read concern, read preference and sessions per operation, not globally.
Failure: idempotency keys, retries, rollback exposure, oplog window, change stream recovery.
Operate: metrics to watch (p99, replication lag, cache dirty %, query targeting, oplog window) and how you’d roll out changes.
Comments on a post: embed recent N (subset) plus a comments collection keyed by postId.
User profile with addresses: embed (bounded, read together).
Products and orders: reference products, but copy name and price into the order line (extended reference + historical accuracy).
Followers: separate edge collection {follower, followee} with indexes both ways; don’t embed unbounded arrays.
Counters: $inc on a small document; shard or bucket counters that get very hot.
Events/metrics: time series collections or bucket pattern; TTL for retention.

qs.q: Why copy product name and price into an order line?
o: Orders must reflect the price at purchase time, and it avoids a join on read
qs.e: Extended reference doubles as historical record.

qs.q: Best model for a user’s followers (could be millions)?
o: Separate edge collection with indexes on follower and followee
qs.e: Unbounded arrays break the 16 MB limit and update cost.

qs.q: Comments on blog posts, usually showing the latest 10. Model?
o: Embed latest 10 (subset) and store all in a comments collection
qs.e: Fast common read, bounded document.

qs.q: A global ‘likes’ counter on a viral post is a hot document. Fix?
o: Split into N counter shards and sum on read (or periodic aggregation)
qs.e: DDIA’s hot‑key splitting.

qs.q: Which data should be embedded?
o: Bounded data read together with its parent
qs.e: Locality wins when bounded and co‑read.

qs.q: An app’s main query is ‘orders by customer, newest first’. First index?
qs.e: Equality then sort.

qs.q: Why model access patterns before schema in MongoDB?
o: Document design and indexes are optimised for the reads you’ll actually do
qs.e: No query optimizer can fix a poor document shape.

qs.q: A ‘last 30 days only’ retention requirement suggests…
o: TTL index or time series expireAfterSeconds
qs.e: Automatic expiry via the oplog.

qs.q: Where should an idempotency key live for order creation?
o: In the order document with a unique index
qs.e: The database rejects duplicates end to end.

qs.q: Feeding Elasticsearch/Kafka from MongoDB safely uses…
o: Change streams with persisted resume tokens
qs.e: CDC from the system of record.

qs.q: When is a separate collection better than embedding for one‑to‑many?
o: When the ‘many’ side is unbounded or queried independently
qs.e: E.g. log lines, order history over years.

qs.q: Which metric best shows poor shard key choice in production?
o: Uneven data/ops per shard and high broadcast (scatter) query ratio
qs.e: Imbalance and targeting.

qs.q: Which read preference for an analytics dashboard that tolerates minutes of lag?
qs.e: Protect the primary’s OLTP workload.

qs.q: Why prefer $set updates over full replacements in a multi‑version app fleet?
o: Older app versions won’t drop fields they don’t know
qs.e: Forward compatibility in practice.

qs.q: How would you keep a ‘total orders per customer’ figure cheap to read?
o: Computed pattern: $inc a counter on order insert (or $merge periodically)
qs.e: Move work to the write path.

qs.q: A chat app has channels with up to 10M messages. Message storage?
o: Messages collection (or buckets per channel per hour) indexed by channel and time
One doc per day for all channels
qs.e: Bounded documents, efficient range reads.

qs.q: Boss: design an order service handling 5k orders/s at peak with no double orders. Core choices?
o: Idempotency key unique index, retryable writes, w:majority, transactions only for true multi‑doc invariants, outbox via change streams
qs.e: Correctness first, then scale.

qs.q: Boss: design a leaderboard updated 50k times/s. Approach?
o: Partitioned score documents with $inc, periodic $merge/aggregation into a top‑N view
qs.e: Avoid a single hot document; precompute reads.

qs.q: Boss: design a notification inbox with read/unread state for 100M users.
o: Notifications collection sharded by userId (+ time), index {userId, read, createdAt}, TTL old ones
qs.e: Targeted queries per user; retention.

qs.q: Boss: interviewer pushes ‘why not Postgres for this?’ Strong answer?
o: Name the access pattern and model fit (document locality, flexible schema, built‑in sharding) and when Postgres would win (heavy relational joins, complex multi‑entity transactions)
qs.e: Balanced trade‑off reasoning scores highest.

qs.q: Boss: a multi‑region app must keep working if one region fails, with zero data loss. Setup?
o: Replica set members across three regions, w:majority, priorities for preferred region, tested failover
qs.e: Majority must survive any single region.

qs.q: Boss: product search must reflect DB changes within seconds and survive crashes. Design?
o: Change stream consumer with resume tokens persisted after indexing; rebuild path from snapshot if token expires
qs.e: CDC with recovery plan.
